questions.technical: Latency is time per request, split for LLMs into time to first token and time per output token. Throughput is total tokens or requests per second across all users. Batching more requests raises hardware utilization and throughput and lowers cost per token, but each request waits longer and decode steps slow down. Continuous batching, adding and removing sequences at every step instead of waiting for a full batch, recovers much of that latency. Other levers: model size and quantization, speculative decoding, prompt caching, shorter prompts and outputs, routing easy requests to smaller models, and batch APIs for non-interactive work. Set the latency target first, such as p95 time to first token, then minimize cost per token within it.

probes.q: What is speculative decoding?
probes.a: A small draft model proposes several tokens and the large model verifies them in one pass, keeping the large model's output distribution while generating faster.

probes.q: How would you cut a customer's LLM bill?
probes.a: Measure token use per feature, trim prompts, cache repeated prefixes, route simple requests to a smaller model, move offline jobs to batch inference, and consider dedicated capacity at steady high volume.

questions.aws: Amazon Bedrock offers on-demand inference, batch inference for offline jobs, Provisioned Throughput for steady volume, prompt caching, and Intelligent Prompt Routing between models; SageMaker AI adds real-time, serverless, asynchronous, and batch options.
questions.trap: Optimizing average latency. Users feel the tail, so set targets on p95 or p99, and track time to first token separately from total time.

questions.q: What are quantization and distillation, and how do they cut inference cost?
questions.plain: Quantization is saving a photo at lower quality: the file gets much smaller and usually looks almost the same. Distillation is a master teaching an apprentice: the apprentice is smaller and faster and learns to do one job nearly as well. Both make AI cheaper to run; quantization shrinks the same model, distillation trains a new, smaller one.
questions.technical: Quantization stores weights, and sometimes activations or the KV cache, in fewer bits: FP16 or BF16 uses 2 bytes per parameter, INT8 one byte, INT4 half a byte, so a 7B model's weights fall from about 14 GB to about 3.5 GB at 4 bits. Post-training methods such as GPTQ, AWQ, and NF4 (from QLoRA) keep quality loss small, but loss grows at very low bit widths and varies by task, so evaluate on your own data. Speed gains depend on hardware and kernel support. Distillation trains a small student model on a large teacher's outputs so the student approaches teacher quality on a target task at a fraction of the cost. Pruning removes low-importance weights. These stack: distill, then quantize.

probes.q: When is quantization a bad idea?
probes.a: When the task is sensitive to small accuracy losses and you have not evaluated it, or when the hardware lacks fast kernels for the format, so you lose quality without gaining speed.

probes.q: What is the catch with distillation?
probes.a: The student is good on the kind of data it was trained on and can be much worse outside it, and it inherits the teacher's mistakes.

questions.aws: Amazon Bedrock Model Distillation uses a teacher model to generate responses and fine-tunes a smaller student model for your use case; AWS Inferentia2 supports FP16, BF16, and INT8 among its data types for cheaper inference.
questions.resume: In ModelScope, I compared Llama-3.2-3B and Gemma-2-2B across 8 quantization configs (FP16, INT8, INT4, NF4) on a T4 GPU. INT4 came in at 2299 MB, 62% below FP16, at 13.7 tok/s, with MMLU within a point of baseline.
questions.trap: Assuming lower precision is always faster. It is always smaller, but speed depends on whether the hardware and kernels are optimized for that format.

questions.q: In your benchmark, INT8 lost to INT4 on both memory and speed. Why can a format with more bits be slower, and what would you tell a customer?
questions.plain: Smaller is not automatically faster. Think of a shipping box that is lighter but needs a special tool to open: if the warehouse has no fast tool for that box, unpacking takes longer than the weight saved. Speed depends on whether the hardware and software have a fast path for that exact format.
questions.technical: Quantized inference speed depends on the kernel path, not just bit width. Weight-only formats are usually dequantized on the fly inside matrix-multiply kernels; well-optimized INT4 kernels move a quarter of FP16's bytes and win when decode is memory-bound. Some popular INT8 paths, such as the LLM.int8() method in bitsandbytes, route outlier features through a separate FP16 computation (mixed-precision decomposition), which protects accuracy but adds overhead and can make INT8 slower than expected at small batch sizes. Results also shift with GPU generation, batch size, sequence length, and library version. So the advice is not 'INT8 is slow' but 'benchmark candidate formats on the target hardware and serving stack, measuring memory, tokens per second, and task accuracy together'.

probes.q: So is INT8 generally a poor choice?
probes.a: No. With hardware-native INT8 kernels, for example engines that quantize both weights and activations, INT8 can be fast and accurate. My result is specific to my library, GPU, and batch settings.

probes.q: What would you measure before recommending a format?
probes.a: Peak memory, time to first token, tokens per second at the expected batch size, and accuracy on the customer's own tasks, all on the actual target hardware.

probes.q: Why did INT4 keep quality?
probes.a: Formats like NF4 place quantization levels to match the bell-shaped distribution of weights and scale small blocks separately, which preserves most information. Quality still varies by task, so it must be evaluated.

questions.resume: In ModelScope, I ran 8 quantization configs on a T4 GPU. INT4 used 2299 MB, 62% below FP16, at 13.7 tok/s with MMLU within a point of baseline, while INT8 was strictly dominated: 53% more memory than INT4 and 2.1x lower throughput. I present that as a finding about my setup, not a rule about INT8.
questions.trap: Turning one benchmark into a rule such as 'INT8 is always slower'. Performance is a property of model, format, kernel, hardware, and batch size together.

questions.q: What is a graph neural network, and why use one for fraud detection?
questions.plain: Fraudsters rarely act alone; they reuse cards, devices, and addresses. A regular model looks at each transaction like a single photo. A graph neural network looks at the whole web of connections, like a detective's board with strings between suspects, so a transaction tied to known bad accounts looks suspicious even when it seems normal on its own.
questions.technical: A graph has nodes (transactions, cards, devices, emails) and edges (relationships). A GNN learns node representations by message passing: at each layer, a node aggregates transformed features from its neighbors and combines them with its own, so after k layers it reflects its k-hop neighborhood. Heterogeneous graphs have several node and edge types; relational GNNs such as R-GCN learn separate weights per relation type. Full-graph training does not fit in memory at scale, so neighbor sampling (GraphSAGE-style) trains on sampled subgraphs in mini-batches. Fraud is rare, so pair it with class-weighted or focal loss and evaluate with ROC-AUC and PR-AUC. Hard parts: building the graph at inference time, neighborhood lookup latency, and new nodes with no history.

probes.q: Why not just add 'number of shared devices' as a feature to XGBoost?
probes.a: You should try that first, and it captures part of the signal. A GNN learns multi-hop patterns and combinations of relationships that are hard to hand-engineer.

probes.q: What is neighbor sampling?
probes.a: Instead of using every neighbor of every node, sample a fixed number per layer for each mini-batch, which bounds memory and compute on large graphs.

probes.q: How would you serve it in real time?
probes.a: Keep the graph in a graph database, fetch a sampled neighborhood for each new transaction, and score it, caching embeddings for stable entities to meet latency targets.

questions.aws: Amazon Neptune stores and queries graphs, and Amazon Neptune ML trains graph neural networks on Neptune data using the Deep Graph Library with Amazon SageMaker AI.
questions.resume: I built a GNN fraud model on the heterogeneous IEEE-CIS fraud graph, 726K nodes and 19.5M edges, using a HeteroRGCN with neighbor sampling and focal loss for the 3.5% fraud rate. It reached 0.923 ROC-AUC, +0.03 over a tuned XGBoost.
questions.trap: Claiming a GNN always beats tabular models. The gain depends on whether relationships carry signal; tuned gradient boosting is the baseline to beat, and the GNN adds real serving complexity.

questions.q: How do you take a model from notebook to production and roll out a new version safely?
questions.plain: Treat a model like a new medicine: it gets a batch number, passes trials, gets signed off, and goes to a small group before everyone. A model registry is the pharmacy's record of every version and who approved it, and an A/B test is the trial that proves the new one is actually better.
questions.technical: MLOps applies CI/CD discipline to models. Version the code, data snapshot, and hyperparameters for reproducibility; automate training and evaluation in a pipeline; register each candidate in a model registry with metrics, lineage, and an approval status; deploy approved versions through infrastructure as code. Roll out progressively: a shadow deployment scores live traffic without its answers being used; a canary sends a small share of traffic; an A/B test compares business metrics with statistical significance, with automatic rollback if guardrail metrics degrade. Keep the previous version ready for instant rollback, and log inputs and predictions for monitoring and future training.

probes.q: Shadow test versus A/B test?
probes.a: A shadow test sends copies of real traffic to the new model without affecting users, which safely checks errors and latency. An A/B test lets some users get the new model's answers, which measures real business impact.

probes.q: What goes into a model registry entry?
probes.a: The model artifact and version, references to training data and code, evaluation metrics, approval status, and who approved it, so any production prediction can be traced back.

questions.aws: Amazon SageMaker AI provides Pipelines for automated workflows, Model Registry with model groups, versions, approval status, and lineage, and endpoints that split traffic across production variants and support shadow testing.
questions.resume: At Oracle, I built a CLI toolchain on Jenkins CI/CD with scripted pre-deployment validation, adopted by 4 teams, which shortened release cycles 34% and cut failed deploys from 11% to 4%. I apply the same gated-release thinking to promoting models.
questions.trap: Declaring success from offline metrics alone. Offline gains often shrink in production; only a controlled online test shows business impact.

questions.q: What is model drift, and how do you monitor and retrain for it?
questions.plain: A model is a snapshot of the world on the day it was trained, and the world keeps moving. A fraud model trained before a new scam appears is like a map printed before a new highway opened: still useful, but increasingly wrong. Monitoring tells you when the map is out of date; retraining prints a new one.
questions.technical: Data drift: input distributions shift, for example a new product line or customer mix. Concept drift: the relationship between inputs and outcome changes, for example fraudsters switching tactics, so the same inputs now mean something different. Detect data drift by comparing live feature distributions with the training baseline using PSI, KS tests, or distance measures. Detect performance decay with quality metrics once ground truth arrives, which can take weeks for fraud chargebacks, so watch proxies meanwhile: score distributions, alert rates, override rates. Retrain on a schedule, on drift triggers, or both, and send every retrained model through the same evaluation gates and staged rollout. For LLM apps, monitor sampled quality, refusals, and user feedback.

probes.q: What if labels arrive months later?
probes.a: Use input drift and prediction distributions as early warnings, track proxy business metrics, and join predictions with labels by ID when they arrive to compute true performance.

probes.q: Is retraining on a fixed schedule enough?
probes.a: It is a sensible baseline, but drift triggers catch sudden shifts sooner. Always compare the new model against the current one before switching.

questions.aws: Amazon SageMaker Model Monitor is no longer open to new customers; AWS now points to open-source SageMaker AI monitoring solutions built on SageMaker AI MLflow and Evidently AI, with Amazon CloudWatch for endpoint metrics and alarms. Retraining can be triggered with Amazon EventBridge and SageMaker AI Pipelines.
questions.resume: At Oracle, I moved alerting across 37,000+ enterprise tenants from static thresholds to SLOs on CPU, memory, and p99 latency, which cut false-positive pages 41%. I would bring the same idea to model monitoring: alert on meaningful drift against a baseline, not on every wiggle.
questions.trap: Confusing data drift with concept drift. Inputs can look unchanged while their meaning shifts, so input monitoring alone misses concept drift; you need outcome labels too.

questions.q: What is Amazon Bedrock, in one minute?
questions.plain: Amazon Bedrock is like renting a fully staffed professional kitchen instead of building your own restaurant. You pick from leading AI models through one service, pay for what you use, and get ready-made tools for safety, connecting your documents, and testing quality, without buying or managing any GPUs.
questions.technical: Amazon Bedrock is a fully managed service offering foundation models from Amazon (such as Amazon Nova) and providers such as Anthropic, Meta, Mistral AI, and Cohere through one API, including the model-agnostic Converse API. It is serverless: pay per token on demand, or use batch inference and Provisioned Throughput. Building blocks: Knowledge Bases for managed RAG, Guardrails for safety policies, evaluations including LLM-as-a-judge, model customization and distillation, Custom Model Import, prompt caching, and Intelligent Prompt Routing. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore adds agent runtime, gateway, memory, identity, and observability. Prompts and responses are not used to train the base models, and access integrates with IAM, VPC endpoints, AWS KMS encryption, and CloudTrail.

probes.q: How does Bedrock keep customer data private?
probes.a: Prompts and responses are not used to train the base models or shared with model providers, traffic can stay on private paths through VPC endpoints, and IAM controls who can call which model.

probes.q: Why offer many models instead of one?
probes.a: Tasks need different tradeoffs of quality, speed, and cost. Choice lets a customer use a small fast model for simple work and a frontier model where it pays off, and switch as models improve.

questions.aws: Pair Bedrock with Knowledge Bases for RAG, Guardrails for safety, evaluations for quality gates, and AgentCore when the solution needs agents in production.
questions.trap: Describing Bedrock as a single Amazon model. It is a platform for many providers' models plus the tooling around them; Amazon Nova is one model family among several.

questions.q: When would you recommend Amazon Bedrock versus Amazon SageMaker AI versus a task-specific AI service like Amazon Textract?
questions.plain: It is buy, assemble, or build. A task-specific service is buying a finished appliance: Textract already reads invoices, so just plug it in. Bedrock is assembling from premium parts: top AI models you combine with your own data. SageMaker AI is a full workshop for building your own model when nothing off the shelf fits.
questions.technical: Start with the highest-level service that meets the requirement. Task-specific AI services (Textract for documents, Rekognition for images and video, Comprehend for text analytics, plus Transcribe, Translate, and Polly) need no ML expertise, are priced per use, and fit well-defined tasks. Amazon Bedrock fits generative AI, such as chat, summarization, RAG, agents, and content generation, with serverless model access and managed guardrails, knowledge bases, and evaluation. Amazon SageMaker AI fits when the customer needs full control: custom models trained on proprietary data (fraud, forecasting, recommendations), open-weight models on chosen instances, custom containers, or end-to-end MLOps for a data science team. They combine well: Textract extracts invoice fields, Bedrock summarizes exceptions, SageMaker AI hosts a custom risk model.

probes.q: A customer wants to host an open-weight model they fine-tuned. Which service?
probes.a: Bedrock Custom Model Import if the architecture is supported and they want serverless operation; SageMaker AI if they need specific instances, custom serving code, or full control over scaling.

probes.q: Which questions decide it?
probes.a: Is it generative or predictive? Does a managed service already do this task? How much ML skill does the team have? What are the data, latency, cost, and control requirements?

probes.q: Where do assistants like Amazon Q fit?
probes.a: Above all three. Amazon Q Developer is a finished product for end users, not a building block for a custom application.

questions.aws: This mirrors how AWS layers its AI stack: AI services on top, Amazon Bedrock and Bedrock AgentCore for generative AI and agents in the middle, and Amazon SageMaker AI plus Trainium, Inferentia, and GPU instances underneath.
questions.trap: Jumping to SageMaker AI to train a custom model when a managed API already solves the task. Building is slower and costlier to operate; justify it with a requirement the higher-level services cannot meet.

questions.q: What does Amazon SageMaker AI give a data science team, and which inference option would you pick?
questions.plain: SageMaker AI is a fully equipped workshop for building your own AI: workbenches for experiments, machines you rent only while training, a catalog of every model version, and a service counter that serves predictions to your apps. You choose the serving style to match the traffic, like choosing between a 24-hour store, a pop-up shop, or overnight delivery.
questions.technical: Amazon SageMaker AI covers the ML lifecycle: SageMaker Studio and JupyterLab for development, managed training jobs including distributed and Spot training, JumpStart for pretrained and foundation models, Pipelines for automation, Model Registry, managed MLflow for experiment tracking, and deployment. Inference options: real-time endpoints for steady, low-latency traffic; Serverless Inference for intermittent or spiky traffic that tolerates cold starts; Asynchronous Inference, which queues requests and suits large payloads (up to 1 GB) or long processing (up to one hour); and Batch Transform for offline scoring of whole datasets. Autoscaling, multi-model endpoints, and inference components let models share instances to cut cost.

probes.q: A customer scores 50 million records every night. Which option?
probes.a: Batch Transform or a batch job, since no user is waiting. Compute runs only during the job instead of keeping an endpoint up all day.

probes.q: Traffic is a few requests an hour with occasional bursts?
probes.a: Serverless Inference, accepting cold starts, or Asynchronous Inference if callers can receive results later.

questions.aws: SageMaker Neo can compile models for targets such as AWS Inferentia, and SageMaker AI Model Registry plus Pipelines provide the governance path from experiment to production.
questions.trap: Using the old name or treating it as only a notebook service. It is Amazon SageMaker AI (renamed in December 2024), and its value is the managed lifecycle from training through deployment and governance.

questions.q: What are AWS Inferentia and AWS Trainium, and when would you recommend them?
questions.plain: Inferentia and Trainium are chips Amazon designed specifically for AI, the way a delivery company might build its own vans instead of buying general-purpose trucks. Trainium is built for teaching models, Inferentia for running them for customers. For the right workloads, they can lower cost compared with general-purpose GPUs.
questions.technical: AWS Trainium is a purpose-built accelerator for training (EC2 Trn1 and Trn2 instances); AWS Inferentia is built for inference (EC2 Inf2 instances use Inferentia2). Each Inferentia2 chip has two NeuronCore-v2 cores and 32 GiB of high-bandwidth memory, with up to 12 chips per Inf2 instance, and supports data types including FP32, BF16, FP16, and INT8. Both are programmed through the AWS Neuron SDK, which integrates with PyTorch; models are compiled for Neuron before running. Recommend them when the customer runs supported model architectures at sustained scale and price-performance matters. Tradeoffs: a porting and validation step, operator coverage that differs from CUDA, and team familiarity. Always benchmark against GPU instances on the actual model.

probes.q: Does the customer have to rewrite their model?
probes.a: Usually not rewrite, but they must compile it with the Neuron SDK and validate accuracy and speed. Custom operators or unusual architectures can need extra work.

probes.q: Why might Inferentia beat a GPU on cost?
probes.a: It is designed only for inference, so for supported models at steady volume it can deliver more throughput per dollar. Prove it with a benchmark on the customer's model and traffic.

questions.aws: SageMaker Neo can compile models to run on AWS Inferentia, and SageMaker AI endpoints can run on Inf2 instances.
questions.trap: Pitching custom silicon as a drop-in replacement for every GPU workload. It shines on supported models at scale; for quick experiments or unusual architectures, GPUs may be faster to adopt.

questions.q: What do Amazon Textract, Amazon Rekognition, Amazon Comprehend, and Amazon Q do?
questions.plain: These are ready-made AI skills you call like a utility. Textract reads documents, including forms and tables, like a tireless data-entry clerk. Rekognition looks at images and video, like a security guard who never blinks. Comprehend reads text for meaning, like an analyst tagging every customer comment as happy or angry. Amazon Q is an AI assistant for working with AWS and writing code.
questions.technical: Amazon Textract extracts printed and handwritten text plus structure, such as form key-value pairs, tables, and signatures, going beyond plain OCR, with specialized APIs for invoices, receipts, and identity documents. Amazon Rekognition analyzes images and video: labels, face detection and comparison, text in images, and content moderation. Amazon Comprehend provides NLP: entities, key phrases, sentiment, language detection, PII detection, and custom classification. All are pay-per-use APIs needing no ML expertise. Amazon Q Developer is a generative AI assistant for building on AWS, in the console and IDEs. Current status matters: Amazon Q Business is no longer open to new customers (AWS points to Amazon Quick), and Q Developer IDE plugins reach end of support on April 30, 2027, with Kiro suggested.

probes.q: Textract or a multimodal LLM for documents?
probes.a: Textract for high-volume structured extraction with bounding boxes and confidence scores; an LLM through Bedrock to interpret, summarize, or handle messy layouts. Many pipelines use Textract first, then an LLM.

probes.q: What responsible-use issue comes up with Rekognition?
probes.a: Face analysis raises privacy and bias concerns, so customers need consent, clear policies, sensible confidence thresholds, and human review for consequential decisions.

questions.trap: Building a custom model for a problem these services already solve. Check the managed service first, and customize only for a measured gap.
