The database uses locks or multi-version concurrency control (MVCC) to keep concurrent transactions apart. Keep transactions short: long ones hold locks, block other writers, and in MVCC engines keep old row versions around, which bloats storage.

probes.q: What is MVCC?
probes.a: Multi-version concurrency control keeps older versions of rows so readers see a consistent snapshot without blocking writers.

probes.q: Why are long transactions bad?
probes.a: They hold locks longer, raise deadlock risk, and stop cleanup of old row versions.

questions.trap: Putting a slow external API call inside an open transaction. Do the call first, then open a short transaction to write the result.

questions.q: Explain isolation levels and the anomalies they prevent: dirty reads, non-repeatable reads, and phantom reads.
questions.plain: Isolation is about how much you can see of other people's unfinished work. Imagine editing a shared spreadsheet. A dirty read is seeing a number someone typed but has not saved. A non-repeatable read is looking twice at the same cell and getting two answers. A phantom is counting rows twice and finding a new row appeared. Stricter isolation hides more of this, but makes people wait more.
questions.technical: Dirty read: reading another transaction's uncommitted change, which may roll back. Non-repeatable read: reading the same row twice in one transaction and getting different values because someone committed an update in between. Phantom read: rerunning a range query and getting new or missing rows because someone inserted or deleted. Per the SQL standard, read uncommitted allows all three, read committed prevents dirty reads, repeatable read also prevents non-repeatable reads, and serializable prevents all three. Defaults differ: PostgreSQL uses read committed, MySQL InnoDB uses repeatable read. Higher levels cost more locking or more retries.

probes.q: Which level would you pick for a bank balance transfer?
probes.a: Serializable, or read committed with explicit row locks (SELECT ... FOR UPDATE) on the rows being changed. Correctness beats throughput there.

probes.q: What is a lost update?
probes.a: Two transactions read the same value, both modify it, and the second write overwrites the first. Fix it with row locks or optimistic version checks.

probes.q: Why not always use serializable?
probes.a: It lowers concurrency and causes more aborts or lock waits, so throughput drops. Most apps are fine with read committed plus targeted locking.

questions.trap: Saying repeatable read always blocks phantoms. The SQL standard allows phantoms at repeatable read; some engines go further, but only serializable guarantees it.

questions.q: What is normalization, and when would you denormalize?
questions.plain: Normalization means writing each fact down in exactly one place, like keeping one master contact card for each customer instead of copying their address onto every order. Denormalization is deliberately copying some facts so you can read faster, like printing the address on the shipping label so the warehouse does not have to look it up.
questions.technical: Normalization splits data into tables so each non-key fact depends only on the key, which removes duplication and update anomalies (first, second, third normal form is the usual target). It favors write correctness: change an address once. The cost is more joins at read time. Denormalization copies or pre-joins data to cut joins and speed reads, accepting the work of keeping copies in sync. Analytics star schemas and NoSQL single-table designs are intentionally denormalized. Pick based on access patterns and read-to-write ratio.

probes.q: What is an update anomaly?
probes.a: When the same fact is stored in several rows and an update changes some copies but not others, leaving the data contradictory.

probes.q: What is a star schema?
probes.a: A central fact table of events, like sales, surrounded by dimension tables, like product and date. It is denormalized for fast analytics.

questions.aws: DynamoDB data modeling usually denormalizes, designing tables around known query patterns. Redshift commonly uses star schemas.
questions.trap: Treating normalization as always right. It is right for transactional writes; read-heavy and analytics systems often denormalize on purpose.

questions.q: What is a database index, and how does a B-tree index work?
questions.plain: An index is like the index at the back of a textbook. Instead of reading every page to find a topic, you look it up alphabetically and jump straight to the page. A B-tree index keeps the values sorted in a shallow tree, so the database finds any row in a handful of steps even in a huge table.
questions.technical: A B-tree (in practice usually a B+ tree) is a balanced tree of fixed-size pages. Internal nodes hold sorted separator keys and pointers to child pages; leaf nodes hold the sorted keys with pointers to rows, and leaves are linked for range scans. Because each page holds hundreds of keys, the tree stays only a few levels deep even for millions of rows, so a lookup reads a few pages instead of scanning the table. It supports equality, range (BETWEEN, less than), prefix LIKE, and ORDER BY without a separate sort.

probes.q: What queries can a B-tree not help?
probes.a: Leading-wildcard LIKE such as '%son', and functions on the column like LOWER(email) unless you build an expression index.

probes.q: What is a covering index?
probes.a: An index that contains every column the query needs, so the database answers from the index alone without visiting the table.

questions.trap: Thinking an index always helps. If a filter matches a large share of rows, a full scan can be faster, and the optimizer may ignore the index on purpose.

questions.q: If indexes speed up reads, why not index every column?
questions.plain: Every index is another sorted list you must keep up to date. Picture a library with ten card catalogs, one by author, one by title, one by color, and so on. Finding books is easy, but every new book means filing ten cards. Too many indexes make every write slower and use more storage.
questions.technical: Each INSERT, UPDATE of an indexed column, and DELETE must also modify every affected index, which adds I/O, page splits, and lock contention. Indexes consume storage and memory, competing with hot data for the buffer cache. More indexes also give the optimizer more plans to weigh. The practical rule: index the columns used in frequent, selective WHERE filters, join keys, and ORDER BY, and drop indexes that monitoring shows are unused. Write-heavy tables such as event logs should carry few indexes.

probes.q: How do you find unused indexes?
probes.a: Use the engine's index usage statistics, such as pg_stat_user_indexes in PostgreSQL, over a representative period.

probes.q: What is selectivity?
probes.a: How well a value narrows results. A unique email is highly selective; a true or false flag is not.

questions.trap: Adding an index on a low-selectivity column like status and expecting a big win. It mostly adds write cost.

questions.q: What is a composite index, and what is the leftmost prefix rule?
questions.plain: A composite index sorts by more than one thing, like a phone book sorted by last name, then first name. It is great if you know the last name, and even better if you know both. But if you only know the first name, the phone book's order does not help at all. That is the leftmost prefix rule.
questions.technical: A composite index on (a, b, c) sorts by a, then b within a, then c. It can serve filters on a, on a and b, or on a, b, and c, and range scans on the last used column. It generally cannot be used efficiently for a filter on b or c alone. Column order matters: put equality-filtered columns first and the range or sort column last, for example (customer_id, created_at) for 'orders for this customer, newest first'. A single composite index can often replace several single-column indexes.

probes.q: Index on (customer_id, created_at). Does WHERE created_at > X use it well?
probes.a: Not efficiently, because created_at is not the leading column. You would need an index that starts with created_at.

probes.q: How do you order columns?
probes.a: Equality columns first, then the range or ORDER BY column, so the database can seek and then scan in order.

questions.resume: At Oracle, I cut NetSuite search P50 page load by 30%, from 840 to 588 ms, partly by restructuring indexes on the hot predicates so the columns the searches actually filtered on led the index.
questions.trap: Assuming column order in a composite index does not matter. It decides which queries the index can serve.

questions.q: A query got slow. How do you diagnose it with a query plan?
questions.plain: A query plan is the database's route map for answering your question. When a query is slow, you ask the database to show its route, like checking a GPS that is taking back roads. Often you find it is driving down every street, reading the whole table, when a highway, an index, was available or could be built.
questions.technical: Run EXPLAIN to see the chosen plan, and EXPLAIN ANALYZE to execute it with real row counts and timings. Look for full table scans on large tables, nested loop joins over many rows, sorts spilling to disk, and big gaps between estimated and actual rows, which point to stale statistics. Typical fixes: add or reorder an index to match the filter and sort, rewrite predicates so they can use the index (no function wrapped around the column), refresh statistics, or reduce selected columns. Measure P50 and P99 before and after.

probes.q: What does a big estimate vs actual row gap tell you?
probes.a: The optimizer's statistics are stale or skewed, so it picked a bad plan. Analyze the table or add extended statistics.

probes.q: Why can WHERE YEAR(created_at) = 2025 be slow?
probes.a: Wrapping the column in a function hides it from the index. Rewrite as a range on created_at.

probes.q: Which metric do you report?
probes.a: Latency percentiles such as P50 and P99, not just the average, since users feel the tail.

questions.aws: Amazon RDS and Aurora offer Amazon CloudWatch Database Insights to find the top SQL by load before you dig into plans.
questions.resume: At Oracle, I profiled NetSuite search query plans, found SQL that drove full scans, restructured indexes on hot predicates, and rewrote that SQL. Search P50 page load dropped 30%, from 840 to 588 ms.
questions.trap: Adding indexes blindly without reading the plan. Confirm what the engine actually does, change one thing, and remeasure.

questions.q: What are the main types of NoSQL databases?
questions.plain: NoSQL databases are specialists, each shaped for one kind of job. A key-value store is a coat check: hand over a ticket, get a coat. A document store keeps whole files, like a folder per customer. Wide column is a giant ledger with flexible columns. A graph database is a map of who knows whom. A time series database is a heart monitor, readings stamped with times.
questions.technical: Key-value: lookups by a unique key, extremely fast and simple (DynamoDB, Redis). Document: JSON-like documents with nested fields and flexible schema, queryable by fields (MongoDB, Amazon DocumentDB). Wide column: rows keyed by partition key with many dynamic columns, built for huge write volume (Cassandra, Amazon Keyspaces). Graph: nodes and edges for traversing relationships such as fraud rings or recommendations (Amazon Neptune). Time series: timestamped measurements with time-window queries and retention (Amazon Timestream). Each trades general query flexibility for scale or a specific access pattern.

probes.q: When would you choose a graph database?
probes.a: When the questions are about relationships several hops deep, such as friends of friends or accounts sharing a device, where SQL joins get slow.

probes.q: Is DynamoDB key-value or document?
probes.a: Both. It is a key-value store that also holds document-style items with nested attributes.

questions.aws: DynamoDB (key-value and document), DocumentDB (MongoDB compatible), Keyspaces (Cassandra compatible), Neptune (graph), Timestream (time series), ElastiCache and MemoryDB (in-memory).
questions.trap: Saying NoSQL means no schema at all. The schema moves into the application and the access patterns; you still design it carefully.

questions.q: How do you decide between a relational database and a NoSQL database?
questions.plain: Choose relational when you need flexible questions and strict correctness across many related records, like an accounting system. Choose NoSQL when you know exactly how the data will be looked up and need it fast at huge scale, like a shopping cart for millions of shoppers. It is the difference between a general store and a vending machine.
questions.technical: Relational fits when relationships matter, queries are ad hoc or evolving, and multi-row transactions and joins are core, such as ERP, billing, and inventory. NoSQL key-value or document stores fit when access patterns are known up front, scale is large or spiky, latency must stay flat, and data is naturally keyed, such as sessions, carts, profiles, or IoT events. Questions to ask: what are the top queries, read-to-write ratio, growth, consistency needs, and team skills. Many systems use both.

probes.q: What is the cost of NoSQL's speed?
probes.a: Less query flexibility. A new access pattern may need a new index or a data migration.

probes.q: Can a relational database scale horizontally?
probes.a: Reads scale with replicas. Writes need sharding or a distributed SQL engine such as Aurora DSQL.

questions.aws: Typical pairing: Aurora for orders and payments, DynamoDB for carts and sessions, ElastiCache in front of hot reads.
questions.trap: Choosing NoSQL because it is 'web scale' without knowing the access patterns. Unknown or changing queries favor relational.

questions.q: What is BASE and eventual consistency?
questions.plain: Eventual consistency means every copy of the data will agree soon, but maybe not this exact second. It is like posting a new phone number to all your friends: some see it right away, some an hour later, but everyone ends up with the right number. Systems accept that short delay to stay fast and always open.
questions.technical: BASE stands for basically available, soft state, eventually consistent. Instead of every write waiting for all replicas, a write is acknowledged once some replicas have it, and the rest catch up asynchronously. If writes stop, all replicas converge to the same value. Readers may briefly see stale data. Conflicts from concurrent writes need a rule such as last writer wins or version vectors. The payoff is lower latency and higher availability, especially across Regions. Use strong reads only where staleness would hurt.

probes.q: Give an example where eventual is fine and one where it is not.
probes.a: Fine: a like counter or product reviews. Not fine: an account balance check before a withdrawal.

probes.q: What is read-your-writes consistency?
probes.a: A guarantee that a user always sees their own latest write, even if others might still see the old value.

questions.aws: DynamoDB reads are eventually consistent by default and half the cost of strongly consistent reads. DynamoDB global tables default to multi-Region eventual consistency, with a multi-Region strong consistency mode available.
questions.trap: Saying eventual consistency means data might be lost or wrong. Committed writes are durable; only the timing of visibility on other replicas varies.

questions.q: Explain the CAP theorem and how it shapes design choices.
questions.plain: Imagine two bank branches whose phone line goes down. A customer asks one branch for their balance. The branch can refuse to answer until the line is back, which is consistent but unavailable. Or it can answer with what it knows, which is available but maybe out of date. CAP says when the line breaks, you must pick one of those two.
questions.technical: CAP says a distributed data system facing a network partition cannot guarantee both consistency (every read sees the latest write) and availability (every request to a non-failed node gets a response). Since partitions happen in real networks, the real choice is CP or AP during a partition. CP systems reject or delay some requests to avoid stale reads; AP systems keep answering and reconcile later. PACELC extends this: even without a partition, you trade latency against consistency. Many databases let you choose per request.

probes.q: Is a single-node PostgreSQL CA?
probes.a: There is no partition between nodes to tolerate, so CAP does not really apply. Once you add replicas across a network, you face the choice.

probes.q: What does PACELC add?
probes.a: If Partition, choose Availability or Consistency; Else, choose Latency or Consistency. It captures the everyday cost of strong consistency.

probes.q: Where does DynamoDB sit?
probes.a: It is tunable per read: eventually consistent by default, with strongly consistent reads available on tables and local secondary indexes.

questions.trap: Saying 'pick any two of three.' You cannot opt out of partitions, so the meaningful trade is consistency vs availability when one happens.

questions.q: What is database replication, and what is the difference between synchronous and asynchronous?
questions.plain: Replication means keeping live copies of your database somewhere else. Synchronous is like a notary who will not stamp your document until the copy is also filed, which is safe but slower. Asynchronous stamps it right away and files the copy a moment later, which is faster, but if the office burns down in that moment the copy is missing the last page.
questions.technical: In primary and replica setups, all writes go to the primary and changes stream to replicas. Synchronous replication waits for the replica to confirm before acknowledging the commit, giving zero data loss on failover but adding write latency. Asynchronous replication acknowledges first and ships changes after, so writes are fast and replicas can serve reads, but replicas lag and a failover can lose the latest writes. Use synchronous copies for high availability and asynchronous replicas for read scaling, reporting, and cross-Region disaster recovery.

probes.q: In RDS, what is the difference between Multi-AZ and a read replica?
probes.a: A Multi-AZ DB instance keeps a synchronous standby in another AZ for failover and it does not serve reads. Read replicas are asynchronous copies that serve read traffic.

probes.q: What is replication lag and why care?
probes.a: The delay before a replica has a write. A user may write and then not see it on a replica read. Route read-after-write to the primary.

probes.q: Does Multi-AZ help a read-heavy app?
probes.a: Not a single-standby Multi-AZ DB instance. A Multi-AZ DB cluster has two readable standbys, or add read replicas.

questions.aws: RDS Multi-AZ DB instance: one synchronous standby, failover only. RDS Multi-AZ DB cluster: two standbys that can serve reads. Read replicas: asynchronous, for scaling reads and cross-Region copies.
questions.trap: Saying Multi-AZ scales reads. The single-standby Multi-AZ DB instance is for availability; its standby serves no read traffic.

questions.q: What is sharding, how do you choose a partition key, and what is a hot partition?
questions.plain: Sharding splits a huge database into pieces across many machines, like splitting a phone book into A to F, G to M, and so on, each kept at a different desk. The partition key decides which desk a record goes to. A hot partition is when everyone lines up at one desk, say because most names start with S, while the others sit idle.
questions.technical: Sharding horizontally partitions data so each node owns a subset, letting writes and storage scale out. The partition key, often hashed, maps each record to a shard. A good key has high cardinality, spreads traffic evenly, and matches the main access pattern so most queries touch one shard. Bad keys such as a date, a status, or one celebrity customer concentrate traffic and create hot partitions that throttle while other shards idle. Fixes include a higher-cardinality key, adding a random or calculated suffix (write sharding), or caching hot reads.

probes.q: Why is today's date a bad partition key?
probes.a: All of today's writes land on one partition, so it gets hot while older partitions sit idle.

probes.q: What is the downside of sharding?
probes.a: Cross-shard queries and transactions are harder and slower, and rebalancing shards takes care.

questions.aws: DynamoDB hashes the partition key to place items. It has adaptive capacity to absorb some uneven traffic, but a poorly chosen key still throttles. Each DynamoDB partition supports up to 3,000 read units and 1,000 write units per second.
questions.trap: Thinking adding capacity fixes a hot partition. If all traffic hits one key, more total capacity does not spread it; change the key design.

questions.q: How do DynamoDB partition keys and sort keys work, and what are its read consistency options?
questions.plain: In DynamoDB, the partition key is like the drawer in a filing cabinet and the sort key is the order of folders inside that drawer. To find something fast, you name the drawer, then optionally a range of folders, like 'customer 42, orders from March.' Reads can be quick and maybe a second behind, or fully up to date at twice the cost.
questions.technical: The primary key is either a partition key alone or a partition key plus sort key (composite). DynamoDB hashes the partition key to pick the physical partition; items with the same partition key are stored together, ordered by sort key, so Query can fetch a range like begins_with or between. Global secondary indexes add other access patterns; local secondary indexes share the partition key with a different sort key. Reads are eventually consistent by default. Setting ConsistentRead true on GetItem, Query, or Scan gives strongly consistent reads, supported on tables and LSIs but not GSIs or streams.

probes.q: Query vs Scan?
probes.a: Query targets one partition key and is efficient. Scan reads the whole table and should be avoided on large tables.

probes.q: Can you do a strongly consistent read on a GSI?
probes.a: No. GSI reads are always eventually consistent.

probes.q: How do you model one-to-many?
probes.a: Use the parent ID as partition key and a sort key like ORDER#date, so one Query returns the parent's children in order.

questions.aws: DynamoDB is serverless, with on-demand or provisioned capacity, and supports transactions, TTL, streams, and global tables for multi-Region replication.
questions.trap: Designing DynamoDB tables like normalized SQL tables and planning to join later. DynamoDB has no joins; design keys around the queries first.

questions.q: Explain cache-aside and write-through caching.
questions.plain: A cache is a sticky note on your desk with answers you use a lot, so you do not walk to the filing room every time. Cache-aside means you check the note first and only go to the filing room when it is missing, then write it down. Write-through means every time you file something, you also update the sticky note right away.
questions.technical: Cache-aside (lazy loading): the app reads the cache; on a miss it reads the database, then populates the cache with a TTL. Only requested data is cached, and a cache failure is not fatal, but the first read is slow and data can go stale until TTL or invalidation. Write-through: the app writes to the cache and the database on every write, so the cache stays fresh, at the cost of write latency and caching data nobody reads. Teams often combine them: write-through for freshness, TTL to evict cold keys.

probes.q: What is write-behind?
probes.a: The app writes to the cache and the cache flushes to the database later. Fast writes, but risk of loss if the cache fails before flushing.

probes.q: What is a cache stampede?
probes.a: Many requests miss the same expired key at once and all hit the database. Fix with request coalescing, locks, or jittered TTLs.

questions.aws: Amazon ElastiCache supports the Valkey, Redis OSS, and Memcached engines, as a serverless cache or node-based cluster. DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX) is a write-through cache for DynamoDB.
questions.trap: Treating the cache as the source of truth. The database is the truth; the cache is a disposable copy.

questions.q: Why is cache invalidation hard, and how would you handle it?
questions.plain: The hard part of a cheat sheet is knowing when it is out of date. If a price changes and your sticky note still shows the old price, you quote the customer wrong. Invalidation is deciding when to throw the note away. You either give each note an expiry time, or you tear it up the moment the real record changes.
questions.technical: Stale data arises because the cache and database update separately, and with concurrency the order can flip: a slow reader can repopulate the cache with an old value after a writer invalidated it. Strategies: TTLs everywhere as a safety net; delete the cache key after the database commit rather than updating it in place; event-driven invalidation from change data capture so every writer path is covered; versioned keys so new data uses a new key. Match staleness tolerance to the data: seconds for a product page, zero for balances, which should skip the cache.

probes.q: Why delete the key instead of updating it on write?
probes.a: Delete is idempotent and avoids two concurrent writers leaving the cache with the older value.

probes.q: How does change data capture help?
probes.a: It publishes every committed change, such as from DynamoDB Streams, so a consumer invalidates keys no matter which service wrote the data.

probes.q: What does a TTL protect against?
probes.a: Any missed invalidation. Even if an event is lost, the bad entry expires on its own.

questions.trap: Relying only on application code to invalidate. Any batch job or second service that writes directly will leave stale entries; add TTLs or CDC-based invalidation.

questions.q: What is the difference between OLTP and OLAP?
questions.plain: OLTP is the cash register: thousands of quick sales, each touching one record. OLAP is the year-end report: a few big questions that read millions of past sales, like which region grew fastest. You keep them on separate systems so the slow report never makes the checkout line wait.
questions.technical: OLTP (online transaction processing) handles many short, concurrent reads and writes of a few rows each, needs ACID and low latency, and uses normalized, row-oriented storage with indexes on keys. OLAP (online analytical processing) runs fewer, heavy queries that scan and aggregate many rows but only a few columns, over historical data, and uses columnar storage, compression, and massively parallel processing. Data typically flows from OLTP systems into an OLAP warehouse or lake through ETL, ELT, or change data capture.

probes.q: Why not run reports on the production database?
probes.a: Large scans compete for CPU, memory, and I/O and slow customer transactions. Offload to a replica, warehouse, or lake.

probes.q: Name AWS services for each.
probes.a: OLTP: RDS, Aurora, DynamoDB. OLAP: Redshift, Athena over S3, EMR.

questions.aws: Aurora zero-ETL integration with Redshift can replicate transactional data into Redshift for analytics without building a pipeline.
questions.trap: Thinking one database should do both at scale. Row storage is built for transactions; columnar is built for analytics.

questions.q: Compare a data warehouse, a data lake, and a lakehouse.
questions.plain: A warehouse is a tidy store where every item is labeled and shelved, easy to shop but you must organize items before they come in. A lake is a big storage unit where you can dump anything, cheap and flexible but easy to get lost in. A lakehouse is the storage unit with labeled shelves and an inventory list added, so you keep the low cost but gain the order.
questions.technical: A data warehouse stores structured, modeled data with schema-on-write, tuned for fast SQL and BI; it is reliable but pricier and less flexible for raw or unstructured data. A data lake stores raw files of any type in cheap object storage with schema-on-read, great for scale and ML, but without governance it becomes a swamp and lacks transactions. A lakehouse adds an open table format, such as Delta Lake, Apache Iceberg, or Apache Hudi, over lake files, giving ACID transactions, schema enforcement, time travel, and upserts, so BI and ML share one copy.

probes.q: What problem does a table format like Iceberg solve?
probes.a: Plain files lack transactions, so concurrent writes and updates corrupt or confuse readers. The table format tracks file versions and gives ACID commits.

probes.q: Schema-on-write vs schema-on-read?
probes.a: Write: validate shape when loading, as in a warehouse. Read: store raw and apply a schema at query time, as in a lake.

questions.aws: Warehouse: Amazon Redshift. Lake: Amazon S3 with the AWS Glue Data Catalog and AWS Lake Formation for governance. Lakehouse: Iceberg tables on S3 queried by Athena, EMR, Glue, or Redshift.
questions.resume: At MSRcosmos, I built a nightly Databricks feed that loaded 17 financial tables and 4.2M rows into Delta Lake with PySpark, which is a lakehouse pattern: open files with transactional table features on top.
questions.trap: Saying a lake replaces a warehouse. Without a catalog, governance, and a table format, a lake is hard to trust for reporting.

questions.q: Why are columnar formats like Parquet faster for analytics?
questions.plain: Picture a survey stored two ways. Row storage keeps each person's whole form together. Columnar storage keeps every answer to question 1 together, then question 2, and so on. If you only want the average age, columnar lets you read one stack of answers instead of flipping through every full form.
questions.technical: Columnar storage writes each column's values contiguously. Analytic queries usually touch a few columns over many rows, so the engine reads only those columns and skips the rest, cutting I/O. Same-typed values compress very well with encodings like dictionary and run-length. Parquet also stores min and max statistics per row group, letting engines skip chunks that cannot match a filter. Row formats like CSV or JSON force reading every byte. The trade-off: columnar is slower for single-row lookups and small frequent updates.

probes.q: How does Parquet save money on Athena?
probes.a: Athena bills by data scanned. Reading only the needed columns of compressed Parquet scans far less than CSV.

probes.q: When is row storage better?
probes.a: For OLTP, where you read or write whole records one at a time.

questions.aws: Amazon Redshift stores tables in columnar format with compression and 1 MB blocks. Athena and Redshift Spectrum read Parquet and ORC on S3 efficiently.
questions.trap: Converting to Parquet but writing millions of tiny files. Small files kill scan performance; compact into larger files.

questions.q: What is the difference between ETL and ELT?
questions.plain: Both move data from where it is made to where it is analyzed. ETL is like washing and chopping vegetables before putting them in the fridge. ELT puts the groceries in the fridge first and preps them later as needed. ELT is popular in the cloud because the fridge is huge and the kitchen is powerful.
questions.technical: ETL extracts from sources, transforms on a separate engine (cleaning, joining, conforming), then loads only the finished data into the target. It suits strict schemas, sensitive data that must be masked before landing, and older warehouses with limited compute. ELT extracts and loads raw data first, then transforms inside the warehouse or lakehouse using its scalable compute, often with SQL. It keeps raw history for reprocessing and speeds up ingestion. The trade-off is storing raw data and governing who can see it.

probes.q: When would you still pick ETL?
probes.a: When regulated data, such as personal or health fields, must be masked or dropped before it lands in shared storage.

probes.q: Why keep raw data in ELT?
probes.a: If transformation logic has a bug or changes, you can rebuild from raw without re-extracting from sources.

questions.aws: AWS Glue runs serverless Spark ETL jobs and crawlers. Zero-ETL integrations, such as Aurora to Redshift, remove the pipeline for common cases.
questions.resume: At MSRcosmos, my nightly Databricks feed extracted 17 financial tables, loaded them into Delta Lake, and transformed them with PySpark, holding full refresh at 22 minutes.
questions.trap: Saying ELT means no transformation. It still transforms; it just does it after loading, inside the target.

questions.q: When would you use batch processing vs streaming?
questions.plain: Batch is like the mail: collected all day and delivered once in a big pile. Streaming is like a text message: each event arrives the moment it happens. Use batch when tomorrow morning is soon enough, such as payroll reports. Use streaming when minutes matter, such as fraud alerts or live dashboards.
questions.technical: Batch processes bounded data on a schedule, which is simpler, cheaper, easy to rerun, and fine for daily reports, model training, and reconciliation. Streaming processes unbounded events continuously with seconds of latency, for fraud detection, monitoring, personalization, and IoT. Streaming adds complexity: ordering, late and duplicate events, exactly-once vs at-least-once delivery, windowing, and state. Many architectures run both, a stream for fresh views and a batch job that recomputes accurate totals.

probes.q: What is at-least-once delivery and how do you cope?
probes.a: An event may arrive more than once, so consumers must be idempotent, for example by deduplicating on an event ID.

probes.q: What is a tumbling window?
probes.a: A fixed, non-overlapping time bucket, such as counting events per minute.

questions.aws: Streaming: Amazon Kinesis Data Streams for real-time ingestion, Amazon Data Firehose to deliver streams into S3, Redshift, or OpenSearch, and Amazon MSK for managed Kafka. Batch: AWS Glue jobs, Amazon EMR, scheduled Athena queries.
questions.resume: At Oracle, I built real-time API diagnostics across 1M+ endpoints on high-throughput event streams, auto-tagging root causes on 400 and 500 series failures. That cut P1 MTTR from 94 to 26 minutes, which a nightly batch could never do.
questions.trap: Defaulting to streaming because it sounds modern. If the business decision happens once a day, batch is cheaper and easier to operate.

questions.q: What are MapReduce and Spark, and why did Spark largely replace MapReduce?
questions.plain: MapReduce splits a giant job across many workers, like counting votes: each precinct counts its own ballots (map), then the totals are combined by candidate (reduce). Spark does the same idea but keeps the work in memory instead of writing every step to disk, like counters passing notes hand to hand instead of mailing them between rooms. That makes it much faster for multi-step work.
questions.technical: MapReduce runs a map phase that turns input splits into key-value pairs, a shuffle that groups by key across the network, and a reduce phase that aggregates each key. It writes intermediate results to disk between jobs, which is robust but slow for multi-stage pipelines and iterative ML. Spark builds a lazy directed acyclic graph of transformations, optimizes it, and keeps intermediate data in memory where possible, with recomputation from lineage for fault tolerance. It offers DataFrames, SQL, streaming, and MLlib in one engine. Shuffles remain the expensive step in both.

probes.q: What is a shuffle and why is it costly?
probes.a: Redistributing data across nodes by key, which means network transfer, serialization, and often disk spill. Minimize wide transformations.

probes.q: What is data skew in Spark?
probes.a: One key holds far more rows, so one task runs much longer than the rest. Fix with salting keys or broadcast joins.

probes.q: What does lazy evaluation buy you?
probes.a: Spark sees the whole plan before running, so it can push filters down, prune columns, and combine steps.

questions.aws: Amazon EMR runs managed Spark, Hadoop, Hive, and Presto clusters, including EMR Serverless. AWS Glue runs serverless Spark jobs. Athena also supports Apache Spark.
questions.resume: At MSRcosmos, I wrote the PySpark jobs behind a nightly Databricks feed of 17 tables and 4.2M rows into Delta Lake.
questions.trap: Saying Spark is fast because it is all in memory. It spills to disk when needed; the bigger gains are avoiding disk between stages and optimizing the whole plan.

questions.q: What is partition pruning, and how do incremental loads keep pipelines fast?
questions.plain: If your files are sorted into folders by month, and someone asks about March, you only open the March folder. That is partition pruning: skipping everything that cannot contain the answer. An incremental load is only adding the new receipts each night instead of re-filing the whole cabinet.
questions.technical: Data is laid out in partitions by a column such as date or region, often as folder paths like date=2026-10-21. When a query filters on that column, the engine reads only matching partitions and skips the rest, cutting I/O, time, and per-scan cost. It only works if queries filter on the partition column directly; choose low-to-moderate cardinality to avoid millions of tiny partitions. Incremental processing reads only new or changed source rows, often by watermark or change data capture, and applies them with a MERGE (upsert) instead of rewriting whole tables.

probes.q: Why not partition by customer ID?
probes.a: Too many partitions and tiny files. Partition by a coarse column like date and use clustering or sort order for finer filtering.

probes.q: What does MERGE do?
probes.a: In one atomic statement it updates rows that match on a key and inserts rows that do not, so reruns stay correct.

probes.q: What breaks pruning?
probes.a: Filtering on a derived expression of the partition column, or not filtering on it at all.

questions.aws: Athena and Redshift Spectrum prune partitions registered in the AWS Glue Data Catalog, and partition projection avoids managing huge partition lists. Iceberg tables support MERGE INTO on Athena.
questions.resume: At MSRcosmos, my nightly Databricks feed loads 17 financial tables and 4.2M rows into Delta Lake. Partition pruning and incremental merges held the full refresh at 22 minutes.
questions.trap: Partitioning on a column nobody filters on. Partitioning only pays off when it matches the common query filters.

questions.q: How does Amazon Aurora differ from standard Amazon RDS?
questions.plain: Standard RDS is like a managed apartment: AWS handles the maintenance, but each database still keeps its own storage. Aurora rebuilt the building so every apartment shares one very sturdy, self-copying storage foundation spread across three locations. Adding a reader is like adding a window onto the same room, not building a new room and copying the furniture.
questions.technical: RDS runs standard engines on instances with attached storage; Multi-AZ adds a synchronous standby, and read replicas copy data asynchronously. Aurora, compatible with MySQL and PostgreSQL, separates compute from a shared distributed cluster volume. Writes are synchronously replicated to six storage nodes across three Availability Zones, independent of how many instances you run. Up to 15 Aurora Replicas read the same volume, so adding one does not copy data, and failover to a replica is typically under 60 seconds. Storage grows automatically. Global Database replicates asynchronously to other Regions.

probes.q: When would you pick RDS over Aurora?
probes.a: When you need Oracle, SQL Server, or MariaDB, a specific engine version, or a small steady workload where RDS costs less.

probes.q: What is Aurora Serverless v2 for?
probes.a: Spiky or unpredictable workloads; capacity scales in fine increments instead of picking a fixed instance size.

probes.q: What is the Aurora cluster endpoint?
probes.a: A DNS name that always points to the current writer, so apps keep working after a failover.

questions.aws: Aurora storage: six storage nodes across three AZs, up to 15 read replicas, I/O-Optimized or Standard pricing, Global Database for cross-Region DR with typical replication latency under a second.
questions.trap: Saying Aurora is just RDS MySQL with a new name. The storage layer is fundamentally different, which is why replicas are cheap to add and failover is fast.

questions.q: What are Athena, Glue, and Lake Formation, and how do they fit together?
questions.plain: Think of S3 as a giant warehouse of files. Glue is the inventory clerk who catalogs what is on each shelf and can repackage goods. Athena is a search desk where you ask questions in plain SQL and pay only for what you look at. Lake Formation is the security guard who decides which people can open which aisles, even which boxes.
questions.technical: Amazon Athena is a serverless, interactive query service that analyzes data directly in S3 using standard SQL; there is no infrastructure, and you pay per query based on data scanned. AWS Glue provides the Data Catalog (table definitions Athena, EMR, and Redshift Spectrum share), crawlers that infer schemas, and serverless Spark ETL jobs. AWS Lake Formation builds and governs the data lake, with centralized permissions down to database, table, column, row, and cell level. Together they form a serverless lake: data in S3, metadata in Glue, access in Lake Formation, SQL in Athena.

probes.q: How do you lower Athena cost?
probes.a: Store data as compressed Parquet or ORC, partition by common filters, and select only needed columns, since you pay for bytes scanned.

probes.q: Athena or Redshift?
probes.a: Athena for ad hoc, infrequent queries over S3 with no setup. Redshift for heavy, frequent, concurrent BI with tuned performance.

questions.aws: Amazon Quick Sight (formerly QuickSight, now part of Amazon Quick) builds dashboards on top of Athena and Redshift.
questions.trap: Thinking Athena stores your data. It only queries data that stays in S3.

questions.q: A customer asks, 'Which database should I use?' Walk me through choosing an AWS service for several workloads.
questions.plain: There is no single best database, just as there is no single best vehicle. A delivery van, a race car, and a bus each fit a job. I start by asking what questions the app asks of its data, how fast, and how much. Then I match: an orders system to a relational database, a shopping cart to a key-value store, reports to a warehouse, and so on.
questions.technical: Start with access patterns, scale, latency, consistency, and team skills. Relational with transactions and joins, such as orders, ERP, or billing: Aurora or RDS. Key-value at massive scale with flat latency, such as carts, sessions, or gaming state: DynamoDB. Sub-millisecond cache or leaderboards: ElastiCache. Large-scale BI over structured history: Redshift. Ad hoc SQL over files in S3: Athena. Full-text search and log analytics: OpenSearch Service. Relationships like fraud rings: Neptune. Metrics over time: Timestream. Streams of events: Kinesis. Dashboards: Quick Sight. Most solutions use several, joined by events.

probes.q: A startup wants a mobile app backend that might go viral. What do you suggest?
probes.a: DynamoDB on-demand for core data, since it scales without capacity planning, with Cognito and Lambda, adding OpenSearch Service only if they need search.

probes.q: A retailer wants product search with typo tolerance. Which service?
probes.a: Amazon OpenSearch Service, fed from the primary database, which stays the source of truth.

probes.q: When do you push back on purpose-built databases?
probes.a: When a small team would have to run five engines. One well-chosen relational database often covers more than people expect.

questions.aws: Common pairings: Aurora plus ElastiCache for a web app, DynamoDB plus Streams plus OpenSearch Service for searchable items, Kinesis to S3 to Athena or Redshift for analytics.
questions.trap: Leading with a product name before asking about access patterns. Ask what the app needs to read and write, how often, and how fresh, then pick.

domains.name: Security
domains.summary: How systems keep data private, correct, and available, and how AWS splits that job with the customer, so an SA can design safe architectures and explain risk to a business audience.

sources.label: AWS KMS: cryptography essentials and envelope encryption
Amazon Cognito: user pools and identity pools

cheatsheet.def: Confidentiality (only the right people see it), integrity (it is not changed silently), availability (it is there when needed).
cheatsheet.probe: Name a control for each: encryption for confidentiality, hashing or signatures for integrity, redundancy and DDoS protection for availability.

cheatsheet.def: Authentication proves who you are; authorization decides what you may do.
cheatsheet.probe: OIDC is for authentication, OAuth 2.0 is for authorization. A 401 means not authenticated, a 403 means authenticated but not allowed.

cheatsheet.def: Hashing is one-way and fixed length; encryption is two-way with a key.
cheatsheet.probe: Passwords are hashed with a slow, salted algorithm, never encrypted.

cheatsheet.def: Symmetric uses one shared key and is fast; asymmetric uses a public and private key pair and is slower.
cheatsheet.probe: TLS uses asymmetric crypto to agree on keys, then symmetric crypto for the bulk data.

cheatsheet.def: Encrypt data with a data key, then encrypt the data key with a KMS key and store it next to the data.
cheatsheet.probe: The KMS key never leaves the KMS HSMs unencrypted; only the small data key travels to KMS.

cheatsheet.def: Give each person or workload only the permissions it needs, for only as long as it needs them.
cheatsheet.probe: Prefer roles with temporary credentials over long-lived access keys.

cheatsheet.def: Never trust a request because of where it comes from on the network; verify identity, device, and context on every request.
cheatsheet.probe: It does not mean removing the network perimeter; it means the perimeter is no longer the only check.

cheatsheet.def: Everything starts as an implicit deny; an allow is needed to proceed; any explicit deny anywhere wins.
cheatsheet.probe: An explicit deny in an identity policy, resource policy, SCP, or boundary overrides every allow.

cheatsheet.def: An AWS Organizations guardrail that caps the maximum permissions of IAM users and roles in member accounts.
cheatsheet.probe: SCPs never grant permissions and do not affect the management account or service-linked roles.

cheatsheet.def: Standard is automatic, at no extra charge, against common network and transport layer DDoS; Advanced is a paid tier with more detection, response team access, and cost protection.
cheatsheet.probe: Layer 7 floods are handled together with AWS WAF rules.

cheatsheet.def: CloudTrail records who called which API and when; Config records what each resource looked like over time and checks it against rules.
cheatsheet.probe: CloudTrail answers who did it; Config answers what changed and is it compliant.

cheatsheet.def: Managed threat detection that analyzes CloudTrail management events, VPC Flow Logs, and Route 53 Resolver DNS logs.
cheatsheet.probe: You do not have to turn those logs on yourself, and GuardDuty detects; it does not block.

cheatsheet.term: Cognito user pool vs identity pool
cheatsheet.def: A user pool signs users in and issues JWTs; an identity pool trades a trusted token for temporary AWS credentials.
cheatsheet.probe: User pool answers who is this user; identity pool answers which AWS resources may they reach.

cheatsheet.def: AWS secures the cloud itself; the customer secures what they put in the cloud.
cheatsheet.probe: The line moves with the service: more customer work on EC2, less on Lambda or S3.

steps.label: Redirect to sign in, with PKCE
Data, if token and scope valid

questions.q: What is the CIA triad?
questions.plain: It is the three things security protects. Think of a bank vault: only the right people can open it (confidentiality), nobody can quietly swap the cash for fake bills (integrity), and the branch is actually open when you need your money (availability).
questions.technical: Confidentiality means data is readable only by authorized parties, enforced with access control and encryption at rest and in transit. Integrity means data is not altered without detection, enforced with hashing, digital signatures, checksums, and change control. Availability means systems and data are reachable when needed, enforced with redundancy across Availability Zones, backups, autoscaling, and DDoS protection. Most security decisions trade these off. Aggressive lockouts improve confidentiality but can hurt availability. I use the triad to frame a customer conversation: which of the three matters most for this workload, and what is the cost of losing each one.

probes.q: Which leg does ransomware hit?
probes.a: Mainly availability, because files are encrypted and unusable. Modern ransomware also steals data first, so it hits confidentiality too.

probes.q: Give one AWS control per leg.
probes.a: KMS encryption for confidentiality, S3 Object Lock or CloudTrail log file integrity validation for integrity, multi-AZ deployments and AWS Shield for availability.

questions.aws: Maps to the AWS Well-Architected Security and Reliability pillars: encryption with KMS, integrity with log file validation and versioning, availability with multi-AZ and Shield.
questions.trap: People treat security as only confidentiality. A system that is perfectly locked but down, or readable but silently corrupted, has still failed.

questions.q: Explain the AWS shared responsibility model to a CFO.
questions.plain: AWS is like a landlord of a secure office building. The landlord guards the doors, the walls, and the power. You still decide who gets a key to your office and you lock your own filing cabinets.
questions.technical: AWS is responsible for security of the cloud: physical data centers, hardware, the global network, and the virtualization layer. The customer is responsible for security in the cloud: identity and access, data classification and encryption choices, network configuration such as security groups, and patching anything they manage. The split shifts by service. On Amazon EC2 the customer patches the guest operating system. On AWS Lambda or Amazon S3, AWS runs more of the stack, so the customer focuses on IAM, data, and code. Compliance inherits the same way: AWS provides audited controls through AWS Artifact reports, and the customer proves their own configuration.

probes.q: Who patches the OS on EC2 vs Lambda?
probes.a: On EC2 the customer does. On Lambda AWS manages the runtime environment, and the customer keeps their own code and dependencies up to date.

probes.q: If an S3 bucket is left public, whose fault is it?
probes.a: The customer's. Access configuration is security in the cloud. S3 Block Public Access exists to make the safe setting easy.

probes.q: Where do I get AWS compliance reports?
probes.a: AWS Artifact provides on-demand access to AWS audit reports such as SOC reports.

questions.aws: Managed and serverless services move more of the line to AWS, which is a real security argument for them, not only a cost one.
questions.trap: Saying the cloud provider handles security. Most cloud breaches come from customer-side misconfiguration, such as overly broad permissions or exposed storage.

questions.q: What is the difference between authentication and authorization?
questions.plain: Authentication is the hotel front desk checking your ID. Authorization is your room key card, which opens your room and the gym but not someone else's room.
questions.technical: Authentication verifies identity, using something you know, have, or are, and results in an identity or session, often a token. Authorization runs after that, on every request, and decides whether that identity may perform a specific action on a specific resource. In HTTP terms, 401 Unauthorized really means not authenticated, while 403 Forbidden means authenticated but not allowed. In AWS, signing in or assuming a role is authentication, and IAM policy evaluation is authorization. Keeping them separate lets you change sign-in methods without rewriting permissions, and the reverse.

probes.q: Which standard is for which?
probes.a: OpenID Connect is for authentication. OAuth 2.0 is for delegated authorization.

probes.q: Can you have authorization without authentication?
probes.a: Yes, in a limited way. A public read on an object or a Cognito guest identity is authorization for an anonymous caller.

questions.aws: IAM Identity Center or an external identity provider handles authentication for people; IAM policies handle authorization for every API call.
questions.trap: Using the words interchangeably, or assuming that being signed in means being allowed. Every request still needs an authorization check.

questions.q: What is MFA and why does it matter so much?
questions.plain: MFA means you need two different kinds of proof to get in, like a bank card plus a PIN. A thief who steals your password still cannot get in without your phone or security key.
questions.technical: Multi-factor authentication combines at least two factor types: something you know (password), something you have (authenticator app, hardware key), or something you are (biometric). Two passwords are not MFA. It sharply reduces risk from phished or reused passwords. Factors differ in strength: SMS codes can be intercepted through SIM swapping, time-based one-time passwords are better, and FIDO2 security keys or passkeys are phishing resistant because they are bound to the real site's origin. On AWS, protect the root user and all human access with MFA, and prefer phishing-resistant factors for administrators.

probes.q: Why is SMS the weakest option?
probes.a: Codes can be redirected through SIM swapping or intercepted, and users can be tricked into reading them out.

probes.q: What is MFA fatigue?
probes.a: An attacker spams push approvals until the user taps approve. Number matching or phishing-resistant keys stop it.

questions.aws: Enable MFA on the AWS account root user and enforce it for workforce users in IAM Identity Center. Amazon Cognito user pools support TOTP and SMS MFA for app users.
questions.trap: Thinking a password plus a security question is MFA. Both are something you know, so it is a single factor.

questions.q: What is single sign-on, and how would you set it up for a company on AWS?
questions.plain: SSO is one company badge that opens every door you are allowed through, instead of a separate key for each room. When someone leaves, security takes back one badge and every door locks for them at once.
questions.technical: SSO lets users authenticate once with a central identity provider, which then vouches for them to many applications using SAML 2.0 or OpenID Connect. Benefits: one place for MFA and password policy, fast offboarding, and fewer passwords to phish. On AWS, the recommended pattern for a workforce is AWS IAM Identity Center. Connect it to the existing identity provider, such as Microsoft Entra ID or Okta, sync users and groups with SCIM, then define permission sets that map groups to IAM roles in each account of the AWS Organization. Users get short-lived credentials instead of long-lived IAM user access keys.

probes.q: SAML vs OIDC?
probes.a: Both carry a signed statement of who the user is. SAML uses XML assertions and is common in older enterprise apps. OIDC uses JSON Web Tokens on top of OAuth 2.0 and suits web, mobile, and APIs.

probes.q: What is SCIM for?
probes.a: Automatic provisioning and deprovisioning of users and groups from the identity provider into the target system.

probes.q: What is the main risk of SSO?
probes.a: The identity provider becomes a single high-value target, so it needs strong MFA and monitoring.

questions.aws: AWS IAM Identity Center (formerly AWS SSO) with permission sets across AWS Organizations accounts; Amazon Cognito covers customer-facing app sign-in instead.
questions.trap: Creating an IAM user per employee in every account. That multiplies long-lived credentials and makes offboarding error prone.

questions.q: How do OAuth 2.0 and OpenID Connect differ, and how does the authorization code flow work?
questions.plain: OAuth is a valet key: it lets an app do a few specific things on your behalf without ever seeing your real password. OpenID Connect adds a name tag to that key, so the app also learns who you are.
questions.technical: OAuth 2.0 is a delegated authorization framework. An authorization server issues an access token with scopes that an API checks. It does not define who the user is. OpenID Connect is an identity layer on top of OAuth 2.0 that adds an ID token, a signed JWT with claims about the user. In the authorization code flow, the app redirects the user to the authorization server, the user signs in and consents, the server redirects back with a short-lived code, and the app exchanges that code at the token endpoint for tokens. PKCE binds the code to the app that started the flow, so a stolen code is useless. PKCE is now recommended for all clients, not only mobile apps.

probes.q: Why not return the token directly in the redirect?
probes.a: That was the old implicit flow. Tokens in URLs leak through browser history and logs, so the code exchange plus PKCE replaced it.

probes.q: Which token does the API accept?
probes.a: The access token. The ID token is for the client app to learn who signed in, not for calling APIs.

probes.q: What flow do machine-to-machine calls use?
probes.a: The client credentials grant, where the service authenticates as itself with no user involved.

questions.aws: Amazon Cognito user pools act as an OIDC provider and OAuth 2.0 authorization server; API Gateway can validate the resulting tokens.
questions.trap: Calling OAuth an authentication protocol. Using an OAuth access token as proof of identity is exactly the gap OIDC was created to fill.

questions.q: What is a JWT, and what are the common mistakes with it?
questions.plain: A JWT is like a concert wristband with a tamper-proof seal. Staff can read it at a glance and know it is real without phoning the box office, but anyone can read what is printed on it, so you never print secrets there.
questions.technical: A JSON Web Token has three base64url parts: header, payload of claims, and signature. The signature, made with a secret (HMAC) or a private key (RSA or ECDSA), lets any service verify the token was issued by a trusted party and not modified, without a database lookup. That is why JWTs suit stateless APIs. A signed JWT is encoded, not encrypted, so anyone can read the claims. Validation must check the signature against the expected algorithm and key, plus expiry, issuer, and audience. Because JWTs are hard to revoke before they expire, keep access tokens short-lived and use refresh tokens for renewal.

probes.q: How do you revoke a JWT early?
probes.a: Keep lifetimes short, revoke the refresh token, or keep a deny list of token IDs, which brings back some state.

probes.q: What is the alg none attack?
probes.a: A library that trusts the algorithm named in the header might accept an unsigned token. Always pin the expected algorithm.

questions.aws: Cognito user pools issue JWT ID and access tokens; API Gateway HTTP APIs have a built-in JWT authorizer, and REST APIs can use a Cognito or Lambda authorizer.
questions.trap: Putting sensitive data in the payload because it looks scrambled. Base64url is an encoding anyone can reverse.

questions.q: What is the difference between symmetric and asymmetric encryption?
questions.plain: Symmetric is a house key: the same key locks and unlocks, so you must hand a copy to anyone who needs in. Asymmetric is a mailbox with a slot: anyone can drop a letter in using the public slot, but only the owner's private key opens the box.
questions.technical: Symmetric encryption, such as AES, uses one shared secret key for both encryption and decryption. It is fast and suits large data, but the key must be distributed securely. Asymmetric encryption, such as RSA or elliptic curve schemes, uses a key pair: what the public key encrypts only the private key decrypts, and what the private key signs anyone can verify with the public key. It is much slower, so real systems combine both. TLS uses asymmetric cryptography to authenticate the server and agree on a session key, then switches to symmetric encryption for the actual traffic. Envelope encryption follows the same idea.

probes.q: Why not use asymmetric encryption for everything?
probes.a: It is far slower and limited in how much data one operation can handle, so it is used for key exchange and signatures.

probes.q: What does AWS KMS use for symmetric keys?
probes.a: AES-256 in Galois Counter Mode, inside FIPS-validated hardware security modules.

questions.aws: AWS KMS supports symmetric keys (the default) and asymmetric RSA and elliptic curve keys for encryption, signing, or key agreement.
questions.trap: Saying asymmetric is more secure, so always better. It solves key distribution, not strength, and is too slow for bulk data.

questions.q: How is hashing different from encryption, and how should passwords be stored?
questions.plain: Encryption is a locked box: with the key you get the original back. Hashing is a blender: you can check that two smoothies came from the same fruit, but you can never turn the smoothie back into fruit. Passwords go in the blender, with a pinch of a unique spice per person, so two people with the same password still get different smoothies.
questions.technical: A hash function maps any input to a fixed-length digest and is one-way: there is no key to reverse it. It is used for integrity checks and password verification. Encryption is reversible with a key and is used for confidentiality. Passwords must be hashed, never encrypted, so a leaked database does not reveal them. Use a slow, purpose-built algorithm such as Argon2, bcrypt, scrypt, or PBKDF2, not a fast hash like SHA-256 alone. Add a unique random salt per user, stored next to the hash. The salt defeats precomputed rainbow tables and makes identical passwords produce different hashes. A pepper is an extra secret kept outside the database.

probes.q: Why must a password hash be slow?
probes.a: Attackers who steal hashes guess offline. A deliberately slow, memory-hard function makes each guess expensive.

probes.q: Is the salt secret?
probes.a: No. It only needs to be unique and random per user. Its job is to break precomputation, not to be hidden.

probes.q: What is a hash collision?
probes.a: Two different inputs with the same digest. That is why MD5 and SHA-1 are no longer used for security.

questions.aws: Amazon Cognito user pools store and verify user passwords for you, which removes this whole problem from the customer's code.
questions.trap: Encrypting passwords so they can be recovered, or hashing them with fast unsalted SHA-256. Both make a database leak far worse.

questions.q: What is a digital signature, and how do certificates and PKI build on it?
questions.plain: A digital signature is a wax seal only you can make but anyone can check. A certificate is a passport: a trusted government (the certificate authority) vouches that this seal really belongs to this website, so your browser believes it.
questions.technical: To sign, the sender hashes the message and signs the hash with a private key. Anyone with the public key can verify it, which proves integrity and origin, and gives non-repudiation because only the key holder could sign. The remaining problem is trusting that a public key belongs to who it claims. Public key infrastructure solves that: a certificate authority signs an X.509 certificate binding a public key to a domain name. Browsers and operating systems ship with trusted root CAs, and a server presents a chain from its certificate up to a root. Certificates expire and can be revoked, so automated renewal matters.

probes.q: Where else are signatures used besides TLS?
probes.a: JWTs, code and container image signing, software updates, and AWS request signing with Signature Version 4.

probes.q: What happens if a certificate expires?
probes.a: Clients reject the connection and users see errors, which is why managed automatic renewal is valuable.

questions.aws: AWS Certificate Manager issues public certificates at no extra cost for integrated services such as Elastic Load Balancing, Amazon CloudFront, and API Gateway, and renews them automatically. AWS Private CA covers internal certificates. AWS KMS can sign and verify with asymmetric keys.
questions.trap: Saying a signature encrypts the message. A signature proves who sent it and that it was not changed; the content can still be readable.

questions.q: Walk me through what TLS does when I open an HTTPS site.
questions.plain: Before any secrets are shared, your browser and the website check each other's ID and agree on a private code only the two of them know. After that, everything they say is in that code, so anyone listening in on the cafe Wi-Fi hears gibberish.
questions.technical: TLS gives confidentiality, integrity, and server authentication over TCP. In TLS 1.3, the client sends a ClientHello with supported cipher suites and an ephemeral key share. The server replies with its key share, its certificate, and a signature proving it holds the matching private key, then a Finished message. Both sides derive the same symmetric session keys from the ephemeral Diffie-Hellman exchange, so this takes one round trip. The client validates the certificate chain against trusted roots and checks the host name. Bulk data then uses an authenticated cipher such as AES-GCM. Ephemeral keys give forward secrecy: stealing the server key later does not decrypt past sessions. Mutual TLS adds a client certificate.

probes.q: What is forward secrecy?
probes.a: Session keys come from throwaway Diffie-Hellman keys, so a later leak of the server's long-term private key cannot decrypt recorded traffic.

probes.q: Where should TLS terminate on AWS?
probes.a: Often at an Application Load Balancer or CloudFront using an ACM certificate. Re-encrypt to the targets when policy requires encryption end to end.

probes.q: What does TLS not protect?
probes.a: Data at rest, the server itself, and some metadata such as destination IP addresses.

questions.aws: ACM certificates on Elastic Load Balancing, CloudFront, and API Gateway; security policies on load balancers choose allowed TLS versions and ciphers.
questions.trap: Thinking the padlock means the site is trustworthy. It only means the connection is encrypted to whoever owns that domain.

questions.q: What is the difference between encryption at rest and in transit, and do you need both?
questions.plain: In transit is the armored truck moving the money. At rest is the vault where the money sits overnight. A robber can try either one, so you protect both.
questions.technical: Encryption in transit protects data moving over a network, usually with TLS, against eavesdropping and tampering. Encryption at rest protects stored data, such as disks, databases, object storage, and backups, against stolen media, snapshots shared by mistake, or direct storage access. They guard different threats, so a sound design uses both. Neither replaces access control: an authorized but malicious user still reads decrypted data. Client-side encryption, done before data reaches the service, adds protection even from the storage layer, at the cost of managing keys in the application.

probes.q: Is S3 encrypted at rest by default?
probes.a: Yes. Since January 2023, new objects in S3 are encrypted with S3 managed keys by default. You can choose KMS keys for more control and auditing.

probes.q: How do you force TLS to an S3 bucket?
probes.a: A bucket policy that denies requests where the aws:SecureTransport condition is false.

questions.aws: Most AWS storage services integrate with AWS KMS for at-rest encryption; TLS endpoints and ACM handle in transit.
questions.trap: Believing encryption at rest stops a hacker who gets into the application. The app decrypts data for any caller it authorizes, so access control still decides.

questions.q: What is envelope encryption and why does AWS KMS use it?
questions.plain: You lock your documents in a box with an everyday key, then lock that key inside a small safe that never leaves the bank. You keep the locked-up key taped to the box. To open the box, you ask the bank to unlock the little key for you, and the bank writes down every time you asked.
questions.technical: Envelope encryption encrypts data with a data key, then encrypts that data key under another key, the KMS key. The application calls GenerateDataKey and receives a plaintext data key and the same key encrypted under the KMS key. It encrypts the data locally with the plaintext key, discards the plaintext key, and stores the encrypted data key alongside the ciphertext. To read, it sends the small encrypted data key to KMS Decrypt, gets the plaintext key back, and decrypts locally. Benefits: large data never travels to KMS, KMS keys never leave its FIPS-validated HSMs unencrypted, every use is authorized by key policy and logged in CloudTrail, and re-keying only re-encrypts small data keys.

probes.q: Why not just call KMS Encrypt on the data?
probes.a: KMS Encrypt takes at most 4 KB of plaintext, and sending bulk data over the network for every operation is slow. Data keys keep bulk crypto local.

probes.q: What happens if someone steals the database?
probes.a: They get ciphertext and encrypted data keys, which are useless without permission to call KMS Decrypt with that KMS key.

probes.q: What does key rotation change?
probes.a: KMS adds new key material for new encryptions and keeps old material to decrypt older data keys, so existing data stays readable.

questions.aws: S3, EBS, RDS, and DynamoDB use this pattern under the hood with KMS; the AWS Encryption SDK gives the same pattern for client-side encryption.
questions.trap: Thinking the KMS key is sent to your application. It never leaves KMS unencrypted; only data keys come back to you.

questions.q: How do you manage encryption keys on AWS?
questions.plain: Keys are like the master keys of a building. You keep them in one guarded key room, decide in writing who can use each one, change locks on a schedule, and keep a log of every time a key was checked out.
questions.technical: AWS KMS centralizes key management. Keys are created and used inside FIPS-validated HSMs and are never exported in plaintext. Every KMS key has a key policy, the primary access control, which can be combined with IAM policies and grants. That allows separation of duties: administrators who manage a key do not have to be able to use it to decrypt data. Options include AWS managed keys, customer managed keys with your own policies and optional automatic rotation, and imported key material. Every API call is logged in AWS CloudTrail. Deleting a key requires a waiting period because data encrypted under it becomes unrecoverable.

probes.q: AWS managed vs customer managed key?
probes.a: AWS managed keys are created for a service and you cannot change their policy. Customer managed keys give you control of policy, rotation, and cross-account sharing.

probes.q: Why is key deletion delayed?
probes.a: Deleting a key makes everything encrypted under it unreadable, so KMS enforces a waiting period that lets you cancel. Disabling the key is the safer first step.

questions.aws: AWS KMS, with AWS CloudHSM for customers who need single-tenant HSMs under their exclusive control.
questions.trap: Storing keys in code or config files next to the data they protect. That is a lock with the key taped to it.

questions.q: Where should an application keep its database password and API keys?
questions.plain: Not on a sticky note on the monitor, which is what hard-coding in source code is. Keep it in a locked key cabinet that hands it only to the right app on request, and that changes the lock for you on a schedule.
questions.technical: Secrets belong in a dedicated secrets manager, not in source code, container images, or plain environment files. The app fetches the secret at runtime using its IAM role, so no credential is needed to get the credential. AWS Secrets Manager encrypts secrets with KMS, controls access with IAM and resource policies, logs access in CloudTrail, and supports automatic rotation. Managed rotation covers many AWS managed secrets without a Lambda function. For other secrets, a Lambda rotation function runs createSecret, setSecret, testSecret, and finishSecret, moving the AWSPENDING version to AWSCURRENT only after the new credential tests successfully. Apps should cache secrets and handle rotation gracefully.

probes.q: Secrets Manager vs Parameter Store?
probes.a: Parameter Store SecureString parameters are encrypted and cheap for config, but Secrets Manager adds built-in rotation, cross-account sharing, and replication across Regions.

probes.q: A secret was committed to Git. What do you do?
probes.a: Rotate it immediately, because history and clones keep it. Then remove it from history and add secret scanning to the pipeline.

questions.aws: AWS Secrets Manager with rotation; Amazon RDS can manage the master user password in Secrets Manager for you.
questions.trap: Thinking deleting the commit fixes a leaked secret. Once pushed, assume it is compromised and rotate it.

questions.q: What is least privilege, and how do you apply it in practice?
questions.plain: A hotel cleaner gets a key card for the floors they clean today, not a master key for the whole building forever. If the card is lost, the damage is small.
questions.technical: Least privilege means each identity, human or workload, gets only the permissions needed for its task, scoped to specific actions and resources, for as little time as possible. It limits the blast radius of a stolen credential or a bug. In practice: use roles with temporary credentials instead of long-lived access keys, start from narrow policies, add conditions such as source VPC or required tags, and remove unused access over time. Admin access should be just in time and audited. AWS tools help: IAM Access Analyzer can generate policies from actual CloudTrail activity and flag unused access, and last accessed data shows which permissions are never used.

probes.q: Why not start broad and tighten later?
probes.a: Later rarely comes, and broad permissions are where breaches spread. Start narrow and add what logs prove is needed.

probes.q: How do you stop developers from granting themselves admin?
probes.a: Permissions boundaries cap what roles they create can do, and SCPs cap the whole account.

questions.aws: IAM roles, IAM Access Analyzer policy generation and unused access findings, permissions boundaries, and SCPs as account-wide guardrails.
questions.trap: Equating least privilege with a one-time policy review. Needs change, so it is a continuous process driven by usage data.

questions.q: What does zero trust mean, and how is it different from a VPN?
questions.plain: The old model is a castle with a moat: once you are inside the walls, you can wander anywhere. Zero trust is an office where every single door checks your badge, your device, and whether you should be there right now, even if you are already inside the building.
questions.technical: Zero trust, described in NIST SP 800-207, removes implicit trust based on network location. Every request is authenticated and authorized using identity, device posture, and context, and access is granted per application or resource with least privilege. A traditional VPN authenticates once and places the user on the network, so a compromised laptop can reach anything routable. Zero trust instead puts an identity-aware proxy or policy check in front of each app and assumes breach, so it also wants segmentation, encryption everywhere, and continuous monitoring. On AWS, IAM already evaluates every API call this way; for private applications, AWS Verified Access grants per-app access without a VPN.

probes.q: Does zero trust mean dropping firewalls and private subnets?
probes.a: No. Network controls stay as one layer. Zero trust says they are not enough on their own.

probes.q: What signals feed a zero trust decision?
probes.a: User identity and MFA, device health, location, time, and the sensitivity of the resource.

questions.aws: IAM authorization on every request, AWS Verified Access for application access without a VPN, and VPC Lattice auth policies for service-to-service calls.
questions.trap: Treating zero trust as a product you buy. It is an architecture principle applied across identity, network, and data.

questions.q: What is defense in depth, and how does network segmentation fit in?
questions.plain: A museum does not rely on one lock. It has a fence, guards at the door, cameras in the halls, alarms on the cases, and an insurance policy. A burglar has to beat every layer, and each one buys time.
questions.technical: Defense in depth stacks independent controls so one failure does not mean a breach: identity, network, compute, application, data, and detection layers. Network segmentation is one layer. It splits the environment into zones so a compromise in one cannot reach everything. On AWS: public subnets hold only load balancers, app and database tiers sit in private subnets, security groups allow only needed ports between tiers and are stateful, network ACLs add stateless subnet rules, and separate accounts isolate environments. On top sit WAF at the edge, IAM least privilege, KMS encryption, and GuardDuty and CloudTrail for detection.

probes.q: Security group vs network ACL?
probes.a: Security groups attach to resources, only allow, and are stateful, so return traffic is automatic. Network ACLs attach to subnets, allow and deny, and are stateless.

probes.q: Why use separate AWS accounts?
probes.a: An account is the strongest isolation boundary, which limits blast radius between prod, dev, and teams.

questions.aws: VPC subnets, security groups, network ACLs, AWS WAF, AWS Network Firewall, and a multi-account setup with AWS Organizations.
questions.resume: At Oracle, I built a CLI toolchain on Jenkins with scripted pre-deployment validation that 4 teams adopted. It was a reliability gate, but it is the same layered idea: a check that stops a bad change before it reaches production, and it brought failed deploys from 11% to 4%.
questions.trap: Stacking many copies of the same control and calling it depth. Layers should fail independently, such as network plus identity plus encryption.

questions.q: What is SQL injection and how do you prevent it?
questions.plain: Imagine a form that says write your name, and someone writes: my name is Bob, and also give me everyone's bank details. If the clerk reads the whole line as instructions, they just obeyed the attacker. Injection is data being mistaken for commands.
questions.technical: Injection happens when untrusted input is concatenated into something an interpreter executes, such as a SQL query, OS command, or LDAP filter. With SQL, input like a quote followed by OR 1=1 can change a query's logic to dump or alter data.
