The fix is to keep code and data separate: parameterized queries or prepared statements, so input is always treated as a value. Add allow-list validation, least-privilege database accounts so a successful injection can do less, and safe ORM use without raw string building. A WAF with SQL injection rules is a useful extra layer, not the fix.

probes.q: Does escaping quotes solve it?
probes.a: Not reliably. Escaping is easy to get wrong across encodings. Parameterized queries are the real fix.

probes.q: Is there an AI version of this?
probes.a: Prompt injection is similar: instructions hidden in untrusted text override the system's intent. Treat model input as untrusted and limit what tools the model can call.

questions.aws: AWS WAF managed rule groups include SQL injection protections; Amazon RDS IAM authentication and least-privilege database users limit damage.
questions.trap: Relying on a WAF or input blocklists instead of parameterized queries. Filters get bypassed; separating code from data does not.

questions.q: Explain XSS and CSRF, and how they differ.
questions.plain: XSS is someone slipping a fake instruction card into your restaurant's menu, so every diner who reads it follows the attacker's instructions. CSRF is someone tricking a regular customer into signing an order slip they did not read, and the kitchen trusts it because the customer's signature is real.
questions.technical: Cross-site scripting injects attacker script into a page that other users load, so it runs with the site's privileges in their browser and can steal data or act as them. In the 2021 OWASP Top 10, XSS is grouped under Injection. Defenses: context-aware output encoding, avoid writing raw HTML, a Content Security Policy, and HttpOnly cookies. Cross-site request forgery makes a logged-in user's browser send an unwanted request to a site that trusts its cookies, such as a transfer form auto-submitted from another site. Defenses: anti-CSRF tokens, SameSite cookies, and checking the Origin header. XSS abuses the user's trust in the site; CSRF abuses the site's trust in the user's browser.

probes.q: Does XSS defeat CSRF tokens?
probes.a: Yes. Script running on the real site can read the token, which is why XSS is usually more severe.

probes.q: Are APIs using bearer tokens in headers exposed to CSRF?
probes.a: Much less, because the browser does not attach those headers automatically the way it attaches cookies.

questions.aws: AWS WAF managed rules cover common XSS patterns at CloudFront, ALB, or API Gateway; the application still needs encoding and CSRF tokens.
questions.trap: Mixing them up, or thinking HTTPS prevents either one. Both work perfectly over an encrypted connection.

questions.q: What is broken access control, and why is it so common?
questions.plain: It is a hotel where your key card opens your room, but if you change the room number on the door sign, the door opens anyway. The lock checks that you have a card, not that it is your room.
questions.technical: Broken access control means users can act outside their intended permissions. It topped the 2021 OWASP Top 10. Classic forms: insecure direct object references, such as changing an ID in the URL to read another customer's invoice; missing checks on admin endpoints that rely on a hidden button; privilege escalation by editing a role field; and overly permissive CORS. It is common because authentication is centralized, but authorization logic is scattered across every endpoint and easy to forget. Fixes: deny by default, enforce checks server side on every request using the authenticated identity, check object ownership, centralize policy in middleware, and test authorization explicitly.

probes.q: Is hiding the admin button enough?
probes.a: No. Attackers call the API directly. The server must enforce every permission.

probes.q: What is the cloud equivalent?
probes.a: Overly broad IAM policies or a bucket policy that grants access to everyone. IAM Access Analyzer flags resources shared outside your account or organization.

questions.aws: Amazon Verified Permissions provides a managed policy engine (using the Cedar language) for fine-grained app authorization; IAM Access Analyzer covers AWS resources.
questions.trap: Assuming a logged-in user can only reach what the UI shows them. Authorization must be checked per object, on the server.

questions.q: How would you protect a public website on AWS from DDoS and web attacks?
questions.plain: A DDoS attack is thousands of fake shoppers crowding the store entrance so real customers cannot get in. You put a huge, staffed lobby in front (CloudFront and Shield) that absorbs the crowd, plus a bouncer (WAF) who checks each person against a list of known troublemakers.
questions.technical: A distributed denial of service attack floods a target from many sources to exhaust bandwidth, connections, or application capacity. Layered approach: serve through Amazon CloudFront and Route 53, which run on the large AWS edge network. AWS Shield Standard applies automatically at no extra charge against common network and transport layer attacks such as SYN floods. AWS WAF on CloudFront, an Application Load Balancer, or API Gateway filters layer 7 requests with managed rule groups, rate-based rules, and bot control. Shield Advanced is a paid tier adding enhanced detection, layer 7 mitigation with WAF, access to the Shield Response Team, and cost protection for scaling charges during an attack. Autoscaling absorbs what remains.

probes.q: When is Shield Advanced worth it?
probes.a: For business-critical, internet-facing apps where downtime is costly and you want expert response help and protection from attack-driven scaling bills.

probes.q: What is a rate-based rule?
probes.a: A WAF rule that blocks or challenges a source IP or key once its request rate goes over a threshold.

probes.q: Does a security group stop a DDoS?
probes.a: It drops unwanted traffic at the resource, but a large flood can still saturate capacity, so absorb it at the edge first.

questions.aws: CloudFront, Route 53, AWS Shield Standard and Advanced, AWS WAF, and Auto Scaling together form the AWS DDoS resiliency pattern.
questions.trap: Thinking you must buy Shield to have any DDoS protection. Shield Standard is on by default; Advanced adds more.

questions.q: How do you know who did what in an AWS account?
questions.plain: CloudTrail is the security camera footage for your account. It records who walked in, which door they opened, and when. When something goes wrong, you rewind the tape.
questions.technical: AWS CloudTrail records API activity: who called which action, from where, when, and whether it succeeded. Event history shows the last 90 days of management events at no extra charge. For long-term audit, create an organization trail that delivers logs to a central S3 bucket in a separate log archive account, with log file integrity validation so tampering is detectable. Data events, such as S3 object reads or Lambda invokes, are optional and extra cost. Pair it with CloudWatch Logs for application logs and alarms on sensitive events, such as root user sign-in or a trail being stopped. Good audit logging is centralized, immutable, and actually reviewed.

probes.q: How do you stop an attacker from deleting the evidence?
probes.a: Send logs to a separate, locked-down account, use S3 Object Lock or tight bucket policies, and enable integrity validation.

probes.q: CloudTrail vs CloudWatch?
probes.a: CloudTrail records API calls for audit. CloudWatch collects metrics and logs and raises alarms on them.

questions.aws: AWS CloudTrail organization trails, CloudTrail Lake for SQL queries over events, and Amazon CloudWatch alarms.
questions.trap: Assuming logs exist because the service exists. Only 90 days of management events are kept by default; long-term and data-event logging must be set up.

questions.q: How do AWS Config and AWS Security Hub help keep an environment compliant?
questions.plain: Config is a building inspector who photographs every room each time something changes and checks it against the fire code. Security Hub is the front desk dashboard where every inspector and alarm in the building reports, so you see the worst problems first.
questions.technical: AWS Config records the configuration of resources over time and evaluates them with Config rules, for example S3 buckets must block public access or EBS volumes must be encrypted. It can trigger automatic remediation through Systems Manager Automation, and conformance packs bundle rules. AWS Security Hub, whose posture management feature is now called Security Hub CSPM, runs continuous checks against standards such as AWS Foundational Security Best Practices, CIS, PCI DSS, and NIST, and it aggregates findings from GuardDuty, Amazon Inspector, Macie, and partners in a standard format. Most of its checks use service-linked Config rules, so Config must be recording. EventBridge can route findings to tickets or auto-remediation.

probes.q: Config vs CloudTrail?
probes.a: Config shows what a resource looked like and whether it is compliant. CloudTrail shows who made the API call that changed it.

probes.q: Detect or prevent?
probes.a: Config and Security Hub detect and can remediate after the fact. SCPs and IAM prevent. You want both.

questions.aws: AWS Config rules and conformance packs, AWS Security Hub CSPM standards, and EventBridge for automated response.
questions.trap: Turning on Security Hub without AWS Config recording and wondering why controls show no data.

questions.q: What does Amazon GuardDuty do?
questions.plain: GuardDuty is a burglar alarm company watching your building's cameras around the clock. It knows what break-ins look like, so it calls you when a door opens at 3 a.m. from a known thief's address.
questions.technical: GuardDuty is a managed threat detection service. Once enabled, it analyzes foundational data sources automatically: CloudTrail management events, VPC Flow Logs, and Route 53 Resolver DNS query logs. You do not have to enable those logs yourself, since it reads independent streams of them. It uses threat intelligence and machine learning to flag things like credential use from unusual locations, instances talking to known command-and-control servers, or crypto-mining DNS lookups. Optional protection plans extend it to S3 data events, EKS, runtime monitoring, malware scanning, RDS logins, and Lambda network activity. It detects and reports findings; response comes through EventBridge, Lambda, or Security Hub.

probes.q: Does GuardDuty block attacks?
probes.a: No. It produces findings. You wire automated responses, such as isolating an instance, through EventBridge.

probes.q: GuardDuty vs Macie?
probes.a: GuardDuty looks for malicious activity across the account. Macie looks for sensitive data and access risk in S3.

questions.aws: Enable GuardDuty in every Region and across the organization with a delegated administrator account, since attackers favor Regions you do not watch.
questions.trap: Thinking you must first turn on VPC Flow Logs or a CloudTrail trail for GuardDuty to work. It consumes its own copies of the foundational sources.

questions.q: What is Amazon Macie for?
questions.plain: Macie is an auditor that walks through your storage rooms, opens a sample of the boxes, and tells you which ones contain Social Security numbers or credit cards, and which rooms were left unlocked.
questions.technical: Amazon Macie is a data security service for Amazon S3. It uses machine learning and pattern matching to discover sensitive data such as personally identifiable information, financial data, and credentials. It keeps an inventory of S3 general purpose buckets and evaluates them for security and access control, raising policy findings when a bucket becomes public, is shared, or is unencrypted. Automated sensitive data discovery samples objects continuously for broad visibility, while discovery jobs give targeted, deeper scans. Custom data identifiers, regular expressions you define, catch company-specific data. Findings go to EventBridge and Security Hub for response.

probes.q: Why does a company need it?
probes.a: You cannot protect or delete sensitive data you do not know you have, and regulations like privacy laws require knowing where it lives.

probes.q: Does it scan databases?
probes.a: Macie focuses on S3. Other stores need other tools or exports to S3.

questions.aws: Macie findings feed Security Hub CSPM; pair with S3 Block Public Access and KMS encryption to fix what it finds.
questions.trap: Confusing Macie with GuardDuty. Macie is about what data you have and who can reach it; GuardDuty is about attacker behavior.

questions.q: Explain IAM users, groups, roles, and policies.
questions.plain: A user is a named employee badge. A group is a department, so you give badges to the whole department at once. A role is a visitor pass that anyone approved can borrow for a few hours. Policies are the written rules that say which doors a badge or pass opens.
questions.technical: An IAM user is a long-term identity with its own credentials, now mostly reserved for edge cases, since people should sign in through IAM Identity Center or federation. A group is a collection of users for attaching policies; groups are not principals and cannot be nested. A role has no long-term credentials: a trusted principal, such as an EC2 instance, a Lambda function, another account, or a federated user, assumes it through AWS STS and gets temporary credentials. Policies are JSON documents with Effect, Action, Resource, and optional Condition. Identity-based policies attach to users, groups, and roles; resource-based policies, like S3 bucket policies, attach to resources and name a principal.

probes.q: Why roles over access keys for an app on EC2?
probes.a: The role delivers short-lived credentials that rotate automatically, so there is no long-lived key to leak.

probes.q: What is a trust policy?
probes.a: The resource policy on a role that says who is allowed to assume it.

questions.aws: AWS IAM with AWS STS for temporary credentials and IAM Identity Center for people.
questions.trap: Creating IAM users with access keys for applications. Use roles, and lock the root user away with MFA.

questions.q: How does AWS decide whether a request is allowed when several policies apply?
questions.plain: Think of a strict club. By default, nobody gets in. You need at least one written invitation. But if any bouncer has your name on a do-not-admit list, you are out, no matter how many invitations you hold.
questions.technical: Every request starts as an implicit deny. AWS gathers all applicable policies: identity-based, resource-based, permissions boundaries, session policies, and Organizations SCPs and RCPs. An explicit deny in any of them ends evaluation with deny. Otherwise, the guardrail types must all allow: SCPs, RCPs, boundaries, and session policies act as filters, so effective permissions are the intersection. Within one account, an allow in either the identity policy or the resource policy is enough, since those two combine as a union. Across accounts, both sides must allow: the caller's identity policy and the target's resource policy. If nothing explicitly allows the action, the implicit deny stands.

probes.q: A user has AdministratorAccess but cannot delete a bucket. Why?
probes.a: Likely an explicit deny somewhere: an SCP, a permissions boundary, or the bucket policy. An explicit deny beats any allow.

probes.q: How do you debug it?
probes.a: Use the IAM policy simulator and check the access denied message, which often names the policy type that denied it.

probes.q: What is a permissions boundary?
probes.a: A managed policy that sets the maximum permissions an identity-based policy can give a user or role. It does not grant anything itself.

questions.aws: Policy evaluation logic in AWS IAM, with SCPs and RCPs from AWS Organizations as account-wide filters.
questions.trap: Thinking the most specific or the most recent policy wins. Order does not matter; explicit deny always wins, then an allow is required.

questions.q: What do service control policies do in AWS Organizations?
questions.plain: An SCP is a company-wide rule from head office, like no branch may open an office outside the US. It does not hire anyone or hand out keys. It only sets the outer limit, and each branch manager still decides who gets which keys inside it.
questions.technical: SCPs are organization policies attached to the root, organizational units, or accounts. They set the maximum available permissions for IAM users and roles in member accounts, including the member account root user. They never grant permissions: a user still needs an identity or resource policy that allows the action, and the effective permission is the intersection. An account only gets what every SCP above it allows. Important exceptions: SCPs do not affect the management account, and they do not restrict service-linked roles. Typical uses: deny leaving the organization, restrict allowed Regions, protect CloudTrail and GuardDuty from being disabled, and require encryption. Test on a small OU before the root.

probes.q: Why keep workloads out of the management account?
probes.a: SCPs cannot restrict it, so it should hold as little as possible and be tightly controlled.

probes.q: SCP vs RCP?
probes.a: SCPs cap what your principals can do. Resource control policies cap what can be done to your resources, including by principals outside your organization.

probes.q: Allow list or deny list strategy?
probes.a: Deny lists, keeping FullAWSAccess and adding targeted denies, are easier to maintain. Allow lists are stricter but need updates as services are adopted.

questions.aws: AWS Organizations with AWS Control Tower, which applies SCP-based preventive controls as part of a landing zone.
questions.trap: Saying an SCP gives an account access to a service. SCPs only filter; without an IAM allow, nothing is permitted.

questions.q: In Amazon Cognito, what is the difference between a user pool and an identity pool?
questions.plain: The user pool is the front desk that checks your ID and gives you a visitor badge. The identity pool is the coat check that swaps that badge for a ticket to a specific locker, which here means a temporary key to specific AWS resources.
questions.technical: A user pool answers who is this user. It is a user directory and OIDC identity provider that handles sign-up, sign-in, MFA, and federation with social and enterprise providers through SAML or OIDC, and it issues JWT ID, access, and refresh tokens to your app or API. An identity pool answers which AWS resources may this user reach. It exchanges a trusted token, from a user pool, a social provider, or a SAML or OIDC provider, for temporary, limited-privilege AWS credentials from STS, mapped to IAM roles by rules or by attributes for access control. It can also give guest users limited credentials. Neither requires the other; use both when users sign in and the app calls AWS services such as S3 directly.

probes.q: My app only calls my own API behind API Gateway. Do I need an identity pool?
probes.a: No. A user pool and an API Gateway authorizer that validates its tokens is enough.

probes.q: How do you stop one user reading another user's S3 files?
probes.a: Identity pool roles with policies scoped by the user's identity ID or principal tags in the resource path.

questions.aws: Cognito user pools for customer identity; identity pools for direct, scoped AWS access from web and mobile apps.
questions.trap: Thinking identity pools store users or passwords. They broker AWS credentials; the user directory is the user pool or an external provider.

questions.q: Walk me through how you would respond to a security incident, for example leaked AWS access keys.
questions.plain: It is like a kitchen fire. First you stop it spreading, then you put it out, then you clean up and figure out why it started so it does not happen again, and you keep notes the whole time for the insurance company.
questions.technical: Follow a standard lifecycle: prepare, detect and analyze, contain, eradicate, recover, and learn. For leaked keys: detect through GuardDuty, a scanner, or an AWS notice. Contain by deactivating the key, and for a role, revoke active sessions. Analyze with CloudTrail: what did the key call, from where, which resources were created or read. Eradicate by deleting the key, removing any backdoor users, roles, or policies, and terminating rogue resources such as crypto-mining instances. Recover from known-good state and rotate related secrets. Then run a blameless review and add a preventive control, such as roles instead of keys or secret scanning in CI. Preparation, with runbooks and pre-approved access, makes the rest fast.

probes.q: Why not delete the compromised instance immediately?
probes.a: You may destroy evidence. Isolate it with a restrictive security group and snapshot its disks first.

probes.q: What makes detection fast?
probes.a: Centralized logs, GuardDuty findings routed through EventBridge to on-call, and alerts tied to runbooks.

questions.aws: GuardDuty and Security Hub for detection, CloudTrail and Amazon Detective for investigation, EventBridge and Lambda or Systems Manager for automated containment.
questions.resume: My closest experience is operational incidents rather than security breaches. At Oracle, I built real-time API diagnostics across 1M+ endpoints that auto-tagged root causes on 400 and 500 series failures with runbook context, which cut P1 MTTR from 94 to 26 minutes. The lesson carries over: tag and route the signal with its runbook, and response gets much faster.
questions.trap: Jumping straight to cleanup. Contain first, preserve evidence, and scope the blast radius with logs before declaring it fixed.

questions.q: A customer wants an AI agent to approve financial transactions automatically. What security controls would you put around it?
questions.plain: Treat the AI like a new junior accountant. It can handle routine, clear-cut items on its own, but anything unusual or high value goes to a senior person to sign off, it only gets the keys it needs, and every decision is written in the ledger.
questions.technical: Treat the agent as an untrusted, privileged workload. Give it a narrow IAM role and tools that expose only the actions it needs, with hard limits such as maximum amounts enforced in code, not in the prompt. Route by risk: auto-approve only above a confidence threshold and within policy, and send exceptions to human reviewers. Treat all model input, including documents it reads, as untrusted, since prompt injection can hide instructions in data. Validate model output against a schema before acting. Log every input, decision, tool call, and approver for audit, and monitor approval rates for drift. Keep secrets in a secrets manager and data encrypted with KMS.

probes.q: Why not just tell the model in the prompt never to approve large amounts?
probes.a: Prompts are not a security boundary. Enforce limits in the tool or API the model calls.

probes.q: How do you pick the confidence threshold?
probes.a: Measure error rates against human decisions on historical cases, then set the threshold where the remaining risk is acceptable and adjust from monitoring.

questions.aws: Amazon Bedrock Guardrails for content and prompt-attack filtering, scoped IAM roles for agent tools, Step Functions for human approval steps, and CloudTrail plus CloudWatch for audit.
questions.resume: At MSRcosmos, I built human-in-the-loop review over Sage REST APIs and MCP tool calling for an ERP migration. 83% of records were auto-approved above a confidence threshold and the rest went to people, which took turnaround from 3 days to 5.5 hours for 12 client entities while keeping a person on every uncertain financial record.
questions.trap: Relying on the model to police itself. Controls must live outside the model: permissions, hard limits, validation, and human review.

domains.name: CS fundamentals and coding concepts
domains.summary: How code and computers work under the hood, explained out loud: complexity, data structures, algorithms, design, concurrency, operating systems, distributed systems, and engineering practice, so an SA can reason about a customer's performance and reliability problems and explain the fix simply.

sources.label: Python wiki: TimeComplexity of built-in types
Python docs: function definitions (defaults evaluated once)
AWS SDKs and Tools: retry behavior
Amazon Builders' Library: timeouts, retries, and backoff with jitter

cheatsheet.def: How time or memory grows with input size, ignoring constants: O(1), O(log n), O(n), O(n log n), O(n^2).
cheatsheet.probe: State time and space separately, and remember Big-O ignores constant factors that still matter in practice.

cheatsheet.def: Average cost per operation over any sequence, such as O(1) list appends despite occasional O(n) resizes.
cheatsheet.probe: Amortized is not average case: it is a worst-case guarantee over a whole sequence.

cheatsheet.def: Key to hash to bucket index, then compare keys; O(1) average for get, put, and delete.
cheatsheet.probe: Worst case is O(n) on heavy collisions; resizing keeps the load factor low.

cheatsheet.def: Tree in an array where the parent beats its children; peek O(1), push and pop O(log n), build O(n).
cheatsheet.probe: Only the root is ordered; top k in O(n log k) with a size-k heap.

cheatsheet.def: Ordered tree giving O(log n) search, insert, and delete plus sorted and range queries.
cheatsheet.probe: An unbalanced BST on sorted input degrades to O(n); databases use shallow B-trees.

cheatsheet.def: BFS goes level by level with a queue; DFS goes deep with a stack. Both O(V + E).
cheatsheet.probe: BFS gives shortest paths only on unweighted graphs; weighted needs Dijkstra.

cheatsheet.def: DP reuses answers to overlapping subproblems; greedy commits to the best local choice.
cheatsheet.probe: Greedy fails on coins 1, 3, 4 for amount 6; DP handles it.

cheatsheet.def: Quicksort: O(n log n) average, O(n^2) worst, in place. Merge sort: O(n log n) always, stable, O(n) extra.
cheatsheet.probe: Name quicksort's worst case and how random pivots or introsort avoid it.

cheatsheet.def: Single responsibility, open-closed, Liskov substitution, interface segregation, dependency inversion.
cheatsheet.probe: Have one concrete example per letter, such as Square versus Rectangle for Liskov.

cheatsheet.def: Outcome depends on thread timing around shared state, such as count += 1.
cheatsheet.probe: The GIL does not make read-modify-write atomic; use a lock or avoid shared state.

cheatsheet.def: Needs all four: mutual exclusion, hold and wait, no preemption, circular wait.
cheatsheet.probe: Break one; a global lock order removes circular wait.

cheatsheet.def: Stack: per-thread call frames, fast, auto-freed. Heap: dynamic objects, freed manually or by GC.
cheatsheet.probe: GC languages still leak through reachable but unused objects.

cheatsheet.def: Per-process address spaces mapped to physical pages through page tables and the TLB.
cheatsheet.probe: It is about translation and isolation, not just swap; thrashing when the working set exceeds RAM.

cheatsheet.def: During a partition choose consistency or availability; models range from linearizable to eventual.
cheatsheet.probe: Partition tolerance is not optional; 'pick two' is the wrong framing.

cheatsheet.def: Retry only idempotent ops on transient errors, with timeouts, capped exponential backoff, and jitter.
cheatsheet.probe: Without jitter clients retry in lockstep; without idempotency a retry can double-charge.

questions.q: What is Big-O notation? Explain time and space complexity with examples.
questions.plain: Big-O describes how the work grows as the job gets bigger, not how long it takes today. Finding a word in a dictionary by jumping to the right section stays quick even if the dictionary doubles in size; reading every page to find it takes twice as long. Space complexity is the same idea for how much desk space you need while you work.
questions.technical: Big-O is an upper bound on how running time or memory grows with input size n, ignoring constants and lower-order terms. Common classes: O(1) for a dict lookup, O(log n) for binary search, O(n) for one scan, O(n log n) for merge sort, O(n^2) for comparing every pair, O(2^n) for trying every subset. Space complexity counts extra memory beyond the input: reversing a list in place is O(1) extra space, building a set of seen items is O(n). I state both, because the usual trade is spending memory to save time, like a hash set turning an O(n^2) pair search into O(n).

probes.q: Does O(n) always beat O(n^2)?
probes.a: Only for large enough n. Big-O drops constants, so on tiny inputs a simple O(n^2) loop can beat an O(n) approach with heavy overhead. Measure when it matters.

probes.q: What is the complexity of two nested loops over two different lists?
probes.a: O(n times m), not O(n^2), unless the lists are the same size. Name each input separately.

probes.q: Big-O versus Big-Theta?
probes.a: Big-O is an upper bound; Big-Theta is a tight bound from above and below. In interviews people say Big-O but usually mean the tight bound.

questions.aws: A DynamoDB Scan reads every item in the table, so its cost grows with table size, while a Query on the partition key goes straight to the matching items. It is the same O(n) scan versus keyed lookup idea.
questions.resume: At USC Sports Analytics I cut DQN training time from 52 to 31 minutes by vectorizing replay-buffer sampling and removing a data-loader stall. That was a constant-factor win found by profiling, a good reminder that Big-O starts a performance conversation but does not finish it.
questions.trap: Saying Big-O measures speed in seconds. It measures growth rate. Two O(n) programs can differ 100x in real time, and constants matter in practice even though Big-O ignores them.

questions.q: What is the difference between best, average, and worst case? Give an example where they differ.
questions.plain: It is your commute with green lights all the way, on a normal day, and on the day there is a crash on the highway. Same route, very different times. When delays are costly, engineers plan around the bad day.
questions.technical: Best, average, and worst case describe the same algorithm on different inputs of the same size. Quicksort is the classic example: best and average O(n log n), worst O(n^2) when pivots keep splitting badly, for instance always picking the first element of already-sorted data. Hash table lookups are O(1) on average but O(n) in the worst case if many keys collide. Linear search is O(1) if the target is first and O(n) if it is last or missing. For latency-sensitive systems I care about worst case and tail latency, not just the average, because the slow case is what a customer remembers.

probes.q: How does quicksort avoid its worst case in practice?
probes.a: Random or median-of-three pivots, and many libraries switch to heapsort if recursion gets too deep (introsort), which caps the worst case at O(n log n).

probes.q: Is worst case the same thing as Big-O?
probes.a: No. Big-O is a kind of bound; you can give a Big-O for the best, average, or worst case. They get mixed up because worst case is the one usually quoted.

probes.q: How does p99 latency relate to this?
probes.a: p99 is the operational cousin of worst case: the slowest 1% of requests. Averages hide it.

questions.trap: Saying quicksort is O(n log n), full stop. Its average is O(n log n) but its worst case is O(n^2). Merge sort is the one that guarantees O(n log n) on every input.

questions.q: What does amortized cost mean? Use a dynamic array as the example.
questions.plain: Think of a gym membership: one big payment up front, then each visit is free. Averaged over the year, each visit is cheap even though one day was expensive. Amortized cost is that per-operation average over a long run of operations.
questions.technical: Amortized analysis averages the cost over a sequence of operations, and the guarantee holds for any sequence, not just typical inputs. A Python list or Java ArrayList appends in O(1) amortized time. Usually an append writes into spare capacity; when the array is full it allocates a bigger block and copies everything, which is O(n). Because capacity grows by a multiple rather than a fixed amount, those copies are rare enough that n appends cost O(n) in total, so O(1) each on average. The catch: one individual append can still take O(n), which matters when you have a hard latency limit.

probes.q: Is amortized the same as average case?
probes.a: No. Average case averages over likely inputs and a bad input can beat it. Amortized is a worst-case guarantee over a whole sequence of operations.

probes.q: Why must the array grow by a multiple instead of a fixed amount?
probes.a: Growing by a fixed 10 slots means a full copy every 10 appends, which totals O(n^2) for n appends. Doubling, or any fixed percentage, keeps the total linear.

probes.q: Another example of amortized cost?
probes.a: A hash table that resizes when its load factor gets high: inserts are O(1) amortized even though each resize rehashes every key.

questions.trap: Claiming every append is O(1). Each one is O(1) amortized; the append that triggers a resize is O(n).

questions.q: Array versus linked list: how do they differ, and when would you use each?
questions.plain: An array is a row of numbered lockers: you can walk straight to locker 500, but squeezing a new locker into the middle means shifting all the others down. A linked list is a scavenger hunt where each clue points to the next: easy to slip in a new clue, but to reach the 500th clue you have to follow the first 499.
questions.technical: An array stores elements next to each other in memory, so access by index is O(1) and it is very cache friendly, but inserting or deleting in the middle is O(n) because elements shift. Appending to a dynamic array is O(1) amortized. A linked list stores nodes connected by pointers: access by position is O(n), but insert or delete is O(1) once you already hold the neighboring node. Linked lists cost extra memory per node and scatter across memory, so in practice arrays win most of the time. Linked lists earn their place in queues, in LRU caches paired with a hash map, and wherever you splice often.

probes.q: Why are arrays often faster even when Big-O says it is a tie?
probes.a: Contiguous memory lets the CPU cache prefetch neighbors. Chasing pointers through a linked list causes cache misses, a big constant-factor cost.

probes.q: Is inserting into a linked list really O(1)?
probes.a: Only if you already have the node. Finding the position first is O(n).

probes.q: What does Python's list use underneath?
probes.a: A dynamic array of references, so indexing is O(1) and inserting at the front is O(n). For fast operations at both ends, use collections.deque.

questions.trap: Saying linked lists are faster for inserts in general. They are O(1) only once you are at the right spot; getting there is O(n), and cache misses often make them slower than arrays in real code.

questions.q: How does a hash map work, and what happens on a collision?
questions.plain: A hash map is a coat check. You hand over your coat, the attendant applies a fixed rule that says hook 42, and gives you a ticket. When you come back, the same rule takes them straight to hook 42 instead of searching the whole room. If two coats end up on the same hook, they hang both there and check the tags.
questions.technical: A hash map runs the key through a hash function, turns the hash into a bucket index, for example hash mod table size, and stores the key and value there. A lookup repeats those steps and then compares the stored key for equality, so lookup, insert, and delete are O(1) on average. A collision is two keys landing in the same bucket. Chaining keeps a small list per bucket; open addressing probes for another free slot, which is what CPython's dict does. When the table gets too full, it resizes and rehashes, keeping collisions rare. The worst case is O(n) if everything collides.

probes.q: What makes a good hash function?
probes.a: It is deterministic, fast, and spreads keys evenly across buckets. Equal keys must always produce equal hashes.

probes.q: Why can't you use a Python list as a dict key?
probes.a: Lists are mutable. If a key changed after insertion, its hash would change and you could never find it again, so Python requires hashable keys such as strings, numbers, or tuples of those.

probes.q: What is a hash flooding attack?
probes.a: An attacker sends many keys that collide on purpose, turning O(1) lookups into O(n). Randomized string hashing, which Python uses by default, defends against it.

questions.aws: DynamoDB uses the same idea at scale: it hashes the partition key to decide which partition stores an item, which is why a partition key with many distinct, evenly used values avoids hot partitions.
questions.trap: Saying hash maps are always O(1). They are O(1) on average with a good hash function and resizing; worst case is O(n). Also, they do not keep keys sorted: Python dicts preserve insertion order, which is not the same as sorted order.

questions.q: What is the difference between a stack and a queue? Where would you use each?
questions.plain: A stack is a pile of plates: the last plate you put on top is the first one you take off. A queue is the line at a coffee shop: first come, first served.
questions.technical: A stack is last in, first out: push and pop happen at the top, both O(1). It powers function call frames, undo history, expression parsing, and depth-first search. A queue is first in, first out: enqueue at the back, dequeue at the front, both O(1) with a linked list, a ring buffer, or Python's collections.deque. Queues power breadth-first search, task scheduling, and buffering between a fast producer and a slow consumer. In Python, a list makes a fine stack but a poor queue, because list.pop(0) shifts every element and costs O(n).

probes.q: How do you build a queue from two stacks?
probes.a: Push onto an inbox stack. To dequeue, if the outbox is empty, pop everything from the inbox onto the outbox, then pop the outbox. Each element moves at most twice, so it is O(1) amortized.

probes.q: What is a priority queue?
probes.a: A queue where the most important item comes out first instead of the oldest. It is usually built on a heap.

probes.q: Why put a queue between two services?
probes.a: It decouples them. The producer keeps working even if the consumer is slow or briefly down, and the consumer drains the backlog at its own pace.

questions.aws: Amazon SQS is a managed queue between services. Standard queues deliver at least once with best-effort ordering; FIFO queues preserve order and deduplicate, which matters when order is part of correctness.
questions.trap: Using a Python list as a queue with pop(0). It works, but it shifts every element, O(n) per dequeue. Use collections.deque and popleft().

questions.q: What is a heap, and when would you use one?
questions.plain: A heap is like an emergency room triage desk. It does not keep every patient in perfect order; it just always knows who is most urgent right now, and it can update that quickly when someone new walks in.
questions.technical: A binary heap is a complete binary tree, usually stored in an array, where every parent is smaller than its children in a min-heap, or larger in a max-heap. Peeking at the top is O(1), insert and pop are O(log n) because an element bubbles up or down one level at a time, and building a heap from n items is O(n). It is the standard way to implement a priority queue. Uses include task schedulers, Dijkstra's shortest path, merging k sorted lists, and finding the top k items in O(n log k) with a heap of size k. Python's heapq module is a min-heap on a plain list.

probes.q: How do you get a max-heap from Python's heapq?
probes.a: Push negated values, or tuples with a negated priority, since heapq works as a min-heap.

probes.q: Heap or sorting for the top k items?
probes.a: Sorting is O(n log n). A min-heap of size k scans once in O(n log k) with O(k) memory, which wins when k is much smaller than n or the data is streaming.

probes.q: Is a heap the same as heap memory?
probes.a: No, it is an unlucky name clash. The heap data structure is a priority queue; heap memory is the region where dynamically allocated objects live.

questions.trap: Thinking a heap is sorted. Only the root is guaranteed to be the minimum or maximum; siblings have no order, and searching a heap for an arbitrary value is O(n).

questions.q: What is a binary search tree, and why does balance matter?
questions.plain: A binary search tree plays 'higher or lower'. At each step you go left for smaller and right for bigger, so you throw away about half of what is left. If the tree gets lopsided, it turns into one long line and you are back to checking items one at a time.
questions.technical: A tree is a hierarchy of nodes with one root and no cycles. A binary search tree adds an ordering rule: everything in a node's left subtree is smaller and everything in its right subtree is larger. Search, insert, and delete cost O(height). When the tree is balanced, height is about log n, so operations are O(log n). Insert already-sorted data into a plain BST and it degenerates into a linked list with O(n) operations. Self-balancing trees such as AVL and red-black trees rotate nodes to keep height O(log n). An in-order walk returns keys in sorted order, which a hash map cannot do. Databases use B-trees, which are wide and shallow, to minimize disk reads.

probes.q: BST or hash map?
probes.a: Hash map: O(1) average lookups but no order. Balanced BST: O(log n), plus sorted iteration, range queries, and finding the next larger key.

probes.q: Why do databases use B-trees instead of binary trees?
probes.a: Each B-tree node holds many keys and matches a disk or memory page, so the tree is only a few levels deep and a lookup reads very few pages.

probes.q: Where are red-black trees used?
probes.a: In ordered maps such as Java's TreeMap and C++ std::map, which guarantee O(log n) operations.

questions.aws: Amazon RDS and Amazon Aurora run engines such as PostgreSQL and MySQL that use B-tree indexes by default, so the same reasoning applies when a customer's query is slow: check whether it can descend an index or is scanning the table.
questions.resume: At Oracle I cut NetSuite search P50 page load by 30%, from 840 to 588 ms, by profiling query plans, restructuring indexes on hot predicates, and rewriting SQL that drove full scans. An index is a tree the database can descend in a few steps instead of reading every row.
questions.trap: Saying a BST is always O(log n). Only a balanced one is. A plain BST fed sorted input becomes a linked list with O(n) operations.

questions.q: What is a trie, and what is it good for?
questions.plain: A trie is how phone autocomplete thinks. Words that start the same share the same path: 'car', 'cart', and 'care' all walk through c, a, r. Type a few letters and you are already standing at every word that begins with them.
questions.technical: A trie, or prefix tree, stores strings one character per level: each edge is a character, and a flag marks where a complete word ends. Insert and lookup take O(L), where L is the length of the word, no matter how many words are stored. Its strength is prefix queries: finding every word that starts with 'pre' means walking three edges and collecting that subtree. Uses include autocomplete, spell checking, IP routing by longest prefix match, and word games. The cost is memory, since each node holds links to its children; a compressed trie, or radix tree, merges single-child chains to save space.

probes.q: Trie or hash set for a dictionary of words?
probes.a: A hash set also answers 'is this exact word present' quickly, but it cannot list words by prefix without scanning everything. Pick a trie when prefixes matter.

probes.q: Where do tries show up in networking?
probes.a: Routers do longest prefix match on IP addresses, which fits a binary trie or radix tree naturally.

probes.q: How do you cut a trie's memory use?
probes.a: Use a radix tree that merges single-child chains, or store each node's children in a small dict holding only the characters actually used.

questions.trap: Saying trie lookup is O(log n). It depends on the key length L, not on the number of stored words n.

questions.q: How do you represent a graph, and when would you choose an adjacency list over a matrix?
questions.plain: A graph is a map of relationships: people and friendships, cities and roads. You can keep a giant grid with a box for every possible pair of people, or give each person a contact list of just their friends. For most real networks the contact lists are far smaller.
questions.technical: A graph has vertices and edges, which can be directed or undirected, weighted or not. An adjacency matrix is a V by V grid: O(1) to check whether one edge exists, but O(V^2) memory no matter how few edges there are. An adjacency list stores each vertex's neighbors: O(V + E) memory and fast iteration over neighbors, which is exactly what BFS, DFS, and Dijkstra need. Real-world graphs such as social networks, road maps, and payment networks are sparse, so adjacency lists are the default. A matrix suits small, dense graphs or cases where constant-time edge checks dominate.

probes.q: What is a DAG and why does it matter?
probes.a: A directed acyclic graph has no cycles. Build systems, task schedulers, and data pipelines are DAGs, and a topological sort gives a valid order to run the steps.

probes.q: How do you detect a cycle?
probes.a: In a directed graph, run DFS and look for an edge back to a node still on the current path. In an undirected graph, use union-find, or DFS that ignores the edge back to the parent.

probes.q: When is a graph database worth it?
probes.a: When the questions are about relationships many hops deep, like fraud rings or recommendations, which would take many expensive joins in SQL.

questions.aws: Amazon Neptune is the managed graph database. It supports property-graph queries with Gremlin and openCypher, and RDF graphs with SPARQL.
questions.resume: In my GNN fraud detection project the IEEE-CIS data formed a heterogeneous graph with 726K nodes and 19.5M edges. A dense matrix over 726K nodes is out of the question, so sparse edge-based representations are the only practical choice, and I used neighbor sampling to keep each training step bounded.
questions.trap: Defaulting to an adjacency matrix. For sparse graphs it wastes O(V^2) memory; an adjacency list needs only O(V + E).

questions.q: Explain binary search. What does it require, and what is its complexity?
questions.plain: Binary search is how you find a name in a printed phone book. Open to the middle, see whether the name comes before or after, and ignore the half that cannot contain it. With a million names it takes about 20 flips.
questions.technical: Binary search finds a target in sorted data by comparing against the middle element and discarding half the range each step, so it runs in O(log n) time and O(1) space when written as a loop. Its hard requirement is sorted data with fast random access, such as an array, not a linked list. The classic bugs are off-by-one errors: pick one invariant, for example lo <= hi with an inclusive hi, and always move lo to mid + 1 or hi to mid - 1 so the range shrinks. The idea generalizes to any yes-or-no condition that flips once, like the smallest server size that meets a deadline, or git bisect finding the commit that broke a build.

probes.q: Why does (lo + hi) / 2 matter in some languages?
probes.a: In Java or C++ with fixed-size integers, lo + hi can overflow. lo + (hi - lo) / 2 avoids it. Python integers do not overflow.

probes.q: Can you binary search a linked list?
probes.a: Not efficiently. Reaching the middle costs O(n), so you lose the whole benefit.

probes.q: What is git bisect?
probes.a: Binary search over commit history: mark one good and one bad commit, and git halves the range until it finds the commit that introduced the bug.

questions.trap: Forgetting the data must be sorted, or writing a loop condition that skips the last element. And sorting first just to search once costs O(n log n), more than a single O(n) scan.

questions.q: Compare merge sort and quicksort.
questions.plain: Merge sort splits a deck of cards among friends, each sorts a small pile, and then the piles are merged back together; it always takes about the same time. Quicksort picks one card as a divider and throws smaller cards to one side and bigger cards to the other, then repeats on each side. It is usually faster, but a bad choice of divider over and over makes it crawl.
questions.technical: Both are divide and conquer. Merge sort splits the input in half, sorts each half, and merges them: O(n log n) on every input and stable, but it needs O(n) extra memory for arrays. Quicksort partitions around a pivot and recurses on each side: O(n log n) on average, O(n^2) in the worst case with consistently bad pivots, in place with O(log n) average stack space, and not stable. Quicksort is often faster on arrays because it moves data in a cache-friendly way. Merge sort suits linked lists and external sorting of data too big for memory. Python's built-in sort is Timsort, a stable hybrid of merge sort and insertion sort.

probes.q: What does stable mean?
probes.a: Equal elements keep their original relative order. It matters when you sort by a second key, like sorting orders by date after sorting them by customer.

probes.q: Can a sort beat O(n log n)?
probes.a: Not a comparison sort in general; n log n is the lower bound. Counting sort or radix sort can be linear when keys are small integers or fixed-length strings.

probes.q: How do you sort data that does not fit in memory?
probes.a: External merge sort: sort chunks that fit in memory, write them out as sorted runs, then merge the runs.

questions.trap: Saying quicksort is always O(n log n) or always faster. It averages O(n log n) with an O(n^2) worst case; merge sort guarantees O(n log n) and stability at the cost of extra memory.

questions.q: BFS versus DFS: how do they differ, and when do you use each?
questions.plain: Searching for a lost child in a mall: BFS checks every store near the entrance first, then the next ring of stores, so the closest match turns up first. DFS walks one corridor all the way to the end before backing up and trying the next one.
questions.technical: Breadth-first search explores level by level using a queue. On an unweighted graph it finds the shortest path in number of edges, and its memory grows with the widest level. Depth-first search follows one path as deep as it goes using a stack or recursion, then backtracks. Its memory grows with the depth, and it suits cycle detection, topological sort, connected components, and exhaustive searches such as puzzles. Both run in O(V + E) on an adjacency list, and both need a visited set on graphs with cycles or they loop forever. For shortest paths with weights, use Dijkstra instead.

probes.q: Why can recursive DFS crash?
probes.a: Each level is a stack frame. A very deep graph can exceed the recursion limit, about 1000 frames in CPython by default, so use an explicit stack for deep graphs.

probes.q: Which one finds shortest paths in a weighted graph?
probes.a: Neither. Use Dijkstra's algorithm with a priority queue for non-negative weights, or Bellman-Ford when weights can be negative.

probes.q: How would you compute degrees of separation in a social network?
probes.a: BFS from one person, counting levels; bidirectional BFS from both people cuts the search space dramatically.

questions.trap: Saying DFS finds the shortest path. It finds a path. BFS finds the shortest path, and only on unweighted graphs.

questions.q: What is recursion, and what can go wrong with it?
questions.plain: Recursion is a set of Russian nesting dolls: to get to the middle you open a doll, then the doll inside it, and so on until you reach the tiny solid one that does not open. That tiny doll is the base case. Without it, you would keep reaching forever.
questions.technical: A recursive function solves a problem by calling itself on a smaller version of the same problem. It needs a base case that returns without recursing, and every call must move closer to that base case. Each call adds a stack frame, so recursion uses O(depth) memory. A missing or unreachable base case causes infinite recursion, which Python stops with RecursionError after about 1000 frames by default. Naive recursion can also redo work: plain recursive Fibonacci is exponential, about O(2^n), and memoization fixes it. Python does not optimize tail calls, so deep linear recursion is better written as a loop.

probes.q: When is recursion the natural choice?
probes.a: Tree-shaped problems: walking a file system or a JSON document, divide-and-conquer sorts, and backtracking searches.

probes.q: What is memoization?
probes.a: Caching a function's results by its arguments so repeat calls return instantly. In Python, functools.lru_cache or functools.cache.

probes.q: Is recursion slower than a loop?
probes.a: Often slightly, because of call overhead, and it risks stack overflow. Any recursion can be rewritten with a loop and an explicit stack.

questions.trap: Thinking recursion is free. Each call costs a stack frame, and without a reachable base case the program crashes.

questions.q: What is dynamic programming, and how do you recognize a DP problem?
questions.plain: Dynamic programming means writing down answers you have already worked out so you never redo them. If you just added up a column of ten numbers and someone adds one more, you do not start over; you take your total and add the new number.
questions.technical: DP applies when a problem has overlapping subproblems and optimal substructure, meaning the best answer is built from the best answers to smaller pieces. There are two styles: top-down memoization, which is recursion plus a cache, and bottom-up tabulation, which fills a table from the smallest cases upward. Fibonacci drops from exponential to O(n). Classic problems are coin change, longest common subsequence, edit distance, knapsack, and Bellman-Ford shortest paths. My recipe: define the state, write the recurrence, set the base cases, pick an evaluation order, then shrink memory if each row only needs the previous one. Time is roughly the number of states times the work per state.

probes.q: Memoization or tabulation?
probes.a: Memoization is easier to write and only computes the states you actually need, but it uses recursion depth. Tabulation avoids recursion and makes memory optimizations easier.

probes.q: Where does DP show up in real systems?
probes.a: Diff tools use longest common subsequence, spell checkers use edit distance, and reinforcement learning is built on the Bellman equation, a DP recurrence over states.

probes.q: How do you reduce DP memory?
probes.a: If each row depends only on the previous row, keep two rows instead of the whole table, turning O(n times m) space into O(m).

questions.resume: My DQN agent for NFL fourth-down calls at USC Sports Analytics learns from a Bellman target, which is the dynamic programming recurrence behind reinforcement learning: the value of a decision is its immediate reward plus the discounted value of the best next state.
questions.trap: Calling any recursion with a cache 'DP' without checking that subproblems actually overlap. Merge sort is divide and conquer, not DP, because its halves never repeat.

questions.q: What is a greedy algorithm, and when does greedy fail?
questions.plain: Greedy means always taking the best-looking option right now and never looking back. Making change in US coins, always handing over the biggest coin that fits works perfectly. But with odd coins, say 1, 3, and 4 cents, making 6 cents greedily gives 4 + 1 + 1, three coins, when 3 + 3 needs only two.
questions.technical: A greedy algorithm makes the locally best choice at each step and never revisits it. It is only correct when the problem has the greedy-choice property, usually proven with an exchange argument, plus optimal substructure. Correct examples: interval scheduling by earliest finish time, Huffman coding, Dijkstra with non-negative weights, and Kruskal's and Prim's minimum spanning trees. Greedy fails on coin change with arbitrary denominations and on 0/1 knapsack, where you need DP. Greedy is usually simpler and faster, often a sort plus one scan in O(n log n), so I try it first and then actively hunt for a counterexample.

probes.q: Greedy versus DP in one line?
probes.a: Greedy commits to one choice per step; DP considers every choice for each subproblem and keeps the best.

probes.q: Why does Dijkstra break with negative edges?
probes.a: It greedily finalizes the closest unvisited node, assuming no later path can be cheaper. A negative edge can make a later path cheaper, so you need Bellman-Ford.

probes.q: When is a non-optimal greedy heuristic acceptable?
probes.a: When near-optimal is good enough and speed matters, such as packing jobs onto servers, where exact bin packing is too expensive to solve.

questions.trap: Assuming greedy works because it worked on the example. Always test a counterexample, such as coins 1, 3, and 4 for an amount of 6.

questions.q: Explain the four pillars of object-oriented programming.
questions.plain: Think of a car. Encapsulation: the engine is under the hood and you cannot fiddle with it directly. Abstraction: you just use the pedals and the steering wheel. Inheritance: an electric car is a kind of car and gets the basics for free. Polymorphism: 'press the accelerator' works in any car, and each type responds in its own way.
questions.technical: Encapsulation bundles data with the methods that act on it and hides internal state, so rules are enforced in one place: a BankAccount whose balance changes only through deposit and withdraw. Abstraction exposes what an object does and hides how, through interfaces or abstract base classes. Inheritance lets a subclass reuse and extend a parent's behavior, modeling an is-a relationship. Polymorphism lets code call the same method on different types and get type-specific behavior, like calling area() on any Shape. Together they let you change internals without breaking callers.

probes.q: Encapsulation versus abstraction?
probes.a: Encapsulation hides data and protects its rules. Abstraction presents a simple interface. One is about protection, the other about simplicity, and they reinforce each other.

probes.q: How does Python do encapsulation without private keywords?
probes.a: By convention: a leading underscore means internal, and properties control access. Double underscores trigger name mangling, which is not true privacy.

probes.q: What is duck typing?
probes.a: Polymorphism without a shared base class: if the object has the method you call, it works. Python relies on it heavily.

questions.trap: Treating inheritance as the main point of OOP. Overused inheritance creates fragile hierarchies; most of the design value comes from encapsulation and polymorphism through interfaces.

questions.q: What does 'composition over inheritance' mean, and why is it advised?
questions.plain: Inheritance says a food truck is a kind of restaurant, so it inherits everything a restaurant has, including a dining room it does not need. Composition builds the food truck from parts: a kitchen, a payment system, a vehicle. You can swap one part without rebuilding the whole thing.
questions.technical: Inheritance models is-a and shares code through a parent class, but it couples the child tightly to the parent's internals. Change the base class and every subclass can break, the fragile base class problem. Deep hierarchies also explode when behaviors combine, like a FlyingSwimmingRobotDuck. Composition models has-a: an object holds other objects and delegates work to them, for example a Notifier holding a list of channels such as email and SMS. Behavior can be swapped at runtime and each piece tested alone with a fake. I use inheritance for genuine, stable is-a relationships and composition for sharing behavior.

probes.q: When is inheritance the right call?
probes.a: A true, stable is-a relationship, such as custom exceptions inheriting from Exception, or framework classes designed to be subclassed.

probes.q: How does the Liskov substitution principle relate?
probes.a: A subclass must work anywhere its parent is expected. If you have to override a method just to raise 'not supported', the inheritance is wrong.

probes.q: How does composition help testing?
probes.a: You can inject a fake collaborator, like a fake payment gateway, without subclassing or patching anything.

questions.aws: The AWS CDK is built on composition: you assemble higher-level constructs out of smaller ones, for example one construct that bundles a queue, a function, and the permissions between them, rather than extending deep class trees.
questions.trap: Saying inheritance is bad. It is fine for true, stable is-a relationships; the advice is to prefer composition when the goal is reusing behavior.

questions.q: Walk me through the SOLID principles.
questions.plain: SOLID is five rules for building software like good modular furniture: each piece has one job; you add new pieces without sawing up old ones; any shelf of the right size fits any matching slot; connectors are small and specific; and pieces plug into a standard socket instead of being glued to one particular wall.
questions.technical: S, single responsibility: a class should have one reason to change, so split report formatting from report emailing. O, open-closed: open for extension, closed for modification, so a new payment type is a new class, not another branch in a giant if-else. L, Liskov substitution: a subtype must work wherever its base type is expected, without surprises. I, interface segregation: many small interfaces beat one fat one, so clients do not depend on methods they never call. D, dependency inversion: high-level code depends on abstractions, and the concrete database or API client is passed in, which also makes the code easy to test.

probes.q: Give a Liskov violation.
probes.a: Square inheriting from Rectangle: setting a square's width silently changes its height, which breaks code that expected an ordinary rectangle.

probes.q: Dependency inversion versus dependency injection?
probes.a: Inversion is the principle: depend on abstractions. Injection is one technique for achieving it: pass dependencies in through the constructor or a parameter.

probes.q: Can SOLID be overdone?
probes.a: Yes. An interface for a class with one implementation and no testing need is speculative complexity. Apply the principles where change is likely.

questions.trap: Reciting the acronym without examples. Interviewers want a concrete before-and-after for each letter, especially single responsibility and dependency inversion.

questions.q: Explain a few design patterns simply: singleton, factory, strategy, observer, and adapter.
questions.plain: Singleton is a building with one front desk that everyone shares. Factory is ordering 'a coffee' and letting the barista pick which machine makes it. Strategy is choosing driving, walking, or transit in a maps app: same destination, different method. Observer is subscribing to a newsletter. Adapter is a travel plug converter.
questions.technical: Singleton guarantees one instance with global access, such as a configuration object or connection pool. Use it sparingly: it is hidden global state and hard to test. Factory centralizes object creation, so callers ask for 'a parser for this file type' without knowing the concrete class. Strategy wraps interchangeable algorithms behind one interface and picks one at runtime, like pricing rules or retry policies. Observer lets a subject notify subscribers of events without knowing who they are, the basis of event systems and pub/sub. Adapter wraps an incompatible interface so it fits the one your code expects, like wrapping a legacy SOAP client behind a clean method.

probes.q: Why do some people call singleton an anti-pattern?
probes.a: It is global mutable state: hidden dependencies, hard to replace in tests, and tricky with threads. Creating one shared instance and passing it in explicitly gives the same benefit.

probes.q: What does strategy look like in Python?
probes.a: Often you just pass a function. First-class functions turn many classic patterns into a single parameter.

probes.q: Observer versus a message queue?
probes.a: Observer is usually in-process and synchronous. A queue or pub/sub service decouples across processes and time, adding durability and retries.

questions.aws: Observer at cloud scale is Amazon SNS or Amazon EventBridge: publishers emit events and any number of subscribers react, without the publisher knowing who they are.
questions.trap: Using patterns as a checklist. A pattern is a name for a solution to a recurring problem; adding one where the problem does not exist is just extra code.

questions.q: What is the difference between a process and a thread?
questions.plain: A process is a separate restaurant with its own kitchen and pantry. Threads are cooks inside one restaurant: they share the same kitchen and ingredients, so they coordinate quickly, but they can also bump into each other or grab the same pan.
questions.technical: A process is a running program with its own virtual address space, open files, and other resources, isolated from other processes by the operating system. A thread is a unit of execution inside a process. Threads share the process's memory and resources, but each has its own stack and registers. Threads are cheaper to create and switch between, and shared memory makes communication fast, but any shared state needs synchronization. Processes are heavier and communicate through pipes, sockets, or shared memory segments, but a crash in one does not corrupt another. That isolation is why browsers often run tabs in separate processes.

probes.q: What does a context switch cost?
probes.a: The OS saves and restores registers and scheduling state. Switching between processes can also mean switching address spaces and losing warm caches, so it costs more than switching threads.

probes.q: When would you use processes over threads in Python?
probes.a: For CPU-bound work on standard CPython, because the GIL lets only one thread run Python bytecode at a time. multiprocessing or ProcessPoolExecutor gives true parallelism.

probes.q: What are coroutines or green threads?
probes.a: Lightweight tasks scheduled by the language runtime rather than the OS, like asyncio coroutines or goroutines, so you can run thousands cheaply.

questions.trap: Saying each thread has its own memory. Threads share their process's heap; only the stack and registers belong to each thread.

questions.q: What is the difference between concurrency and parallelism?
questions.plain: Concurrency is one chef juggling three dishes: chop, stir a pot, check the oven, back to chopping. Parallelism is three chefs each cooking a dish at the same moment. Concurrency is about dealing with many things at once; parallelism is about doing many things at once.
questions.technical: Concurrency means structuring a program so several tasks make progress over overlapping periods, possibly by interleaving on a single core. Parallelism means executing several tasks at literally the same instant on multiple cores or machines. Concurrency helps I/O-bound work: while one request waits on the network, another runs, which is how an event loop like asyncio serves thousands of connections on one thread. Parallelism helps CPU-bound work such as image processing or model training. In standard CPython, threads give concurrency for I/O but, because of the GIL, not parallel Python bytecode; processes or native libraries like NumPy provide parallelism.

probes.q: Is the GIL going away?
probes.a: CPython 3.13 introduced an optional free-threaded build without the GIL, and later releases have kept maturing it, but the default build still has the GIL. Native libraries such as NumPy already release it inside heavy computations.

probes.q: How do you speed up an I/O-bound job?
probes.a: Concurrency: asyncio, a thread pool, or batching requests. More cores will not help if the program is waiting on the network.

probes.q: What is Amdahl's law?
probes.a: The speedup from parallelism is capped by the part that must run serially. If 10% of the work is serial, you can never go faster than 10x, however many cores you add.

questions.aws: AWS Lambda scales by running more execution environments side by side as requests arrive, so throughput grows without you managing threads or servers.
questions.trap: Using the two words interchangeably. A single-core machine can run things concurrently but never in parallel.

questions.q: What is a race condition, and how do locks fix it?
questions.plain: Two people share a bank account with $150 and both withdraw $100 at the same moment from different ATMs. Both machines read $150, both decide there is enough, and both pay out. A lock is the rule that only one transaction can touch the account at a time, so the second one sees the updated balance.
questions.technical: A race condition is when the result depends on the timing of threads touching shared state, typically a read-modify-write like count += 1, which is a read, an add, and a write that another thread can interleave with. A lock, or mutex, makes a critical section mutually exclusive: acquire, update, release, ideally with a context manager so it is released even on an exception. Alternatives include atomic operations, thread-safe queues, immutable data, or keeping state inside one thread. Locks cost throughput under contention, and holding several risks deadlock, so keep critical sections short. Races across machines need database transactions, conditional writes, or optimistic concurrency with version numbers.

probes.q: Does Python's GIL prevent race conditions?
probes.a: No. The GIL protects the interpreter's own internals, but a thread can be switched out between the read and the write in count += 1, so your code still needs a lock.

probes.q: What is optimistic concurrency control?
probes.a: Read a version number, write only if it has not changed, and retry if someone else got there first. It works well when conflicts are rare.

probes.q: Why are race conditions hard to debug?
probes.a: They depend on timing, so they appear under load and vanish when you add logging or attach a debugger.

questions.aws: DynamoDB conditional writes let you say 'update this item only if its version is still 7', which gives optimistic locking across many servers without a separate lock service.
questions.trap: Believing a race needs multiple cores. Interleaving on a single core is enough, and the GIL does not make compound operations atomic.

questions.q: What is a deadlock? Name the four conditions and explain how to prevent it.
questions.plain: Two cars meet in the middle of a one-lane bridge from opposite ends. Each waits for the other to back up, and neither will. Everyone is stuck forever, even though neither driver did anything wrong alone.
questions.technical: A deadlock is a set of threads each waiting for a resource held by another, so none can ever proceed. Coffman's four conditions must all hold at once: mutual exclusion, a resource can be held by only one thread; hold and wait, a thread holds one resource while waiting for another; no preemption, a resource cannot be taken away; and circular wait, a cycle of threads each waiting on the next. Break any one and deadlock is impossible. The most practical fix is a global lock order, every thread takes lock A before lock B, which removes circular wait. Others: acquire all locks at once, use try-lock with a timeout and back off, or detect cycles and abort a victim, as databases do.

probes.q: How do databases handle deadlocks?
probes.a: They detect cycles in a wait-for graph, abort one transaction as the victim, and return an error that the application should retry.

probes.q: Deadlock versus livelock versus starvation?
probes.a: Deadlock: everyone is blocked. Livelock: everyone keeps reacting to each other but nothing progresses, like two people stepping aside in a hallway in sync. Starvation: one thread never gets the resource because others keep winning.

probes.q: Can a single thread deadlock itself?
probes.a: Yes, by acquiring a non-reentrant lock it already holds. Python's threading.RLock lets the same thread acquire it again.

questions.trap: Naming only circular wait. All four conditions are required together, and prevention means breaking at least one; consistent lock ordering is the usual answer.

questions.q: What is the difference between stack and heap memory?
questions.plain: The stack is a notepad on your desk for the task in front of you: quick to write on, and the page is torn off automatically when you finish. The heap is a storage warehouse: room for big or long-lived things, but someone has to track what is in there and clear out what nobody needs anymore.
questions.technical: The stack holds function call frames: local variables, arguments, and return addresses. Allocating is just moving a pointer, so it is very fast, and memory is freed automatically when the function returns. It is small and fixed in size per thread, so very deep recursion overflows it. The heap holds data whose size or lifetime is not known in advance, such as objects, lists, and strings. It is larger and flexible but slower to allocate, can fragment, and must be freed manually, as in C and C++, or by a garbage collector, as in Java, Python, and Go. In Python every object lives on the heap; a function's frame just holds references to them.

probes.q: Why is stack allocation faster?
probes.a: It is a pointer bump with no search for free space and no bookkeeping, and that memory is usually already in the CPU cache.

probes.q: What causes a stack overflow?
probes.a: Recursion that goes too deep, or very large local arrays that exceed the thread's stack size.

probes.q: Where does a Python integer live?
probes.a: On the heap, like every Python object. The local variable in the frame only holds a reference to it.

questions.trap: Stating 'primitives on the stack, objects on the heap' as a universal rule. It depends on the language: in Python everything is a heap object, and a Java JIT can avoid some heap allocations through escape analysis.

questions.q: How does garbage collection work, and can you still leak memory in a garbage-collected language?
questions.plain: Garbage collection is a cleaning crew that throws away anything nobody is holding onto. A memory leak in these languages is a hoarder: the crew cannot throw anything out because you are technically still holding it, even though you will never use it again.
questions.technical: A garbage collector frees memory that is no longer reachable from roots such as global variables and the active stack frames. CPython uses reference counting, freeing an object the moment its count hits zero, plus a cycle collector for objects that reference each other. The JVM and Go use tracing collectors that mark everything reachable and reclaim the rest; the JVM's are generational, because most objects die young. You can still leak, because anything reachable is kept. Common causes: unbounded caches or global dicts, event listeners never unsubscribed, queues that grow without limit, and closures capturing large objects. Fixes: bounded caches, weak references, and heap profiling, such as Python's tracemalloc.

probes.q: What is a GC pause?
probes.a: Time the collector stops or slows the program to do its work. Modern collectors do most work concurrently to keep pauses short, but pauses can still show up in tail latency.

probes.q: How would you find a leak in production?
probes.a: Watch memory climb over time without leveling off, take heap snapshots at two points, and compare which object types grew.

probes.q: What is a weak reference?
probes.a: A reference that does not keep the object alive. It is useful for caches and listener lists so they do not cause leaks.

questions.trap: Saying garbage collection makes leaks impossible. It only frees unreachable objects; reachable but useless objects leak just fine.

questions.q: How does an operating system schedule work across processes and threads?
questions.plain: A CPU core is a single checkout lane, and the scheduler is the store manager deciding who goes next. Serve one giant cart to completion and everyone behind it waits; give everyone a short turn and the line feels fair and responsive.
questions.technical: The scheduler decides which ready thread runs on each core, and for how long. Preemptive schedulers give each thread a time slice and interrupt it when the slice ends or a higher-priority thread becomes ready. Classic policies: first-come first-served, which is simple but makes short jobs wait behind long ones; shortest job first, which minimizes average wait but needs good predictions; round robin, which gives fair time slices; and priority scheduling, with aging so low-priority work does not starve. Linux used the Completely Fair Scheduler, which tracks how much CPU time each thread has received, for many years, and newer kernels moved to the EEVDF scheduler. The goals trade off: throughput, latency, and fairness.

probes.q: How do schedulers treat I/O-bound versus CPU-bound threads?
probes.a: I/O-bound threads run briefly and then block, so schedulers tend to favor them to keep the system responsive; CPU-bound threads use their full time slices.

probes.q: What is priority inversion?
probes.a: A high-priority task waits on a lock held by a low-priority task, which keeps getting preempted by medium-priority work. Priority inheritance fixes it by temporarily boosting the lock holder.

probes.q: How does this relate to Kubernetes?
probes.a: Kubernetes places pods on nodes based on their resource requests, and CPU limits are enforced by the kernel, which can throttle a container even when the node has idle cores.

questions.trap: Thinking several processes truly run at the same moment on one core. They take very fast turns; only multiple cores give real parallelism.

questions.q: Explain virtual memory and paging.
questions.plain: Virtual memory is a hotel where every guest is told they are in room 101. The front desk secretly maps each guest's 'room 101' to a different real room, so guests can never walk into each other's rooms, and luggage nobody has touched in a while can go to off-site storage and be fetched back when asked for.
questions.technical: Each process gets its own virtual address space. The memory management unit translates virtual addresses to physical memory using page tables, in fixed-size pages, commonly 4 KB, and a cache called the TLB keeps recent translations. Benefits: processes are isolated from each other, a program can use more address space than the RAM it currently occupies, pages load lazily on first use, and shared libraries and copy-on-write after fork share physical pages. Touching a page that is not in RAM causes a page fault: the OS loads it from disk or swap and resumes the program. If the working set is bigger than RAM, the system thrashes, spending its time swapping, and performance collapses.

probes.q: What is a TLB miss?
