probes.a: The translation is not cached, so the hardware or OS walks the page table, costing extra memory accesses. Huge pages reduce misses for big-memory workloads.

probes.q: What is copy-on-write?
probes.a: After fork, parent and child share pages marked read-only; a page is physically copied only when one of them writes to it.

probes.q: Minor versus major page fault?
probes.a: Minor: the page is already in memory, just not mapped for this process yet. Major: it has to be read from disk, which is far slower.

questions.trap: Saying virtual memory means using the disk as RAM. Swap is one feature; the core idea is address translation and isolation, which matters even on a machine with no swap at all.

questions.q: What is a system call, and how does a file system store a file?
questions.plain: A system call is a program ringing the bell at the front desk. It is not allowed into the back office, so it asks the operating system to open a file or send data on its behalf. A file system is a library catalog: it records which shelves hold each book's pages, so you can ask for a book by its title.
questions.technical: Programs run in user mode and cannot touch hardware directly. A system call such as open, read, write, fork, or mmap switches into kernel mode, where the OS checks permissions, does the work, and returns. Each crossing has overhead, which is why buffered I/O batches many small writes into fewer calls. A Unix-style file system maps names to inodes through directories. An inode holds metadata such as size, owner, and permissions, and points to the data blocks on disk. Journaling file systems such as ext4 log changes before applying them, so a crash leaves a consistent state. A write may sit in the page cache in memory until it is flushed; fsync forces it to disk.

probes.q: Why can a successful write still lose data in a crash?
probes.a: The write often lands in the OS page cache, not on disk. Only after fsync, or a later flush, is it durable.

probes.q: What is a file descriptor?
probes.a: A small integer the kernel hands a process to refer to an open file, socket, or pipe in later system calls.

probes.q: Block versus file versus object storage?
probes.a: Block storage is raw disk blocks. A file system adds names, folders, and permissions on top. Object storage keeps whole objects by key with metadata, accessed over an HTTP API.

questions.aws: On AWS this maps to Amazon EBS for block storage attached to an instance, Amazon EFS for a shared file system mounted over NFS, and Amazon S3 for object storage accessed by key through an API.
questions.trap: Thinking a returned write() means the data is on disk. It usually means the kernel accepted it into memory; durability needs fsync.

questions.q: Compiled versus interpreted, and static versus dynamic typing: are they the same thing?
questions.plain: No, they answer two separate questions. Compiled versus interpreted is whether a book is fully translated before you read it, or translated aloud line by line as you go. Static versus dynamic typing is whether a form is checked for mistakes before you hand it in, or only when someone tries to use the wrong field.
questions.technical: Compiled versus interpreted is about how code runs. Ahead-of-time compiled languages such as C, Go, and Rust become machine code before running; interpreted code runs through an interpreter; and many languages are hybrids: Java compiles to bytecode that a JIT turns into machine code, and CPython compiles to bytecode that it then interprets. Static typing checks types before the program runs, as in Java, Go, and TypeScript; dynamic typing checks at runtime, as in Python and JavaScript. The two axes are independent. Strong versus weak typing is a third axis about implicit conversions: Python is dynamic but strong, so 1 + '1' raises an error.

probes.q: What is the tradeoff of static typing?
probes.a: It catches whole classes of bugs before the code runs and helps tooling and refactoring, at the cost of more upfront annotation. Python type hints checked with mypy are an optional middle ground.

probes.q: What is a JIT?
probes.a: A just-in-time compiler that turns frequently run code into machine code while the program runs, using what it observes at runtime to optimize.

probes.q: Is Python compiled?
probes.a: CPython compiles source to bytecode, cached in .pyc files, then interprets that bytecode. 'Interpreted' is a simplification.

questions.trap: Saying Python is untyped, or that interpreted means dynamically typed. Python is strongly and dynamically typed, and the execution model and type checking are separate axes.

questions.q: Explain the CAP theorem in practical terms.
questions.plain: Two branch offices share one customer list, and the phone line between them goes down. Either both offices keep serving customers with lists that may be out of date, or they stop accepting changes until the line is back so nobody sees wrong data. During the outage you cannot have both.
questions.technical: CAP says that during a network partition, a distributed data store must choose between consistency, meaning every read sees the latest write, and availability, meaning every request to a working node gets a response. Partitions are a fact of real networks, so the practical choice is whether the system leans CP or AP when one happens. CP systems refuse or delay some requests to stay correct, like a coordination service that needs a majority. AP systems keep answering and reconcile later, like a shopping cart that merges changes. PACELC adds that even with no partition you trade latency against consistency. CAP's C means linearizability, not the C in ACID.

probes.q: What does PACELC add?
probes.a: If there is a Partition, choose Availability or Consistency; Else, choose Latency or Consistency. It captures the everyday tradeoff when nothing is broken.

probes.q: Is a single-node database CA?
probes.a: Only in the sense that there is no network to partition. Once you replicate across a network, partitions can happen and you must decide how to behave during one.

probes.q: How do you choose for a customer?
probes.a: Ask what a stale read costs. A bank balance or inventory reservation leans consistent; a review count or social feed can be eventually consistent.

questions.aws: DynamoDB lets you choose per read: reads are eventually consistent by default, or strongly consistent with ConsistentRead on tables and local secondary indexes, at twice the read cost. Global secondary indexes only support eventually consistent reads.
questions.trap: Saying 'pick any two of the three' as if you could drop partition tolerance. In a distributed system partitions happen, so the real choice is consistency or availability while one is happening.

questions.q: What are the main consistency models, from strong to eventual?
questions.plain: Strong consistency is one whiteboard everyone looks at: the moment you write on it, everyone sees it. Eventual consistency is mailing a memo to every branch office: everyone gets it, but for a while some offices are still reading the old version.
questions.technical: Linearizability, the strongest common model, makes each operation appear to take effect at a single instant between its start and end, as if there were one copy of the data. Sequential consistency keeps one global order that respects each client's own order, but not necessarily real time. Causal consistency guarantees that causes are seen before effects, so a reply never appears before the message it answers. Session guarantees such as read-your-writes and monotonic reads keep one user's view sensible. Eventual consistency only promises that replicas converge once writes stop. Stronger models cost latency and availability because replicas must coordinate; weaker ones are faster and keep working during partitions.

probes.q: What is read-your-writes?
probes.a: After you update something, your own later reads see the update, even if other users briefly see the old value. It is often what users actually need.

probes.q: How do quorum systems give stronger reads?
probes.a: With N replicas, if writes go to W of them and reads to R of them with R + W greater than N, every read overlaps at least one replica that has the latest write.

probes.q: Where is eventual consistency fine?
probes.a: Like counts, caches, search indexes, and analytics, where brief staleness costs little.

questions.aws: Amazon S3 provides strong read-after-write consistency for object PUTs and DELETEs in all Regions, while bucket configuration changes are eventually consistent. DynamoDB global tables default to multi-Region eventual consistency and offer an optional multi-Region strong consistency mode.
questions.trap: Treating it as a binary choice between strong and eventual. It is a spectrum, and many applications only need read-your-writes or causal consistency, which are cheaper than linearizability.

questions.q: What is idempotency, and why does it matter for retries?
questions.plain: An elevator button is idempotent: pressing it five times still calls one elevator. A vending machine that charges you on every press is not. On unreliable networks you want 'pay for order 123' to behave like the elevator button, so pressing it again after a timeout does not charge the customer twice.
questions.technical: An operation is idempotent if doing it once or many times leaves the same result. Reads, 'set balance to 100', and 'delete item 42' are naturally idempotent; 'add 10 to balance' and 'create an order' are not. It matters because a timeout is ambiguous: the request may have succeeded before the response was lost, so the client cannot tell whether a retry is safe. Make writes safe to retry with an idempotency key, a unique request ID that the server stores with the result and answers repeats from. Other techniques are upserts keyed on a natural ID, conditional writes, and deduplicating consumers, since many queues deliver at least once.

probes.q: Which HTTP methods are idempotent?
probes.a: By the HTTP specification, GET, PUT, and DELETE are idempotent and POST is not, which is why payment APIs add an idempotency key header to POST requests.

probes.q: How long do you keep idempotency keys?
probes.a: At least as long as a client might retry, often hours to a day, with expiry so the store does not grow forever.

probes.q: What about exactly-once delivery?
probes.a: True end-to-end exactly-once delivery is very hard. The practical pattern is at-least-once delivery plus idempotent processing, which gives exactly-once effects.

questions.aws: Powertools for AWS Lambda includes an idempotency utility that returns the stored result for a repeated request, with DynamoDB as the default store. Amazon SQS standard queues deliver at least once, so consumers should be idempotent, and many EC2 APIs accept a client token for the same reason.
questions.resume: At MSRcosmos my nightly Databricks feed loaded 17 financial tables and 4.2M rows into Delta Lake using incremental merges. A merge upserts by key, which is what makes rerunning a load safe instead of duplicating rows.
questions.trap: Saying 'just retry on failure'. Retrying a non-idempotent operation after a timeout can double-charge or double-ship. Make it idempotent first, then retry.

questions.q: How should a client retry failed calls? Explain timeouts, exponential backoff, and jitter.
questions.plain: If a busy shop does not answer, calling back every second makes things worse for everyone. Wait a little, then longer each time, and add a random few seconds so a hundred callers do not all redial at the same instant. And do not stay on hold forever: hang up after a sensible time.
questions.technical: Every remote call needs a timeout, or one slow dependency ties up threads until the whole service stalls; set it from the dependency's measured latency, for example a bit above its p99. Retry only transient failures, such as timeouts, throttling, and 5xx errors, never validation errors, and only for idempotent operations. Exponential backoff waits a base delay times 2^attempt, up to a cap. Jitter randomizes that wait; full jitter picks uniformly between zero and the cap, so clients that failed together do not retry together and cause a thundering herd. Limit the number of attempts, budget retries, and retry at one layer only, because retries at every layer multiply load.

probes.q: Why is retrying at every layer dangerous?
probes.a: If three layers each make 3 attempts, one user request can become 27 calls to the bottom dependency, exactly when it is struggling.

probes.q: What is a retry budget?
probes.a: A cap on retries relative to total traffic, so retries smooth over blips but stop amplifying load during a real outage. AWS SDKs implement this as a retry quota token bucket.

probes.q: How do you pick a timeout value?
probes.a: From the dependency's measured latency, usually above its p99 so normal slow requests still succeed, and within the caller's own deadline.

questions.aws: AWS SDKs retry transient and throttling errors automatically. The standard retry mode uses exponential backoff with full jitter, defaults to 3 total attempts, and has a retry quota that stops retrying when failures are widespread.
questions.trap: Retrying immediately in a tight loop, or adding backoff without jitter so clients retry in lockstep. And never retry a non-idempotent write without an idempotency key.

questions.q: What is a circuit breaker in software?
questions.plain: It works like the breaker in your home's electrical panel. When a dependency keeps failing, the breaker trips and requests fail fast for a while, instead of every request waiting and piling up. After a cool-down it lets one test request through; if that works, normal service resumes.
questions.technical: A circuit breaker wraps calls to a dependency and tracks failures. While closed, calls pass through and failures are counted. When failures cross a threshold, it opens: calls fail immediately or return a fallback, such as cached data or a degraded response, which protects the caller's threads and gives the dependency room to recover. After a timeout it goes half-open and lets a few trial calls through; success closes it, failure opens it again. It complements timeouts and retries: retries handle short blips, while the breaker stops sending traffic to a dependency that is clearly down.

probes.q: What fallback would you use?
probes.a: It depends on the feature: cached or default data for recommendations, queuing the request for later, or a clear error for payments, where guessing is unsafe.

probes.q: Circuit breaker versus retries?
probes.a: Retries assume the failure is brief. A breaker assumes it is not and stops sending traffic, which prevents retry storms.

probes.q: What is a bulkhead?
probes.a: Isolating resources, such as a separate thread or connection pool per dependency, so one slow dependency cannot exhaust everything.

questions.aws: Amazon ECS has a deployment circuit breaker that applies the same idea to releases: if new tasks keep failing to reach a steady state, it marks the deployment failed and can roll back automatically to the last completed deployment.
questions.trap: Confusing a circuit breaker with retries or rate limiting. A breaker reacts to the dependency's health and stops calls entirely while it is open.

questions.q: Explain unit, integration, and end-to-end tests. How do you balance them?
questions.plain: Think of building a car. Unit tests check each part on the bench, like the brakes on their own. Integration tests check parts working together, like the brakes with the wheels. End-to-end tests drive the finished car around the block. You run lots of bench tests because they are quick and cheap, and only a few test drives.
questions.technical: Unit tests check one function or class in isolation, with fakes standing in for slow dependencies; they run in milliseconds and point straight at the failure. Integration tests check real collaborators together, such as code against a real database, queue, or another service's API, and catch wiring, schema, and configuration bugs. End-to-end tests drive the whole system the way a user would, through the UI or public API; they catch what nothing else does but are slow and prone to flakiness. The test pyramid says many unit tests, fewer integration tests, and a handful of end-to-end tests on critical paths, all run automatically in CI on every change.

probes.q: What makes a test flaky, and how do you fix it?
probes.a: Dependence on timing, test order, shared state, or real networks. Use deterministic waits, isolated data per test, and fakes where realism is not the point.

probes.q: Mock versus fake?
probes.a: A fake is a working lightweight implementation, like an in-memory database. A mock records calls so you can assert how it was used. Overusing mocks tests the implementation instead of the behavior.

probes.q: What is a smoke test?
probes.a: A quick check right after deployment that the core paths work at all, such as the homepage loads and login succeeds.

questions.aws: AWS CodePipeline and AWS CodeBuild can run these test stages in a release pipeline, so a failing test stops the deployment.
questions.resume: At Oracle I built a CLI toolchain on Jenkins CI/CD with scripted pre-deployment validation, and 4 teams adopted it. Release cycles got 34% shorter and failed deploys dropped from 11% to 4%, because problems were caught before production instead of after.
questions.trap: Relying mainly on end-to-end tests. They are slow and flaky, so teams start ignoring failures. Most coverage should come from fast unit and integration tests.

questions.q: What is test-driven development, and when is it worth it?
questions.plain: TDD is writing the exam before teaching the lesson. You write down exactly what 'correct' looks like, watch it fail, then do just enough work to pass. It keeps you honest about what you are actually building.
questions.technical: TDD is a short loop. Red: write a small failing test for the next behavior. Green: write the simplest code that passes it. Refactor: clean up with the tests as a safety net. The benefits are that tests exist by construction, the design is pushed toward small units with clear interfaces, and refactoring is safer. It works best for well-understood logic such as parsers, business rules, and bug fixes, where you start with a test that reproduces the bug. It helps less for exploratory prototypes or UI layout, where the target is still moving. The main pitfall is testing implementation details, which makes later refactoring painful.

probes.q: How do you apply TDD to a bug fix?
probes.a: Write a test that reproduces the bug and fails, fix the code, watch the test pass, and keep it so the bug cannot quietly come back.

probes.q: Does TDD guarantee good coverage?
probes.a: It covers the behaviors you thought to specify. It does not find cases you never imagined; property-based tests and code review help there.

probes.q: TDD versus BDD?
probes.a: BDD phrases tests as behaviors in business language, given, when, then, so non-engineers can read them. The underlying loop is similar.

questions.trap: Thinking TDD means writing every test up front. It is one small test at a time, alternating with just enough code.

questions.q: What makes a good code review?
questions.plain: Code review is a second pair of eyes before something ships, like an editor reading an article before it goes to print. A good editor checks that the story is right and clear, not just the commas, and leaves notes that make the writer better next time.
questions.technical: Small, focused changes get better reviews, so I keep a pull request to one purpose with a clear description of what changed, why, and how it was tested. Reviewers check in priority order: correctness and edge cases; security, such as input validation and leaked secrets; design fit and readability; tests that cover the behavior; and performance hot spots such as queries inside loops. Linters and formatters should handle style automatically so people focus on substance. Comments should be specific, explain why, and mark which points are blocking and which are suggestions. Turnaround matters: a review that sits for days blocks the author and encourages giant batched changes.

probes.q: How do you handle a disagreement in review?
probes.a: Ground it in the goal, data, or a team standard rather than preference. If it is still a tie, defer to the author or code owner and write the decision down.

probes.q: What do you look at first?
probes.a: Whether the change does what it claims, safely: the logic, error handling, and anything touching security or data.

probes.q: How big should a pull request be?
probes.a: Small enough to review carefully in one sitting, often a few hundred lines. Bigger work goes in a series of smaller pull requests or behind a feature flag.

questions.aws: Amazon Q Developer can review code for security and quality issues and suggest fixes, which works alongside human review rather than replacing it.
questions.trap: Treating review as a style check or a rubber stamp. Tools handle style; reviewers should focus on correctness, design, security, and tests.

questions.q: Git merge versus rebase: what is the difference, and when do you use each?
questions.plain: Two writers edit copies of the same document. Merging staples both versions together with a note saying 'combined here', keeping the full record of who did what and when. Rebasing retypes your edits on top of the latest version, as if you had started from it, so the history reads as one straight line.
questions.technical: Both bring changes from one branch into another. Merge creates a merge commit with two parents, preserving the true history and never rewriting existing commits. Rebase replays your commits on top of the target branch, creating new commits with new hashes, which gives a linear history that is easier to read and bisect. The rule: never rebase commits other people have already pulled, because rewriting shared history forces everyone to untangle it. A common workflow is rebasing your own feature branch onto main to stay current, then merging or squash-merging into main through a pull request. Conflicts can happen either way; rebase may surface them one commit at a time.

probes.q: What is a squash merge?
probes.a: All of a branch's commits are combined into a single commit on main. History stays clean, but the individual steps are lost.

probes.q: What is a fast-forward merge?
probes.a: If main has not moved since you branched, git just moves the main pointer to your latest commit, and no merge commit is needed.

probes.q: How do you recover from a bad rebase?
probes.a: git reflog shows where the branch pointed before the rebase, and you can reset back to that commit.

questions.trap: Saying rebase is always cleaner, so always use it. Rebasing a shared branch rewrites history others depend on; keep it to your own local or personal branches.

drills.title: Find a pair that sums to a target
drills.what: It checks whether any two different numbers in the list add up to the target, by trying every possible pair.
drills.complexity: O(n^2) time, O(1) extra space. For each of the n numbers it scans the rest of the list, about n^2 / 2 pair checks.
drills.bug: No correctness bug, but it is quadratic. With 100,000 numbers that is about 5 billion comparisons, so it falls over on real data sizes.
drills.plain: Instead of making every guest at a party shake hands with every other guest to find a matching pair, you keep a guest list at the door and check each newcomer against it once.

drills.title: Recursive power with no base case
drills.code:
def power(base, exp):
    # base^exp by repeated squaring
    half = power(base, exp // 2)
    if exp % 2 == 0:
        return half * half
    return half * half * base


print(power(2, 10))
drills.what: It tries to compute base to the power exp by squaring: compute the half power once, square it, and multiply by base one extra time when exp is odd.
drills.complexity: As written it never finishes. Once fixed, it is O(log n) time and O(log n) stack space in the exponent, because exp halves on every call.
drills.bug: There is no base case. Every call recurses, and once exp reaches 0 it keeps calling power(base, 0) forever because 0 // 2 is 0. Python stops it with RecursionError after about 1000 frames. A negative exponent loops too, since -1 // 2 is -1.
drills.plain: It is like telling someone to fold a map in half, then in half again, with no rule for when to stop. Any instruction that repeats itself needs a clear 'you are done now' step.

drills.title: Threads incrementing a shared counter
drills.what: It starts 4 threads that each add 1 to a shared global counter 100,000 times, then prints the total, which should be 400,000.
drills.complexity: O(n) total increments. The problem here is correctness, not speed.
drills.bug: Race condition. count += 1 is three steps: read, add, write. Two threads can read the same old value and both write back that value plus one, so an update is lost and the total can come out below 400,000. A run that happens to print the right answer proves nothing, and the GIL does not make this compound operation atomic.
drills.improve:
Protect the read-modify-write with a lock so only one thread runs it at a time. Locking every single increment is slow, so the better design is to avoid shared state: let each thread count locally and add the per-thread totals once at the end.

lock = threading.Lock()

def worker():
    global count
    for _ in range(100_000):
        with lock:
            count += 1
drills.plain: Two cashiers keep one shared paper tally. Both glance at 10, both write 11, and a sale disappears. The fix is one pen that only one cashier can hold at a time, or each cashier keeps their own tally and you add them up at closing.

drills.title: One database query per customer
drills.what: For each customer ID, it runs a separate query to fetch that customer's orders and sums the order totals.
drills.complexity: n database round trips for n customers. Each query may be fast, but 1,000 customers means 1,000 network round trips, so latency is dominated by the round trips, not the work.
drills.bug: The classic N+1 query problem: a query inside a loop. It looks fine in testing with 5 customers and falls over in production with thousands, and it adds load on the database for no reason.
drills.improve:
Ask the database once and let it do the grouping: one query with IN, or a JOIN with GROUP BY. The f-string only builds the list of ? placeholders; the values still go through parameters, so this stays safe from injection. For very long ID lists, send them in batches.

def order_summaries(db, customer_ids):
    if not customer_ids:
        return []
    marks = ",".join("?" * len(customer_ids))
    rows = db.execute(
        "SELECT customer_id, SUM(total) FROM orders "
        f"WHERE customer_id IN ({marks}) GROUP BY customer_id",
        list(customer_ids),
    ).fetchall()
    totals = dict(rows)
    return [(cid, totals.get(cid, 0)) for cid in customer_ids]
drills.plain: It is like a waiter walking to the kitchen separately for each guest's order, instead of writing down the whole table's order and making one trip.

drills.title: User input pasted into SQL
drills.what: It looks up a user's id and email by name, by pasting the name the user typed straight into the SQL text.
drills.complexity: One query. With an index on name it is a quick lookup; without one, the database scans the whole table, O(n) rows.
drills.bug: SQL injection. An input like ' OR '1'='1 turns the WHERE clause into always true and returns another user's data, and nastier inputs can change or delete data. Even honest input breaks it: a name like O'Brien causes a syntax error.
drills.plain: It is like a bank teller who reads a customer's note aloud as an instruction. If the note says 'and also show me everyone's balance', the teller does it. A parameterized query means the teller only ever reads the note as a name.

drills.title: Mutable default argument
drills.code:
def add_tag(tag, tags=[]):
    tags.append(tag)
    return tags


print(add_tag("urgent"))   # ['urgent']
print(add_tag("billing"))  # ['urgent', 'billing'], surprise
drills.what: It adds a tag to a list of tags and returns the list, starting from an empty list when no list is passed in.
drills.complexity: O(1) amortized per call, but the hidden shared list grows forever.
drills.bug: Python evaluates the default [] once, when the function is defined, not on each call. Every call that omits tags shares and mutates that same list, so tags leak between unrelated callers: the second call returns ['urgent', 'billing'].
drills.improve:
Use None as the default and create a fresh list inside the function. Copying the input with list(tags) also avoids silently mutating the caller's list.

def add_tag(tag, tags=None):
    tags = [] if tags is None else list(tags)
    tags.append(tag)
    return tags
drills.plain: It is like a restaurant that hands every new customer the same notepad 'to start fresh', so each new order arrives with the previous customer's order already written on it.

drills.title: Binary search that misses the last element
drills.what: It searches a sorted list by checking the middle element and throwing away the half that cannot contain the target, returning the index or -1.
drills.complexity: O(log n) time and O(1) space, because the search range halves on every loop.
drills.bug: Off-by-one. hi is inclusive (len - 1), but the loop runs only while lo < hi, so it stops before checking the final remaining element. binary_search([1, 2, 3], 3) returns -1, and every one-element list fails.
drills.improve:
Pick one invariant and stick to it: with an inclusive hi, loop while lo <= hi and move to mid + 1 or mid - 1. Better, use the standard library's bisect module, which is tested and fast.

from bisect import bisect_left

def binary_search(items, target):
    i = bisect_left(items, target)
    return i if i < len(items) and items[i] == target else -1
drills.plain: It is like playing 'guess my number' by halves and giving up one guess too early: when only one number is left, you declare it does not exist instead of saying it.

drills.title: A cache that never forgets
drills.what: It keeps user profiles in a module-level dictionary so that repeat lookups skip the database.
drills.complexity: O(1) average per lookup, but memory grows with every distinct user ever requested, with no upper limit.
drills.bug: Unbounded cache, a memory leak even in a garbage-collected language: the dict keeps every entry reachable, so in a long-running server it grows until the process runs out of memory. Entries never expire either, so a changed profile is served stale forever.
drills.plain: It is like a receptionist who photocopies every visitor's ID and never throws a copy away. Repeat visits are quicker, but the office slowly fills with paper, and some copies are years out of date.

drills.title: Retrying a payment in a tight loop
drills.what: It calls a payment API to charge an order and, on any request error, immediately tries again, forever, until it succeeds.
drills.complexity: Unbounded. During an outage it loops forever at full speed, and with no timeout a single hung connection can block it indefinitely.
drills.bug: Four problems. No timeout, and requests waits indefinitely by default. No backoff or jitter, so many clients hammer a struggling service in sync. No limit on attempts. And it is not idempotent: if the charge succeeded but the response was lost, the retry charges the customer twice. It also retries client errors such as 400, which will never succeed.
drills.plain: It is like redialing a busy store every second, forever, and every time the call drops mid-order you might be placing the order again. Wait longer between tries, give up eventually, and quote an order number so the store knows it is the same order.

drills.title: Reading a huge log into memory
drills.what: It counts how many lines in a log file contain the word ERROR.
drills.complexity: O(n) time in the file size either way, but O(n) memory too: f.read() loads the whole file, and splitlines() makes a second full copy as a list of strings.
drills.bug: On a 20 GB log it tries to hold the file in memory at least twice, so it can crash with MemoryError or get the process killed. It also relies on the platform's default text encoding, which can fail on unexpected bytes.
drills.plain: It is like photocopying an entire encyclopedia just to count the pages that mention one word, instead of flipping through it and keeping a tally.

domains.name: Application development
domains.summary: How modern applications are built, shipped, run, and observed, so an SA can recommend the right architecture and delivery practice and explain the trade-offs in business terms.

sources.label: Amazon SQS: standard vs FIFO queue types
AWS Step Functions: choosing Standard or Express
Amazon API Gateway: REST APIs vs HTTP APIs

cheatsheet.def: Continuous integration merges and tests every change automatically; continuous delivery keeps every build releasable, and continuous deployment ships it automatically.
cheatsheet.probe: Delivery has a human approval before production; deployment does not.

cheatsheet.def: Define servers, networks, and permissions in versioned files that a tool applies, instead of clicking in a console.
cheatsheet.probe: AWS CDK synthesizes AWS CloudFormation templates; CloudFormation does the actual provisioning.

cheatsheet.def: One deployable unit vs many small services owned by separate teams and deployed independently.
cheatsheet.probe: Microservices trade code complexity for operational and network complexity.

cheatsheet.def: A unique client-supplied ID that lets the server recognize a retry and return the original result instead of repeating the action.
cheatsheet.probe: Needed because networks retry and SQS standard queues can deliver duplicates.

cheatsheet.def: A server that keeps no client session in its own memory, so any instance can handle any request.
cheatsheet.probe: Put session state in a shared store such as ElastiCache or DynamoDB, not in sticky sessions.

cheatsheet.def: Add more machines vs make one machine bigger.
cheatsheet.probe: Horizontal needs stateless design but has no single-box ceiling and improves availability.

cheatsheet.def: A queue hands each message to one consumer; pub/sub copies each message to every subscriber.
cheatsheet.probe: SNS to multiple SQS queues is the classic fan-out pattern.

cheatsheet.def: Standard: nearly unlimited throughput, at-least-once delivery, best-effort ordering. FIFO: ordering within a message group and exactly-once processing, with lower throughput.
cheatsheet.probe: Standard consumers must be idempotent.

cheatsheet.def: Event-driven functions billed per request and duration, with a timeout of 3 seconds by default and 15 minutes maximum.
cheatsheet.probe: Long-running jobs belong in Step Functions, ECS, or Fargate.

cheatsheet.def: Standard: up to one year, exactly-once, priced per state transition. Express: up to five minutes, at-least-once (async), priced per execution and duration.
cheatsheet.probe: Use Standard for non-idempotent steps like payments.

cheatsheet.def: Serverless compute for containers on Amazon ECS and Amazon EKS, so you do not manage EC2 instances.
cheatsheet.probe: Fargate is not an orchestrator; ECS or EKS still schedules the containers.

cheatsheet.def: SLI is the measurement, SLO is the target, and the error budget is the allowed failure, 100% minus the SLO.
cheatsheet.probe: A 99.9% monthly SLO allows about 43 minutes of downtime in 30 days.

cheatsheet.def: Canary sends a small slice of traffic to the new version first; blue/green runs two full environments and switches all traffic at once.
cheatsheet.probe: Both make rollback a traffic switch instead of a redeploy.

cheatsheet.term: API Gateway REST vs HTTP API
cheatsheet.def: REST APIs have more features; HTTP APIs are simpler and lower cost.
cheatsheet.probe: API keys, usage plans, request validation, caching, and AWS WAF are REST API features.

questions.q: What is the software development lifecycle, and how does Agile or Scrum change it?
questions.plain: Traditional development is like building a whole house from blueprints and only showing it to the owner at the end. Agile is building one room at a time, showing it every two weeks, and changing the plan based on what the owner actually likes.
questions.technical: The SDLC is the set of phases every product goes through: plan, gather requirements, design, build, test, release, and operate. Waterfall runs these once in sequence, so feedback comes late. Agile runs them in short cycles and favors working software and customer feedback over fixed upfront plans. Scrum is one Agile framework: a product owner keeps a prioritized backlog, the team commits to a sprint goal for usually one to four weeks, holds a short daily standup, then a sprint review with stakeholders and a retrospective on its own process. DevOps extends the same thinking into operations with automation and shared ownership.

probes.q: When is waterfall still reasonable?
probes.a: When requirements are fixed and regulated up front, or when change is very expensive, such as hardware or some government contracts.

probes.q: What is a definition of done?
probes.a: The shared checklist a story must meet, such as tested, reviewed, and deployable, before the team counts it as complete.

questions.aws: AWS working backwards and two-pizza teams fit this model; CodePipeline and similar tools automate the build, test, and release phases.
questions.trap: Thinking Agile means no planning or no documentation. It means planning in smaller increments and adjusting with feedback.

questions.q: What is CI/CD and why does it matter to a business?
questions.plain: It is an assembly line with quality checks at every station. Every small change gets built and tested automatically, so problems are caught in minutes instead of at the end, and shipping becomes a routine button press instead of a risky weekend event.
questions.technical: Continuous integration means developers merge small changes often, and each merge triggers an automated build and test run, so integration problems surface quickly. Continuous delivery means every passing build is packaged and deployable, usually with an approval gate before production. Continuous deployment removes that gate and ships automatically. A typical pipeline: commit, build an artifact or container image, unit and integration tests, security and policy checks, deploy to staging, deploy to production gradually, then monitor and roll back automatically if alarms fire. The business value is smaller, safer, more frequent releases, which the DORA metrics capture: deployment frequency, lead time, change failure rate, and time to restore.

probes.q: Delivery vs deployment?
probes.a: Delivery keeps every build releasable with a human approval. Deployment pushes every passing change to production automatically.

probes.q: What breaks CI in practice?
probes.a: Long-lived branches and flaky or slow tests. Teams stop trusting a pipeline that fails randomly.

questions.aws: AWS CodePipeline orchestrates stages, AWS CodeBuild builds and tests, and AWS CodeDeploy rolls out to EC2, ECS, or Lambda with canary or linear traffic shifting. Many teams use GitHub Actions or Jenkins with the same pattern.
questions.resume: At Oracle, I built a CLI toolchain on Jenkins CI/CD with scripted pre-deployment validation. Four teams adopted it, release cycles got 34% shorter, and failed deploys dropped from 11% to 4%.
questions.trap: Treating CI/CD as just a build server. Without good automated tests and gradual rollout, it only ships bugs faster.

questions.q: What is infrastructure as code, and how do CloudFormation and CDK relate?
questions.plain: Instead of setting up each office by hand and hoping it matches the last one, you write a recipe. Anyone can follow the recipe and get an identical office, and if someone changes the recipe, you can see exactly what changed and who did it.
questions.technical: Infrastructure as code describes resources such as networks, databases, and permissions in version-controlled files that a tool applies. Benefits: repeatable environments, code review for infrastructure changes, easy rebuilds for disaster recovery, and less configuration drift. AWS CloudFormation is declarative: you describe the desired state in a YAML or JSON template, and it creates, updates, or rolls back a stack, with change sets to preview updates and drift detection to spot manual edits. The AWS CDK lets you define the same infrastructure in a general-purpose language such as TypeScript or Python with reusable constructs; it synthesizes CloudFormation templates, which CloudFormation then deploys. Terraform is a popular multi-cloud alternative.

probes.q: What is configuration drift?
probes.a: When live resources no longer match the code because someone changed them by hand. CloudFormation drift detection reports it.

probes.q: Why choose CDK over raw templates?
probes.a: Loops, types, and reusable components make large setups shorter and safer, while still producing standard CloudFormation.

questions.aws: AWS CloudFormation, AWS CDK, and AWS SAM for serverless apps, which also builds on CloudFormation.
questions.trap: Saying CDK replaces CloudFormation. CDK generates CloudFormation; CloudFormation still provisions and tracks the resources.

questions.q: When would you recommend a monolith, microservices, or serverless?
questions.plain: A monolith is one big restaurant kitchen: simple to run when small, but crowded as it grows. Microservices are a food hall of separate stalls that each run on their own. Serverless is a catering service: you send the order and only pay for the meals, without owning a kitchen at all.
questions.technical: A monolith is one deployable unit. It is simplest to build, test, and debug, and is often right for a new product or small team, though scaling and releasing pieces independently gets harder as it grows. Microservices split by business capability, each owning its data and deployed independently, so teams move in parallel and scale hot spots separately. The cost is network calls, distributed failures, data consistency, and much more operational tooling. Serverless, such as Lambda with API Gateway, SQS, and DynamoDB, removes server management and scales to zero, which fits spiky or event-driven work, with limits on run time and some cold-start latency. Many teams start with a modular monolith and split out services where the pain is real.

probes.q: What is the strangler fig pattern?
probes.a: Gradually route features from the old system to new services behind a facade until the old system can be retired.

probes.q: Biggest microservices mistake?
probes.a: Sharing one database across services, which keeps them coupled and loses the main benefit.

questions.aws: Monolith on EC2 or Elastic Beanstalk; microservices on ECS, EKS, or Fargate; serverless with Lambda, API Gateway, Step Functions, and DynamoDB.
questions.trap: Recommending microservices by default. For a small team, they often add more operational cost than they save.

questions.q: What makes a good REST API?
questions.plain: A good API is like a well-organized library. Every book has a clear shelf address, there are a few standard things you can do (borrow, return, renew), and when something goes wrong, the librarian tells you exactly what and why.
questions.technical: REST models the system as resources with stable URLs, usually plural nouns such as /orders/123, manipulated with standard HTTP methods: GET reads, POST creates, PUT replaces, PATCH partially updates, and DELETE removes. GET, PUT, and DELETE should be idempotent. Use meaningful status codes: 200 and 201 for success, 400 for bad input, 401 and 403 for auth, 404 for not found, 409 for conflicts, 429 for throttling, and 5xx for server faults. Return consistent JSON error bodies, support filtering and pagination on lists, version the API, and keep requests stateless, with each call carrying its own authentication. Document it with OpenAPI.

probes.q: PUT vs PATCH?
probes.a: PUT replaces the whole resource and is idempotent. PATCH changes only some fields.

probes.q: When choose gRPC instead?
probes.a: For internal service-to-service calls that need low latency, strong typing, and streaming. REST is friendlier for public and browser clients.

questions.aws: Amazon API Gateway can import OpenAPI definitions and front Lambda, containers, or HTTP backends.
questions.trap: Putting verbs in URLs like /getOrder or returning 200 with an error message inside. Clients and monitoring then cannot tell success from failure.

questions.q: How do you handle API versioning and pagination?
questions.plain: Versioning is like a phone company keeping the old number working while you move to a new plan, so nobody's calls suddenly break. Pagination is a waiter bringing a long menu one page at a time, with a bookmark so you can ask for the next page.
questions.technical: Versioning lets you change an API without breaking existing clients. Common approaches: a version in the path, such as /v2/orders, which is simple and visible, or a header or media type. Prefer additive, backward-compatible changes, and introduce a new version only for breaking ones, with a published deprecation window. For pagination, offset and limit is easy but slow on large tables and can skip or repeat items when data changes between pages. Cursor-based pagination returns an opaque next token encoding the last seen key, so each page is an indexed seek and stays consistent. Always cap page size.

probes.q: What counts as a breaking change?
probes.a: Removing or renaming a field, changing a type, or making an optional input required. Adding an optional field is not.

probes.q: How do AWS APIs paginate?
probes.a: Most return a NextToken, and DynamoDB returns LastEvaluatedKey, which you pass back to get the next page.

questions.aws: API Gateway stages and custom domain base path mappings can route /v1 and /v2 to different backends.
questions.trap: Using large offsets on big datasets. The database still scans and discards all the skipped rows, so later pages get slower.

questions.q: What is an idempotency key, and why do payment APIs need one?
questions.plain: If you press the elevator button five times, the elevator still comes once. An idempotency key gives a payment that same property: if your phone loses signal and resends the payment, the bank sees the same ticket number and charges you once, not twice.
questions.technical: An operation is idempotent if doing it many times has the same effect as doing it once. POST requests that create things, such as charges, are not idempotent by nature, but networks time out and clients retry. With an idempotency key, the client generates a unique ID per logical operation and sends it, usually in a header. The server atomically records the key with the request and result, for example with a conditional write in DynamoDB. If the same key arrives again, it returns the stored result instead of acting again. If the key is reused with a different request body, it rejects it. Keys expire after a retention window. The same idea is needed for message consumers, because at-least-once delivery means duplicates.

probes.q: What if two retries arrive at the same time?
probes.a: The atomic insert lets only one win. The other sees the key as in progress and waits or gets a conflict response.

probes.q: Does SQS FIFO remove the need?
probes.a: It deduplicates within a five-minute window, but side effects in downstream systems should still be idempotent.

questions.aws: Powertools for AWS Lambda includes an idempotency utility backed by DynamoDB; Step Functions Standard workflows give exactly-once step execution.
questions.trap: Assuming retries are safe because the request is identical. Without a key, the server cannot tell a retry from a second real purchase.

questions.q: What is the difference between a stateless and a stateful service, and how do sessions fit in?
questions.plain: A stateless service is a call center where any agent can help you because your case notes are in a shared system. A stateful one is where only the agent you first spoke to remembers you, so if they go home, you start over.
questions.technical: A stateless service keeps no client-specific data in its own memory between requests. Each request carries what is needed, such as a token, or the service reads shared state from a database or cache. Any instance can serve any request, so you can add, remove, or replace instances freely, which makes horizontal scaling and failure recovery simple. A stateful service holds data locally, like databases, in-memory sessions, or WebSocket connections, and needs routing, replication, or careful failover. For web sessions, store session data in a shared store such as ElastiCache for Redis or DynamoDB, or use signed tokens. Sticky sessions on a load balancer work but unbalance load and lose sessions when an instance dies.

probes.q: Is a JWT stateless session handling?
probes.a: Yes, the token carries the claims, but early revocation then needs extra state such as a deny list.

probes.q: Where should state live then?
probes.a: In managed, replicated services built for it: RDS or Aurora, DynamoDB, ElastiCache, or S3.

questions.aws: Stateless app tiers behind an Application Load Balancer in an Auto Scaling group, with state in DynamoDB, ElastiCache, or Aurora.
questions.trap: Calling a service stateless while it writes uploads to local disk. That breaks as soon as a request lands on another instance.

questions.q: Horizontal vs vertical scaling: which would you choose?
questions.plain: Vertical scaling is replacing your delivery van with a bigger truck. Horizontal scaling is adding more vans. A bigger truck eventually hits a size limit and is one point of failure; more vans can keep growing, and if one breaks down the others keep delivering.
questions.technical: Vertical scaling, scale up, moves to a larger instance with more CPU and memory. It needs no code changes, but has a hardware ceiling, usually needs a restart, and leaves a single point of failure. Horizontal scaling, scale out, adds more instances behind a load balancer. It needs stateless design or partitioned data, but grows further, adds redundancy across Availability Zones, and can scale back in to save cost. Stateless web and app tiers almost always scale horizontally. Relational databases often scale up first, then out with read replicas, caching, or sharding. Autoscaling should track a metric that reflects user load, not only CPU.

probes.q: How does a database scale horizontally?
probes.a: Read replicas for reads, caching to take load off, and sharding or a distributed database like DynamoDB for writes.

probes.q: What is target tracking scaling?
probes.a: You set a target, such as average CPU at 50% or requests per target, and Auto Scaling adds or removes capacity to hold it.

questions.aws: EC2 Auto Scaling groups, ECS service autoscaling, Kubernetes autoscalers on EKS, Aurora read replicas, and DynamoDB on-demand capacity.
questions.resume: At Oracle, I containerized NSX services with Docker and Kubernetes and set autoscaling on custom Prometheus metrics instead of CPU alone, which held p99 SLOs at 2x peak load through release surges.
questions.trap: Scaling on CPU by default. Many services are bound by connections, queue depth, or latency, so CPU can look fine while users wait.

questions.q: When should services talk synchronously, and when asynchronously?
questions.plain: Synchronous is a phone call: you wait on the line until you get an answer. Asynchronous is leaving a note in an inbox: you go on with your day, and the work gets done when someone picks it up. If the other person is busy, the phone call fails but the note just waits.
questions.technical: Synchronous calls, such as REST or gRPC, are request and response: the caller waits. They are simple and right when the user needs the answer now, like checking a balance. But they chain latency and failure: if any downstream service is slow or down, the caller is too. Asynchronous communication puts work on a queue or event bus and returns immediately. It decouples producers from consumers, absorbs traffic spikes, allows retries, and lets each side scale and fail independently. The costs are eventual consistency, harder debugging, and the need for idempotent consumers and dead-letter queues. A common pattern: accept an order synchronously, then process payment, inventory, and email asynchronously.

probes.q: How do you tell the user the async work finished?
probes.a: Return a job ID and let the client poll a status endpoint, or push a notification through WebSockets, email, or a callback.

probes.q: What is a dead-letter queue?
probes.a: A queue that receives messages that failed processing a set number of times, so they can be inspected without blocking the main queue.

questions.aws: Synchronous through API Gateway or an Application Load Balancer; asynchronous with SQS, SNS, EventBridge, and Lambda asynchronous invocation with on-failure destinations.
questions.trap: Making everything asynchronous. If the user needs the result to continue, a queue just adds latency and complexity.

questions.q: What is the difference between a queue and pub/sub? How do SQS and SNS fit?
questions.plain: A queue is a deli ticket line: each order is handled by exactly one worker. Pub/sub is a radio broadcast: one announcement, and everyone tuned in hears it. Often you combine them: broadcast the news, and each department keeps its own to-do line.
questions.technical: A queue is point to point: producers send messages, and each message is processed by one of a pool of competing consumers, which spreads work and buffers load. Amazon SQS is a fully managed queue: consumers poll, delete a message after success, and a visibility timeout hides in-flight messages so a crash lets another consumer retry. Pub/sub is one to many: a publisher sends to a topic and every subscriber gets a copy. Amazon SNS pushes to subscribers such as SQS queues, Lambda, HTTP endpoints, email, or SMS. The fan-out pattern publishes once to SNS with an SQS queue per downstream service, so each consumes at its own pace and retries independently.

probes.q: Why put SQS behind SNS instead of subscribing Lambda directly?
probes.a: The queue buffers and retries if the consumer is slow or failing, and lets you control concurrency.

probes.q: Where does Kafka or Kinesis fit?
probes.a: They are durable, ordered logs that multiple consumers can replay at their own offset, suited to streaming and event history.

questions.aws: Amazon SQS, Amazon SNS (both with FIFO variants), Amazon Kinesis Data Streams and Amazon MSK for streaming logs.
questions.trap: Expecting two different services to both receive a message from one SQS queue. They compete for it; use SNS or EventBridge to fan out.

questions.q: What is event-driven architecture, and where does Amazon EventBridge fit?
questions.plain: Instead of the sales team phoning shipping, billing, and marketing every time an order comes in, it just rings a bell that says order placed. Each team listens for the bells it cares about. Sales does not even need to know who is listening, so adding a new team changes nothing for sales.
questions.technical: In event-driven design, services emit events, facts about something that happened such as OrderPlaced, and other services react. Producers do not know or call the consumers, so teams can add new consumers without changing the producer. Amazon EventBridge is a serverless event bus: events from your apps, AWS services, and supported SaaS partners arrive on a bus, rules match event patterns on content, and matched events go to targets such as Lambda, Step Functions, SQS, or API destinations, with optional input transformation. It also offers archive and replay, a schema registry, EventBridge Pipes for point-to-point source-to-target integrations with filtering and enrichment, and EventBridge Scheduler for cron and one-time schedules.

probes.q: EventBridge vs SNS?
probes.a: SNS is high-throughput fan-out to subscribers. EventBridge adds content-based routing rules, many AWS and SaaS sources, schemas, and replay.

probes.q: Events vs commands?
probes.a: An event says something happened and anyone may react. A command asks one specific service to do something.

questions.aws: Amazon EventBridge event buses, Pipes, and Scheduler, often paired with SQS for buffering and Step Functions for multi-step reactions.
questions.trap: Assuming events give you a clear end-to-end flow for free. Without tracing and an event catalog, it gets hard to see who reacts to what.

questions.q: What is a container and how is it different from a virtual machine?
questions.plain: A shipping container holds goods in a standard box that fits on any ship, train, or truck. A software container does the same: the app and everything it needs go in a standard box that runs the same on a laptop, in a data center, or in any cloud.
questions.technical: A container packages an application with its libraries and runtime into an image, and runs it as an isolated process using kernel features such as namespaces and cgroups. Containers share the host operating system kernel, so they start in seconds and are lightweight. A virtual machine virtualizes hardware and runs a full guest operating system, giving stronger isolation but more overhead. A Docker image is built in layers from a Dockerfile, stored in a registry, and is immutable: you ship the same image through test and production. Good practice: small base images, no secrets baked in, pinned versions, image scanning, and running as a non-root user.

probes.q: Why do containers help consistency?
probes.a: The same immutable image runs in every environment, which ends works-on-my-machine problems.

probes.q: Can a container run anywhere?
probes.a: Anywhere with a compatible kernel and CPU architecture. A Linux x86 image will not run natively on a Windows host or an Arm host without the right variant.

questions.aws: Amazon ECR stores and scans images; ECS, EKS, Fargate, and AWS App Runner run them.
questions.resume: At MSRcosmos, I containerized a multi-agent ERP migration with Docker so it could run on AWS, Azure, and GCP, and at Oracle I containerized NSX services on OCI with Docker and Kubernetes.
questions.trap: Saying containers are as isolated as VMs. They share a kernel, which is why Fargate runs each task in its own isolation boundary.

questions.q: Explain pods, deployments, and services in Kubernetes.
questions.plain: Kubernetes is a restaurant manager. A pod is one cook at a station. A deployment is the manager's rule that there must always be five cooks on shift, replacing anyone who leaves. A service is the single order window customers use, no matter which cooks are working behind it.
questions.technical: Kubernetes runs containers across a cluster and constantly reconciles actual state toward declared desired state. A pod is the smallest deployable unit: one or more containers sharing a network identity and storage, and pods are disposable. A deployment declares how many replicas of a pod template to run and manages rolling updates and rollbacks through ReplicaSets. A service gives a stable virtual IP and DNS name in front of a changing set of pods selected by labels, and load balances across them. An ingress or load balancer exposes services externally. ConfigMaps and Secrets inject configuration, and readiness and liveness probes tell Kubernetes when a pod can take traffic or needs a restart.

probes.q: Readiness vs liveness probe?
probes.a: Readiness decides whether a pod receives traffic. Liveness decides whether the container should be restarted.

probes.q: Why not talk to pod IPs directly?
probes.a: Pods are replaced and get new IPs. The service gives one stable address.

questions.aws: Amazon EKS runs a managed Kubernetes control plane; the AWS Load Balancer Controller provisions ALBs and NLBs for ingress and services.
questions.trap: Treating pods like pets that you fix by hand. They are cattle: let the deployment replace them.

questions.q: How does autoscaling work in Kubernetes, and why might you scale on custom metrics?
questions.plain: Imagine a store that adds cashiers based on how warm the room feels. It works sometimes, but the real signal is the length of the checkout line. Scaling on custom metrics means watching the line itself, so you add cashiers before customers walk out.
questions.technical: There are two layers. The Horizontal Pod Autoscaler changes the replica count of a deployment to keep a metric near a target. By default that is CPU or memory, but through the custom and external metrics APIs, for example with a Prometheus adapter, it can use request rate, queue depth, or latency. Node autoscaling, through Cluster Autoscaler or Karpenter, adds nodes when pods cannot be scheduled and removes idle ones. CPU is a poor signal for I/O-bound or latency-sensitive services: CPU stays moderate while requests queue. Good practice: pick a metric that tracks user experience, set resource requests accurately, tune scale-up to be fast and scale-down to be slow, and keep warm headroom for spikes.

probes.q: Why must resource requests be set?
probes.a: The scheduler places pods by requests, and CPU utilization targets are computed against them. Wrong requests mean wrong scaling.

probes.q: What is Karpenter?
probes.a: An open-source node autoscaler, started by AWS, that provisions right-sized nodes directly for pending pods.

probes.q: How do you avoid flapping?
probes.a: Use stabilization windows and slower scale-down so brief dips do not remove capacity you need again a minute later.

questions.aws: On EKS: HPA with CloudWatch or Prometheus metrics, Karpenter or Cluster Autoscaler for nodes; Amazon Managed Service for Prometheus can supply the metrics.
questions.resume: At Oracle, I set Kubernetes autoscaling for NSX services on custom Prometheus metrics instead of CPU alone, and that held our p99 SLOs at 2x peak load through release surges.
questions.trap: Thinking HPA alone handles a spike. If nodes are full, new pods sit pending until node autoscaling adds capacity, which takes longer.

questions.q: How do you choose between ECS, EKS, and Fargate?
questions.plain: ECS and EKS are two different dispatch systems that decide which delivery driver takes which package. Fargate is renting drivers by the hour instead of owning a fleet of vans. You pick a dispatch system, then decide whether to own the vans or rent.
questions.technical: Amazon ECS is the AWS-native container orchestrator: simpler, deeply integrated with IAM, load balancers, and CloudWatch, with no control plane to manage. Amazon EKS is managed Kubernetes: choose it when the team already knows Kubernetes, needs its ecosystem such as Helm and operators, or wants portability across clouds and on premises. AWS Fargate is not an orchestrator. It is serverless compute that both ECS and EKS can use, so you do not provision or patch EC2 instances. Each Fargate task gets its own isolation boundary. Use EC2-backed capacity instead when you need GPUs, special instance types, daemon-style agents, or lower cost at steady high utilization.

probes.q: When is EC2 cheaper than Fargate?
probes.a: For large, steady workloads where you can pack instances densely and use Savings Plans or Spot. Fargate shines for variable or small workloads and low ops effort.

probes.q: Is there a simpler option still?
probes.a: AWS App Runner deploys a web service from an image or source with load balancing and scaling built in.

questions.aws: ECS on Fargate is often the lowest-effort path for a new containerized service; EKS fits Kubernetes-standard organizations.
questions.trap: Saying Fargate competes with ECS. Fargate is a capacity option underneath ECS or EKS.

questions.q: What is AWS Lambda and when is it a good or bad fit?
questions.plain: Lambda is like a taxi instead of owning a car. You do not maintain anything; you pay only for the ride, and a thousand taxis can show up at once if a thousand people need rides. But for a cross-country trip every day, owning the car is cheaper.
questions.technical: AWS Lambda runs your code in response to events, such as an API request, an S3 upload, a queue message, or a schedule, without servers to manage. It scales by running more concurrent copies and bills per request and per millisecond of duration, scaling to zero when idle. Good fits: spiky or unpredictable traffic, event processing, glue between services, and lightweight APIs. Constraints: the timeout defaults to 3 seconds and maxes out at 15 minutes, cold starts add latency to some requests, and functions should be stateless. Poor fits: long-running jobs, constant heavy load where containers or instances are cheaper, and workloads needing special hardware.

probes.q: How do you reduce cold starts?
probes.a: Keep packages small, initialize clients outside the handler, and use provisioned concurrency or SnapStart where supported for latency-critical paths.

probes.q: What if a job takes 40 minutes?
probes.a: Split it into steps with Step Functions, or run it as a container on ECS or Fargate or with AWS Batch.

questions.aws: Lambda with API Gateway for APIs, with SQS or EventBridge for events, and with Step Functions for orchestration.
questions.trap: Assuming serverless is always cheaper. At high, steady utilization, per-request pricing can exceed the cost of containers or instances.

questions.q: What does Amazon API Gateway do, and how do you choose between REST APIs and HTTP APIs?
questions.plain: API Gateway is the reception desk in front of your offices. It checks visitors' badges, turns away crowds, and sends each visitor to the right room. HTTP APIs are a simpler, cheaper desk; REST APIs are the full concierge desk with more services.
questions.technical: API Gateway is a managed front door for APIs. It handles routing, authorization, throttling, CORS, and monitoring in front of Lambda, HTTP backends, or private resources in a VPC. There are REST APIs, HTTP APIs, and WebSocket APIs. REST APIs have more features: API keys and usage plans for per-client throttling, request validation and body transformation, caching, AWS WAF integration, private and edge-optimized endpoints, canary releases, and X-Ray tracing. HTTP APIs are designed with fewer features at a lower price, with native JWT authorizers and automatic deployments. Choose HTTP APIs by default when you do not need REST-only features.

probes.q: How do you protect an API from abuse?
probes.a: Authorizers for identity, throttling limits, usage plans with API keys on REST APIs, and AWS WAF on REST APIs.

probes.q: Are API keys an authentication method?
probes.a: No. They identify a client for usage plans and throttling. Use IAM, Cognito, JWT, or Lambda authorizers for real authorization.

questions.aws: Amazon API Gateway REST, HTTP, and WebSocket APIs; an Application Load Balancer is an alternative front door for containers.
questions.trap: Picking HTTP APIs and later needing AWS WAF, caching, or API keys, which are REST API features. Check requirements first.

questions.q: When would you use AWS Step Functions, and Standard or Express workflows?
questions.plain: Step Functions is a project manager with a checklist. It knows which task comes next, what to do if one fails, when to wait for a human signature, and it keeps a record of exactly where every job is.
questions.technical: Step Functions orchestrates multi-step workflows as state machines defined in Amazon States Language, with built-in retries, error catching, parallel branches, maps over items, waits, and direct integrations with many AWS services. It replaces fragile chains of functions calling functions. Standard workflows run up to one year, use exactly-once execution, keep execution history for 90 days, support callbacks with task tokens for human approvals, and are priced per state transition, which suits long, auditable, non-idempotent processes like order fulfillment or payments. Express workflows run up to five minutes, are priced by executions, duration, and memory, and suit high-volume event processing. Asynchronous Express is at-least-once and synchronous Express is at-most-once, so steps should be idempotent.

probes.q: Can you switch a workflow from Standard to Express later?
probes.a: No. The type is fixed when you create the state machine, so you create a new one.

probes.q: How do you add a human approval step?
probes.a: Use the wait for task token callback pattern in a Standard workflow, sending the token to the approver and resuming when it comes back.

questions.aws: Step Functions with Lambda, ECS tasks, SQS, DynamoDB, and Amazon Bedrock as task steps.
questions.trap: Choosing Express for a payment flow because it is cheaper. At-least-once execution can repeat a non-idempotent step.

questions.q: When would you choose an SQS FIFO queue over a standard queue?
questions.plain: A standard queue is a busy mail room that handles huge volume but might occasionally deliver a letter twice or out of order. A FIFO queue is a numbered ticket counter: strictly in order, no duplicates, but it serves fewer people per minute.
questions.technical: Standard queues offer nearly unlimited throughput, at-least-once delivery, so occasional duplicates, and best-effort ordering. Consumers must be idempotent. FIFO queues guarantee first-in, first-out order within a message group ID and exactly-once processing, using a deduplication ID or content-based deduplication within a five-minute window. Throughput is lower: 300 API calls per second per action without batching, 3,000 messages per second with batches of 10, and higher in high-throughput mode. Message groups allow parallelism: order is kept per group, such as per customer, while different groups process concurrently. Choose FIFO when order or no-duplicate processing is a business requirement, such as price updates or account ledger events.

probes.q: How do you scale a FIFO queue?
probes.a: Use many message group IDs so groups process in parallel, use batching, and enable high-throughput mode.

probes.q: What happens if one message in a group keeps failing?
probes.a: It blocks later messages in that group until it succeeds or moves to a dead-letter queue, so set a redrive policy.

questions.aws: SQS standard and FIFO queues, SNS FIFO topics for ordered fan-out, and Lambda event source mappings that respect FIFO group order.
questions.trap: Choosing FIFO for everything to be safe. It caps throughput, and most workloads are better served by standard queues with idempotent consumers.

questions.q: What are logs, metrics, and traces, and why do you need all three?
questions.plain: Metrics are your car dashboard: speed and fuel at a glance. Logs are the mechanic's detailed notes on what happened. Traces are a GPS record of the whole trip, showing exactly where you were stuck in traffic.
questions.technical: Metrics are numeric time series, such as request rate, error rate, latency percentiles, and saturation. They are cheap to store, good for dashboards and alerts, and answer is something wrong. Logs are timestamped event records with detail. Structured JSON logs with a request ID answer what exactly happened. Traces follow one request across services as a tree of timed spans and answer where the time or the error came from. Together they move from alert to cause: a metric alarm fires, a trace shows which service is slow, and that service's logs show why. Use percentiles like p99, not averages, and propagate a correlation ID everywhere.

probes.q: Why p99 and not average latency?
probes.a: Averages hide the slow tail. The p99 shows what the unluckiest 1% of users experience, and heavy users hit the tail often.

probes.q: What is OpenTelemetry?
probes.a: A vendor-neutral standard and SDKs for emitting traces, metrics, and logs, so you can switch backends without re-instrumenting.

questions.aws: Amazon CloudWatch for metrics, logs, alarms, and dashboards; AWS X-Ray for distributed traces and service maps, commonly instrumented with OpenTelemetry; Amazon Managed Grafana and Managed Service for Prometheus as open-source options.
questions.resume: At Oracle, I ran Prometheus and Grafana observability across 37,000+ enterprise tenants and built 47 dashboards and alert rules.
questions.trap: Logging everything and calling it observability. Without metrics to detect and traces to locate, you search a haystack during an outage.

questions.q: Explain SLIs, SLOs, and error budgets.
questions.plain: An SLI is the thermometer reading, such as how many orders went through fine. The SLO is the promise: 99.9% of orders go through fine. The error budget is the small allowance for things going wrong; while you have budget left, you can move fast, and when it is spent, you slow down and fix reliability.
questions.technical: A service level indicator is a measured ratio of good events to total events from the user's view, such as requests served successfully under 300 milliseconds. A service level objective is the target for that SLI over a window, such as 99.9% over 30 days. A service level agreement is a contract with penalties, usually looser than the internal SLO. The error budget is 100% minus the SLO: 99.9% over 30 days allows about 43 minutes of bad time. It turns reliability into a shared decision: while budget remains, ship features; when it burns too fast, prioritize reliability work. Alert on burn rate, how fast the budget is being consumed, rather than on every blip.

probes.q: Why not target 100%?
probes.a: It is impossibly expensive, users cannot tell the difference beyond some point, and it freezes all change.

probes.q: What is a burn rate alert?
probes.a: An alert when errors consume the budget faster than planned, for example at a rate that would exhaust a month's budget in a few days.

questions.aws: Amazon CloudWatch Application Signals supports defining SLOs on service metrics; CloudWatch alarms can alert on SLI thresholds.
questions.resume: At Oracle, I moved alerting from static thresholds to SLOs on CPU, memory, and p99 latency across 47 dashboards and alert rules, which cut false-positive pages by 41%.
questions.trap: Confusing SLO and SLA. The SLA is the external contract; the SLO is the stricter internal target that protects it.

questions.q: How do you design alerting that wakes people up only when it matters?
questions.plain: A smoke alarm that goes off every time you make toast gets its battery pulled, and then it is useless in a real fire. Good alerting rings only for real fire, meaning something customers actually feel, and tells you which room it is in.
questions.technical: Page on symptoms, not causes: alert when users are hurt, such as error rate, latency against the SLO, or failed checkouts, rather than on every high CPU or a single host failing, which redundancy should absorb. Every page must be actionable, urgent, and linked to a runbook; anything else becomes a ticket or a dashboard. Use SLO burn-rate alerts with a fast window for sudden outages and a slow window for gradual leaks. Reduce noise by grouping related alerts, setting sensible evaluation periods, and reviewing every page after on-call shifts to tune or delete. Cause-level signals stay on dashboards for diagnosis. Track the false-positive rate as a metric.

probes.q: Should high CPU ever page someone?
probes.a: Only if it predicts imminent user impact that automation cannot fix, such as a database about to saturate. Usually it is a dashboard signal.

probes.q: How do you combine many alarms?
probes.a: CloudWatch composite alarms can page only when several conditions are true together, cutting duplicate noise.

questions.aws: CloudWatch alarms and composite alarms, routed through SNS or incident tools, with runbooks in Systems Manager.
questions.resume: At Oracle, I replaced static threshold alerts with SLO-based alerting on CPU, memory, and p99 latency, and that cut false-positive pages by 41%. I also added auto-tagging of root causes on 400 and 500 series failures with runbook context, which helped bring P1 MTTR from 94 to 26 minutes.
questions.trap: Adding an alert for every metric to be safe. Alert fatigue is how real incidents get missed.

questions.q: Compare rolling, blue/green, and canary deployments.
questions.plain: Rolling is repainting a hotel one floor at a time while guests stay. Blue/green is building a second identical hotel, then moving every guest over at once, with the old one kept ready. Canary is moving a few guests first and checking they are happy before moving everyone.
questions.technical: A rolling deployment replaces instances in batches. It needs no extra capacity, but old and new versions run side by side, and rollback means rolling back again. Blue/green runs a full new environment next to the old one, tests it, then switches traffic at the load balancer or DNS. Rollback is an instant switch back, at the cost of double capacity during the cutover. Canary shifts a small share of traffic, such as 5%, to the new version, watches error and latency metrics against the old version, then promotes in steps or rolls back automatically. All need backward-compatible database changes, because both versions touch the same data during the transition.

probes.q: How do you handle database schema changes?
probes.a: Expand and contract: add new columns or tables compatible with both versions, migrate, and remove the old ones only after the old version is gone.

probes.q: What metrics gate a canary?
probes.a: Error rate, p99 latency, and key business metrics, compared with the baseline, with alarms wired to automatic rollback.

questions.aws: AWS CodeDeploy supports in-place and blue/green deployments, with canary and linear traffic shifting for Lambda and ECS and automatic rollback on CloudWatch alarms; API Gateway REST APIs have canary releases; ALB weighted target groups split traffic.
questions.trap: Thinking blue/green makes database rollback free. Traffic switches back instantly; data written by the new version does not.

questions.q: What are feature flags and how do they relate to rollback?
questions.plain: A feature flag is a light switch wired into new code. The code ships to everyone with the switch off, and you turn it on for a few people, then everyone. If something goes wrong, you flip the switch off in seconds instead of rebuilding the house.
questions.technical: Feature flags decouple deploying code from releasing a feature. New code ships dark behind a runtime toggle, then is enabled for internal users, a percentage of customers, or specific segments, and turned off instantly if metrics degrade, with no redeploy. That makes rollback for a feature a configuration change in seconds. Code-level rollback still matters for bad builds: keep previous artifacts versioned and immutable, automate the rollback path, and test it. Flags carry costs: stale flags become technical debt and hidden branches, so set owners and expiry dates, and remove flags after full rollout.

probes.q: Flag vs canary?
probes.a: A canary splits traffic between two deployed versions. A flag switches a feature inside one version, often per user. They complement each other.

probes.q: What is the danger of leaving flags in?
probes.a: Combinations multiply untested code paths, and an old flag flipped by mistake can resurrect retired behavior.
