cheatsheet.def: On-demand IT resources over the internet with pay-as-you-go pricing.
cheatsheet.probe: Renting electricity from the grid instead of running your own generator.

cheatsheet.def: Rent raw servers, rent a platform to run your code, or rent finished software.
cheatsheet.probe: Who manages what: the higher the model, the less you manage.

cheatsheet.def: Shared provider cloud, dedicated cloud, a mix with on-premises, or several providers.
cheatsheet.probe: Hybrid mixes on-premises with cloud; multi-cloud means more than one provider.

cheatsheet.def: Variable expense, economies of scale, stop guessing capacity, speed and agility, stop running data centers, go global in minutes.
cheatsheet.probe: Name them in AWS's words.

cheatsheet.def: A Region is a geographic area with multiple isolated AZs; an AZ is one or more data centers with separate power and networking.
cheatsheet.probe: Spread across AZs for high availability; across Regions for disaster recovery.

cheatsheet.def: A site close to users that caches content and serves DNS and edge security.
cheatsheet.probe: Used by CloudFront, Route 53, and Global Accelerator; you do not run EC2 there.

cheatsheet.term: HA vs fault tolerance vs DR
cheatsheet.def: HA: brief blips are OK. Fault tolerance: no visible interruption. DR: recovering from a major disaster.
cheatsheet.probe: Fault tolerance costs more than HA because spares are always running.

cheatsheet.def: RPO: how much data you can lose. RTO: how long you can be down.
cheatsheet.probe: RPO looks back to the last good copy, RTO looks forward to recovery.

cheatsheet.def: Backup and restore, pilot light, warm standby, multi-site active/active: cheapest and slowest to costliest and fastest.
cheatsheet.probe: Pilot light cannot serve traffic until switched on; warm standby can, at reduced capacity.

cheatsheet.def: Scalability is the ability to grow; elasticity is growing and shrinking automatically with demand.
cheatsheet.probe: Elastic means you also scale in and stop paying.

cheatsheet.def: On-Demand, Savings Plans, Reserved Instances, Spot.
cheatsheet.probe: Spot is cheapest but can be interrupted with a two-minute warning.

cheatsheet.def: Operational excellence, security, reliability, performance efficiency, cost optimization, sustainability.
cheatsheet.probe: There are six; sustainability was added last.

cheatsheet.def: Retire, retain, rehost, relocate, repurchase, replatform, refactor.
cheatsheet.probe: Rehost is lift and shift; replatform is lift, tinker, and shift.

cheatsheet.def: AWS secures the cloud itself; the customer secures what they put in the cloud.
cheatsheet.probe: The split shifts with the service, but data and access are always the customer's.

questions.q: What is cloud computing, in plain English?
questions.plain: Cloud computing means renting computers, storage, and software over the internet and paying only for what you use. It is like getting electricity from the power grid instead of running your own generator: you flip a switch, it works, and you pay for the kilowatts, not the power plant.
questions.technical: Cloud computing is the on-demand delivery of IT resources, such as compute, storage, databases, networking, and higher-level services, over the internet with pay-as-you-go pricing. The provider owns and operates the hardware and data centers; customers provision resources through an API or console in minutes and release them when done. Key traits are self-service, broad network access, pooled resources shared across many customers, rapid elasticity, and measured usage. That shifts IT from large up-front purchases to an operating expense tied to actual use.

probes.q: What does 'pooled resources' mean?
probes.a: The provider serves many customers from the same large fleet, isolated from each other, which is how it gets economies of scale.

probes.q: Is the cloud just someone else's computer?
probes.a: Partly, but the value is the automation, global reach, managed services, and pay-per-use on top of the hardware.

questions.aws: AWS offers more than 200 services across compute, storage, databases, analytics, AI, and more, all provisioned by API.
questions.trap: Defining cloud as 'storing files online.' Storage is one piece; the real idea is renting any IT resource on demand and paying per use.

questions.q: How does the cloud change IT spending from capital expense to operating expense?
questions.plain: Before the cloud, a company had to buy servers up front, like buying a delivery truck before knowing how many packages it would ship. With the cloud, it is more like using a rideshare: you pay per trip. Money stays free for the business, and if a project fails, you stop paying instead of owning idle hardware.
questions.technical: Capital expense (capex) is a large up-front purchase, such as servers, storage, and data center space, depreciated over years and sized for forecast peak. Operating expense (opex) is ongoing spend tied to consumption. Cloud moves most IT to opex: no purchase cycle, no overprovisioning for peak, and costs that track usage. It lowers the cost of experiments and speeds time to market. The flip side is that spend becomes variable and needs governance, tagging, budgets, and commitment discounts for steady usage.

probes.q: Is cloud always cheaper?
probes.a: Not automatically. It is cheaper when you right-size, turn off idle resources, and use the right pricing model. Lift and shift with no tuning can cost more.

probes.q: How do you keep variable spend under control?
probes.a: Tag resources by owner, set AWS Budgets alerts, review Cost Explorer, and commit with Savings Plans for the steady baseline.

questions.aws: AWS's first stated advantage of cloud is 'Trade fixed expense for variable expense.'
questions.trap: Promising a customer the cloud is cheaper by default. The honest pitch is that cost follows usage and can be optimized, with agility as the bigger win.

questions.q: What are the six advantages of cloud computing, as AWS describes them?
questions.plain: In short: pay as you go instead of buying up front, get bulk-discount prices because AWS buys at huge scale, stop guessing how much you will need, move faster, stop spending on running buildings full of servers, and reach customers worldwide in minutes. It is like switching from owning a fleet of cars to a rideshare service everywhere you travel.
questions.technical: From the Overview of AWS whitepaper: 1. Trade fixed expense for variable expense: pay only for what you consume. 2. Benefit from massive economies of scale: aggregated usage across customers lowers pay-as-you-go prices. 3. Stop guessing capacity: scale up and down with minutes of notice instead of sitting on idle or insufficient hardware. 4. Increase speed and agility: resources are a click away, so lead time drops from weeks to minutes. 5. Stop spending money running and maintaining data centers. 6. Go global in minutes: deploy in multiple Regions for lower latency.

probes.q: Which one matters most to a startup?
probes.a: Usually speed and agility plus variable expense: they can test ideas cheaply and shut down what fails.

probes.q: Which one matters most to a global enterprise?
probes.a: Often go global in minutes and stop guessing capacity, for launches in new markets and seasonal peaks.

questions.trap: Listing 'cheaper' and 'more secure' as the six. Use AWS's own six phrases; security is covered by the shared responsibility model, not this list.

questions.q: Explain IaaS, PaaS, and SaaS with examples.
questions.plain: Think of pizza. IaaS is renting a kitchen: you bring ingredients and cook. PaaS is a pizza shop where you pick toppings and they bake it. SaaS is pizza delivered to your door: you just eat. The further along you go, the less you manage and the less you control.
questions.technical: IaaS (infrastructure as a service) gives virtual machines, storage, and networks; you manage the operating system, runtime, and app. Examples: Amazon EC2, Amazon EBS, Amazon VPC. PaaS (platform as a service) gives a managed environment where you deploy code or data and the provider runs the OS, patching, and scaling. Examples: AWS Elastic Beanstalk, Amazon RDS, AWS Lambda (often called serverless or FaaS). SaaS (software as a service) is a finished application used through a browser or API. Examples: Salesforce, Microsoft 365, Amazon Connect.

probes.q: Where does serverless fit?
probes.a: It sits at or above PaaS: you provide only code or configuration, with no servers to manage and billing per use.

probes.q: Why would someone choose IaaS over PaaS?
probes.a: For full control of the OS and software, for legacy apps that need specific setups, or for licensing reasons.

questions.aws: EC2 is IaaS; RDS, Elastic Beanstalk, and Lambda are managed or platform services; Amazon Connect and Amazon Quick are SaaS-style offerings.
questions.trap: Classifying by vendor instead of by who manages what. The test is which layers the customer still operates.

questions.q: What does serverless mean, and when is it a good fit?
questions.plain: Serverless does not mean there are no servers. It means you never see or manage them. It is like a taxi instead of owning a car: you do not worry about the engine, parking, or insurance, and you pay only for the ride. When no one is riding, you pay nothing.
questions.technical: Serverless services run your code or store your data without you provisioning, patching, or scaling servers. They scale automatically, including to zero, and bill per request or per unit of work. Examples: AWS Lambda for functions, Amazon API Gateway, DynamoDB, S3, Step Functions, and Fargate for containers. Good fits are event-driven work, spiky or unpredictable traffic, and small teams. Weaker fits are long-running, steady, high-utilization compute, where reserved capacity can be cheaper, and workloads needing special hardware or very low cold-start latency.

probes.q: What is a cold start?
probes.a: The extra delay when a new function environment starts for the first request. Provisioned concurrency or lighter runtimes reduce it.

probes.q: Is serverless always cheaper?
probes.a: Not for constant heavy load. Per-request pricing wins for spiky traffic; steady high load can be cheaper on reserved instances or containers.

questions.aws: AWS Lambda functions can run up to 15 minutes per invocation; longer jobs suit ECS on Fargate or Step Functions orchestration.
questions.trap: Saying serverless means no operations at all. You still own code quality, permissions, monitoring, and cost.

questions.q: What are public, private, hybrid, and multi-cloud?
questions.plain: Public cloud is like a hotel: shared building, your own locked room, someone else runs it. Private cloud is owning your own house. Hybrid is keeping your house but booking hotel rooms when relatives visit. Multi-cloud is staying at more than one hotel chain.
questions.technical: Public cloud: a provider such as AWS runs shared infrastructure, with logical isolation between customers, on demand. Private cloud: cloud-style self-service on infrastructure dedicated to one organization, usually on premises. Hybrid cloud: on-premises or private systems connected to a public cloud, integrated for workloads, data, or bursting. Common drivers are data residency, low-latency plant equipment, and gradual migration. Multi-cloud: using more than one public cloud provider, for best-of-breed services, acquisitions, customer requirements, or regulatory pressure. Hybrid and multi-cloud can coexist.

probes.q: What AWS services support hybrid?
probes.a: AWS Outposts runs AWS infrastructure on premises; AWS Direct Connect and Site-to-Site VPN link data centers to VPCs; AWS Storage Gateway bridges storage.

probes.q: Hybrid vs multi-cloud in one line?
probes.a: Hybrid mixes on-premises with cloud. Multi-cloud uses more than one cloud provider.

questions.trap: Using hybrid and multi-cloud as synonyms. Hybrid is about on-premises plus cloud; multi-cloud is about several providers.

questions.q: A customer says they want to be multi-cloud to avoid lock-in. How do you respond?
questions.plain: Being on several clouds can protect you, but it costs something, like a company that keeps accounts at three banks: more paperwork, more fees, and staff who must know three systems. I ask what risk they want to avoid, then design just enough portability for that risk instead of doubling everything.
questions.technical: Start with the driver: regulation, a customer contract, an acquisition, best-of-breed services, or negotiation leverage. Then weigh costs: each cloud needs its own skills, security controls, networking, and monitoring; data egress between clouds adds cost and latency; and the lowest common denominator gives up managed services. Practical patterns: containers and Kubernetes plus infrastructure as code for portable compute, open data formats, and identity federation. Often the better answer is one primary cloud with a documented exit plan, and multi-Region on that cloud for resilience.

probes.q: Does multi-cloud improve availability?
probes.a: Only if the app can actually fail over across clouds, which is hard. Multi-AZ and multi-Region on one cloud usually give more resilience per dollar.

probes.q: What makes workloads portable?
probes.a: Containers, open-source data formats and engines, infrastructure as code, and avoiding proprietary APIs in the core path.

probes.q: What is data gravity?
probes.a: Large datasets are expensive and slow to move, so apps tend to run where the data lives.

questions.aws: Amazon EKS Anywhere and Amazon ECS Anywhere can run containers outside AWS with consistent tooling, and AWS IAM Identity Center can federate identities.
questions.resume: At MSRcosmos, I containerized a multi-agent ERP migration workflow with Docker so it could run on AWS, Azure, and GCP. That portability was a real customer requirement, and containers were the cheapest way to meet it.
questions.trap: Saying multi-cloud is always best practice. It is a trade-off; without a specific driver it often adds cost and complexity without adding resilience.

questions.q: What are AWS Regions and Availability Zones?
questions.plain: A Region is a city where AWS has a cluster of data centers, such as Northern Virginia or Frankfurt. Availability Zones are separate neighborhoods in that city, each with its own power and network, far enough apart that a flood or power cut in one does not hit the others, but close enough to talk quickly. You spread your app across neighborhoods so one bad day does not take you down.
questions.technical: An AWS Region is a separate geographic area, such as us-east-1, that is isolated from other Regions. Each Region contains multiple Availability Zones, at least three in current Regions. An AZ is one or more discrete data centers with redundant power, networking, and connectivity, physically separated from other AZs, linked by low-latency private fiber. Many services are Regional, and data stays in the Region you choose unless you move it. Deploying across multiple AZs protects against a data center or AZ failure; multi-Region protects against a Regional event.

probes.q: Why are AZs close but not too close?
probes.a: Far enough apart to avoid shared disasters, close enough for synchronous replication with low latency.

probes.q: Is an AZ one building?
probes.a: Not necessarily. It is one or more data centers acting as one isolated zone.

questions.aws: RDS Multi-AZ and Aurora replicate synchronously across AZs within a Region; S3 Standard stores data across multiple AZs.
questions.trap: Confusing Regions and AZs, or saying a single EC2 instance is highly available. One instance lives in one AZ; HA needs at least two AZs.

questions.q: What is an edge location and how is it different from a Region?
questions.plain: Edge locations are small outposts in many more cities than Regions, like neighborhood pickup lockers versus the main warehouse. Popular content is copied to the locker near you, so you get it fast. The main warehouse, the Region, still does the real work.
questions.technical: Edge locations are points of presence in many cities worldwide, far more numerous than Regions. They host services that benefit from being near users: Amazon CloudFront caches content and terminates TLS, Amazon Route 53 answers DNS, AWS Global Accelerator brings traffic onto the AWS backbone early, and AWS WAF and AWS Shield filter attacks at the edge. You do not run general EC2 workloads at an edge location. Regions run full services with multiple AZs. Local Zones and Wavelength Zones are separate options that put compute closer to specific metros or 5G networks.

probes.q: How does CloudFront speed up a site?
probes.a: It caches content at edge locations close to users and keeps optimized connections back to the origin for the rest.

probes.q: Global Accelerator vs CloudFront?
probes.a: CloudFront caches HTTP content. Global Accelerator gives static anycast IPs and routes TCP or UDP traffic over the AWS backbone to the best healthy endpoint, without caching.

questions.trap: Thinking edge locations are mini Regions where you deploy servers. They run specific edge services, not your full stack.

questions.q: How would you help a customer choose an AWS Region?
questions.plain: Picking a Region is like picking where to open a store. First, are there laws about where you can operate? Then, is it close to your customers? Does it stock what you need? And what does rent cost there? I walk through those four in that order.
questions.technical: Four factors, usually in this order. Compliance and data residency: laws or contracts may require data to stay in a country or Region. Latency: proximity to end users, measured not assumed. Service availability: not every service or instance type launches in every Region at once, so check the feature list. Cost: prices vary by Region. For DR, pick a second Region far enough away for independent risk that still satisfies residency rules.

probes.q: Can data leave a Region on its own?
probes.a: No. AWS does not move your data out of the Region you choose unless you configure it, such as replication or a cross-Region copy.

probes.q: How do you check latency?
probes.a: Test from user locations to candidate Regions, or use real user monitoring, rather than relying on a map.

questions.trap: Choosing the Region with the lowest price first. Compliance and latency usually decide it; price is a tie-breaker.

questions.q: What is the difference between high availability, fault tolerance, and disaster recovery?
questions.plain: High availability is a store with two cashiers: if one leaves, there is a short wait, but you still check out. Fault tolerance is a plane with two engines: one can fail and passengers do not even notice. Disaster recovery is the plan for when the whole store burns down: where you reopen and how fast.
questions.technical: High availability aims for minimal downtime by removing single points of failure, for example instances in multiple AZs behind a load balancer with health checks and automatic failover. Brief disruptions during failover are acceptable. Fault tolerance means the system keeps operating with no visible interruption when a component fails, usually through fully redundant, active components, at higher cost. Disaster recovery covers recovering from large events such as a Regional outage, data corruption, or ransomware, defined by RPO and RTO targets and implemented with backups, replication, and a recovery site.

probes.q: Is Multi-AZ RDS fault tolerant or highly available?
probes.a: Highly available. Failover to the standby causes a short interruption, so it is not zero-impact fault tolerance.

probes.q: Does HA replace backups?
probes.a: No. Replication copies mistakes and corruption instantly; you still need point-in-time backups for DR.

questions.aws: Aurora stores data on six storage nodes across three AZs and typically fails over to a replica in under 60 seconds, which is high availability, not zero downtime.
questions.trap: Thinking replication is a backup. If someone deletes a table, replication deletes it everywhere; only a backup lets you go back in time.

questions.q: What are RPO and RTO?
questions.plain: RPO is how much work you can afford to lose, like asking how long since you last saved your document. RTO is how long you can afford to be down, like how long until you are back at your desk typing. A one-hour RPO means losing up to an hour of data; a four-hour RTO means being back up within four hours.
questions.technical: Recovery Point Objective (RPO) is the maximum acceptable data loss, measured as time between the last recoverable copy and the disaster. It is driven by backup frequency or replication lag. Recovery Time Objective (RTO) is the maximum acceptable time from disruption to restored service. It is driven by how much of the recovery environment is already running and automated. Both are business decisions set per workload, based on the cost of downtime and data loss. Lower targets cost more, so not every system needs near-zero values.

probes.q: How do you lower RPO?
probes.a: Back up more often or replicate continuously, such as cross-Region replication or Aurora Global Database.

probes.q: How do you lower RTO?
probes.a: Keep more infrastructure pre-provisioned, automate failover with infrastructure as code, and rehearse it.

questions.trap: Mixing them up. RPO is about data, looking back; RTO is about time to recover, looking forward.

questions.q: What are the four disaster recovery strategies on AWS?
questions.plain: Think of four levels of insurance for a restaurant. Backup and restore: keep the recipes in a safe and rebuild if it burns. Pilot light: a second kitchen with the gas on but no staff. Warm standby: a small second kitchen already cooking at low volume. Multi-site active/active: two full restaurants serving customers every day. Each step costs more and recovers faster.
questions.technical: From the AWS DR whitepaper, from lowest cost and slowest recovery to highest: Backup and restore: back up data and infrastructure as code to another Region, restore on disaster; RPO and RTO in hours. Pilot light: data is replicated live and core infrastructure exists, but app servers are switched off until failover; tens of minutes. Warm standby: a scaled-down but fully functional copy runs in another Region and is scaled up on failover; minutes. Multi-site active/active: full workloads serve traffic in multiple Regions; near-zero RTO, though data corruption still needs backups.

probes.q: Which strategy would you suggest for an internal reporting tool?
probes.a: Backup and restore. Hours of downtime is acceptable, so paying for a running second site is wasteful.

probes.q: What is hot standby?
probes.a: A full-capacity copy in a second Region that does not take traffic until failover, a variant of multi-site.

probes.q: What is the most common DR failure?
probes.a: Never testing it. Rehearse failover regularly, ideally automated, so recovery works when needed.

questions.aws: AWS Backup copies backups across Regions and accounts; Aurora Global Database, DynamoDB global tables, and S3 Cross-Region Replication support pilot light and above; AWS Elastic Disaster Recovery implements pilot light for servers; Route 53 and Amazon Application Recovery Controller handle traffic failover.
questions.trap: Assuming active/active means you need no backups. Corruption or a bad deploy replicates everywhere; point-in-time backups are still required.

questions.q: What exactly is the difference between pilot light and warm standby?
questions.plain: With pilot light, the stove's pilot flame is lit but no burners are on: you have to turn them on before you can cook. With warm standby, a couple of burners are already cooking at low heat: you can serve a few guests right away and turn up the heat as more arrive.
questions.technical: Both keep a copy of data and core infrastructure in a DR Region. The AWS whitepaper's distinction: pilot light cannot process requests without additional action first, because app servers are switched off or not deployed and must be turned on and scaled. Warm standby can handle traffic immediately at reduced capacity, because everything is already deployed and running, so it only needs to scale up. Warm standby costs more but gives lower RTO and is easier to test continuously, since the stack is live.

probes.q: Why is warm standby easier to test?
probes.a: The stack is live, so you can send test traffic to it anytime instead of first standing it up.

probes.q: What is the risk of depending on Auto Scaling in DR?
probes.a: Scaling is a control plane action, which can be less available during a large event. Pre-provision enough to handle initial load.

questions.trap: Describing both as 'a smaller copy in another Region.' The real difference is whether it can serve traffic before you act.

questions.q: What is the difference between elasticity and scalability?
questions.plain: Scalability means your restaurant can grow by adding tables. Elasticity means tables appear when the dinner rush starts and disappear when it ends, automatically, so you only pay for tables in use. Every elastic system is scalable, but not every scalable system is elastic.
questions.technical: Scalability is a system's ability to handle more load by adding resources, vertically with a bigger machine or horizontally with more machines, and it may be a manual, planned change. Elasticity is automatic, rapid scaling out and back in to match demand in near real time, so capacity tracks load and you stop paying for idle resources. Elasticity needs stateless or horizontally scalable components, health checks, and a good scaling signal. Cloud makes elasticity practical because capacity is available on demand and billed per use.

probes.q: What makes an app hard to make elastic?
probes.a: State held on one server, such as sessions in memory or local files. Move state to a shared store like ElastiCache, DynamoDB, or S3.

probes.q: Name AWS elastic features.
probes.a: EC2 Auto Scaling, Application Auto Scaling for ECS and DynamoDB, Lambda concurrency, Aurora Serverless v2.

questions.resume: At Oracle, I containerized NSX services on OCI with Docker and Kubernetes and autoscaled them on custom Prometheus metrics instead of CPU alone. That held p99 SLOs at 2x peak load through release surges.
questions.trap: Using the words interchangeably. Elasticity specifically includes automatic scale in, which is where the cost savings come from.

questions.q: What is vertical vs horizontal scaling?
questions.plain: Vertical scaling is buying a bigger truck. Horizontal scaling is adding more trucks. A bigger truck is simple but there is a largest model, and if it breaks, nothing moves. More trucks can grow almost without limit and one breakdown does not stop deliveries, but you need a dispatcher.
questions.technical: Vertical scaling (scale up) moves a workload to a larger instance with more CPU, memory, or I/O. It needs no code change but has a hardware ceiling, often requires a restart, and keeps a single point of failure. Horizontal scaling (scale out) adds more instances behind a load balancer or partitions data across nodes. It improves both capacity and availability and enables elasticity, but requires stateless app tiers and a strategy for shared state. Databases often scale vertically first, then add read replicas or sharding.

probes.q: When is vertical scaling the right call?
probes.a: For a quick fix, a database that is hard to shard, or software licensed per server, until you outgrow the largest size.

probes.q: What do you need for horizontal scaling?
probes.a: A load balancer, stateless instances, health checks, and shared storage or a database for state.

questions.aws: Change an EC2 or RDS instance type to scale up; use an Application Load Balancer with an Auto Scaling group across AZs to scale out.
questions.trap: Assuming scale out is always better. Some workloads, like a single relational writer, scale up more simply until they hit the ceiling.

questions.q: How would you design autoscaling for a service, and what metric would you scale on?
questions.plain: Autoscaling is like a manager calling in extra staff when the line gets long. The key is watching the right signal. Counting how busy staff look, like CPU, can miss the point. Watching how long customers wait, or how many are in line, tells you directly when to call people in.
questions.technical: Pick a metric that tracks user-facing load and leads the problem: requests per target, queue depth, or latency, not only CPU, which can lag or be irrelevant for I/O-bound services. Use target tracking to hold the metric near a set point, with step policies for sharp bursts and scheduled scaling for known peaks. Set minimums across multiple AZs, cooldowns to prevent flapping, and scale-in protection for in-flight work. Pre-warm for launches, since new capacity takes time to start. Validate with load tests at peak and beyond.

probes.q: Why can CPU be a bad scaling metric?
probes.a: An I/O-bound or memory-bound service can be overloaded at low CPU, so users suffer before the scaler reacts.

probes.q: What is target tracking?
probes.a: You set a target value, such as 60% CPU or 1,000 requests per target, and Auto Scaling adds or removes capacity to stay near it.

probes.q: How do you avoid flapping?
probes.a: Use cooldowns or warmup periods, scale in more slowly than out, and avoid noisy metrics.

questions.aws: EC2 Auto Scaling and Application Auto Scaling support target tracking, step, scheduled, and predictive scaling, using CloudWatch metrics including custom ones; SQS queue depth is a common signal for workers.
questions.resume: At Oracle, I autoscaled containerized NSX services on custom Prometheus metrics instead of CPU alone, which held p99 SLOs at 2x peak load through release surges.
questions.trap: Scaling only on CPU because it is the default. Choose the metric that best reflects user pain or backlog.

questions.q: Explain the main AWS pricing models: On-Demand, Savings Plans, Reserved Instances, and Spot.
questions.plain: On-Demand is paying the full hotel rate night by night: total freedom, highest price. Savings Plans and Reserved Instances are like a yearly lease: you promise to stay, you pay much less. Spot is a last-minute empty room at a deep discount, but the hotel can ask you to leave with short notice if a full-price guest shows up.
questions.technical: On-Demand: pay per second or hour with no commitment; best for short, spiky, or unknown workloads. Savings Plans: commit to a consistent amount of usage in dollars per hour for 1 or 3 years for a lower rate; Compute Savings Plans apply across EC2 instance families, Regions, Fargate, and Lambda. Reserved Instances: a 1 or 3 year commitment tied to specific instance attributes; still used for services such as RDS. Spot: spare EC2 capacity at up to 90% off On-Demand, which AWS can reclaim with a two-minute warning, suited to fault-tolerant, flexible work.

probes.q: How would you combine them for a typical web app?
probes.a: Savings Plans for the steady baseline, On-Demand for normal peaks, Spot for stateless batch or extra scale-out capacity.

probes.q: What workloads should not use Spot?
probes.a: Anything that cannot tolerate interruption, such as a single-instance database or a stateful job with no checkpointing.

questions.aws: AWS Cost Explorer recommends Savings Plans and Reserved Instance purchases based on past usage.
questions.trap: Committing to Savings Plans before right-sizing. Shrink and clean up first, then commit to the smaller real baseline.

questions.q: When is Spot a good fit, and how do you design for interruptions?
questions.plain: Spot is like flying standby: very cheap, but you might get bumped. It is great if your trip is flexible, and terrible if you are flying to your own wedding. You make it safe by being able to take the next flight without losing your luggage.
questions.technical: Spot suits stateless, fault-tolerant, flexible work: batch and big data jobs, CI builds, rendering, ML training with checkpoints, and extra web capacity behind a load balancer. Design for interruption: handle the two-minute interruption notice to drain work, checkpoint progress to S3, keep jobs idempotent, diversify across many instance types and AZs, and use allocation strategies that favor capacity-optimized pools. Mix Spot with On-Demand in the same Auto Scaling group so a baseline always remains.

probes.q: Why diversify instance types?
probes.a: Each type and AZ is a separate capacity pool. Spreading across many pools lowers the chance of losing everything at once.

probes.q: Which AWS services use Spot natively?
probes.a: EC2 Auto Scaling groups, EMR, AWS Batch, ECS and EKS capacity providers, and SageMaker AI managed spot training.

questions.trap: Putting a production primary database on Spot to save money. Interruptions make that a data and availability risk.

questions.q: A customer's AWS bill doubled. How would you approach cost optimization?
questions.plain: I would treat it like a household budget review. First, find where the money goes. Then turn off what nobody uses, like lights in empty rooms. Then right-size, like a smaller apartment if you only use half of it. Finally, lock in discounts for what you always use, like a yearly transit pass.
questions.technical: 1. Visibility: Cost Explorer by service, account, and tag; find top drivers and recent changes; enforce cost allocation tags. 2. Eliminate waste: idle instances, unattached EBS volumes, old snapshots, unused Elastic IPs, forgotten dev environments; schedule non-production off at night. 3. Right-size using Compute Optimizer and utilization data; move to Graviton where compatible. 4. Storage: S3 lifecycle policies and Intelligent-Tiering. 5. Architecture: data transfer and NAT gateway costs, caching, serverless for spiky loads. 6. Pricing: Savings Plans for the baseline, Spot for flexible work. 7. Governance: AWS Budgets alerts.

probes.q: What hidden costs often surprise customers?
probes.a: Data transfer out and between AZs, NAT gateway processing, idle load balancers, and log storage.

probes.q: How do you keep costs from creeping back?
probes.a: Tagging policies, budgets with alerts per team, regular reviews, and making each team see its own bill.

probes.q: Which Well-Architected pillar covers this?
probes.a: Cost optimization, which also stresses measuring efficiency and adopting a consumption model.

questions.aws: Tools: AWS Cost Explorer, AWS Budgets, AWS Compute Optimizer, AWS Trusted Advisor, Cost Anomaly Detection, S3 Storage Lens.
questions.trap: Jumping straight to buying Savings Plans. Remove waste and right-size first, or you lock in paying for things you do not need.

questions.q: What is the AWS Well-Architected Framework, and what are its pillars?
questions.plain: The Well-Architected Framework is AWS's building inspection checklist for systems. Like an inspector checking a house's foundation, wiring, and plumbing, it checks six areas: how you run it, how safe it is, whether it stays up, whether it is fast enough, whether it costs too much, and how much energy it wastes.
questions.technical: The framework is a set of design principles, best practices, and review questions for evaluating workloads, organized into six pillars: operational excellence, security, reliability, performance efficiency, cost optimization, and sustainability. A Well-Architected review walks a team through each pillar's questions, surfaces high and medium risks, and produces an improvement plan. The AWS Well-Architected Tool in the console records reviews, and lenses add domain guidance such as serverless, SaaS, machine learning, and generative AI. It is a continuous practice, not a one-time certification.

probes.q: Which pillar was added most recently?
probes.a: Sustainability, the sixth pillar, added in late 2021.

probes.q: What is a lens?
probes.a: Extra questions and guidance for a specific domain, such as the Serverless Lens or the Generative AI Lens.

questions.aws: SAs often run Well-Architected reviews with customers to find risks and plan improvements.
questions.trap: Saying five pillars. There are six; sustainability is the one people forget.

questions.q: Give an example of a trade-off between Well-Architected pillars and how you would explain it to a customer.
questions.plain: Making a system bulletproof costs money, like insuring a car fully versus basic coverage. If an app is used only by staff during work hours, paying for a second Region is like insuring a parked car against highway crashes. I would show the customer the cost of an hour of downtime next to the cost of the protection, and let that drive the choice.
questions.technical: Reliability vs cost: multi-Region active/active cuts RTO toward zero but roughly doubles infrastructure and adds data consistency work. For an internal tool, multi-AZ plus cross-Region backups may meet the business RTO and RPO at a fraction of the cost. Performance vs cost: provisioned capacity cuts latency but sits idle off-peak. Security vs operational speed: strict approvals slow deploys, mitigated by automating guardrails. Frame each choice by quantified business impact: downtime cost per hour, data loss tolerance, and compliance requirements.

probes.q: How do you quantify reliability needs?
probes.a: Ask what an hour of downtime and an hour of lost data cost in revenue, penalties, and reputation, then set RTO and RPO.

probes.q: Where do security and cost align?
probes.a: Removing unused resources and accounts both cuts cost and shrinks the attack surface.

questions.trap: Treating pillars as a checklist to maximize everywhere. The framework expects deliberate trade-offs driven by business priorities.

questions.q: What are the 7 Rs of cloud migration?
questions.plain: Moving to the cloud is like moving house, and each item gets one of seven fates. Throw it out (retire). Leave it behind for now (retain). Move it as is (rehost). Move the whole room in one go on a truck (relocate). Replace it with a new one (repurchase). Move it with small fixes (replatform). Rebuild it to fit the new house (refactor).
questions.technical: From AWS Prescriptive Guidance: Retire: decommission apps with no business value. Retain: keep in place for now, due to compliance, dependencies, or recent investment. Rehost: lift and shift with no changes, for example servers to EC2 with AWS Application Migration Service. Relocate: move at the platform level with no new hardware or rewrites, such as many servers from an on-premises platform to its cloud version, or an RDS instance to another VPC or account. Repurchase: drop and shop, move to SaaS. Replatform: lift, tinker, and shift, such as a database to Amazon RDS. Refactor or re-architect: redesign cloud-native, the most complex and costly.

probes.q: Which strategies does AWS recommend for large migrations?
probes.a: Mostly rehost, replatform, relocate, and retire, then modernize after the move. Refactor during a large migration is usually discouraged.

probes.q: What is the difference between rehost and replatform?
probes.a: Rehost changes nothing. Replatform makes targeted optimizations, such as moving a self-managed database to RDS, without changing core architecture.

probes.q: Why retire anything?
probes.a: Discovery often finds idle or unused apps; shutting them down saves cost and security risk and shrinks the migration.

questions.aws: AWS Migration Hub and AWS Transform help assess and track portfolios; AWS Application Migration Service rehosts servers; AWS Database Migration Service moves databases.
questions.trap: Listing only lift and shift and rewrite. There are seven, and retire and retain are real choices that shrink the scope.

questions.q: A customer has 300 on-premises applications and a data center lease ending in 12 months. How do you plan the migration?
questions.plain: With a hard deadline, I would act like a moving company with a firm move-out date. First, take inventory and throw out what nobody uses. Then move most things as they are, quickly and safely. Only after everything is in the new house do we start remodeling. Trying to remodel during the move is how you miss the deadline.
questions.technical: Assess: discovery of servers, dependencies, and utilization; group apps into move groups by dependency. Assign an R per app: retire idle apps, retain those blocked by compliance or hardware, repurchase where a SaaS fits, and rehost, relocate, or replatform the bulk for speed. Refactor only where business value justifies it, usually after cutover. Build a landing zone with multi-account structure, networking, identity, and guardrails before waves. Run a pilot wave, then repeatable waves with tested rollback. Modernize post-migration once the deadline risk is gone.

probes.q: Why build a landing zone first?
probes.a: Every wave needs consistent accounts, networking, security, and logging; setting it up once avoids rework and risk.

probes.q: What do you do about tightly coupled apps?
probes.a: Migrate them in the same wave so latency-sensitive dependencies are not split across on-premises and cloud.

probes.q: How do you reduce cutover risk?
probes.a: Continuous replication, rehearsed cutovers, clear rollback criteria, and moving low-risk apps first.

questions.aws: AWS Control Tower sets up a governed landing zone; AWS Application Migration Service, AWS Database Migration Service, and AWS DataSync move servers, databases, and files; AWS offers the Migration Acceleration Program for large migrations.
questions.trap: Proposing to refactor everything for the cloud before the deadline. Large migrations succeed by moving fast first and modernizing after.

questions.q: Explain the AWS shared responsibility model.
questions.plain: It is like renting an apartment in a secure building. The landlord handles the building: locks on the front door, the walls, the fire alarms. You handle your own unit: locking your door, who gets a key, and what you keep inside. AWS secures the cloud itself; you secure what you put in it.
questions.technical: AWS is responsible for security of the cloud: physical data centers, hardware, the global network, and the virtualization layer, plus the software of managed services. The customer is responsible for security in the cloud: their data, identity and access management, encryption choices, network configuration such as security groups, and the guest operating system and applications on IaaS. The customer always owns data classification, access policies, and account credentials. AWS provides tools, and the customer must configure them.

probes.q: Who patches the OS on EC2?
probes.a: The customer. On RDS, AWS patches the database engine and underlying OS during maintenance windows.

probes.q: Who is responsible if an S3 bucket is made public by mistake?
probes.a: The customer. AWS blocks public access by default on new buckets, but configuration is the customer's job.

questions.aws: AWS Artifact gives customers AWS's compliance reports, which cover AWS's side of the model.
questions.trap: Assuming 'AWS is secure, so my app is secure.' Most cloud breaches come from customer-side misconfiguration, such as open buckets or leaked keys.

questions.q: How does the shared responsibility split change between EC2, RDS, and Lambda?
questions.plain: The more the service does for you, the more AWS handles. EC2 is renting an empty apartment: you furnish and maintain everything inside. RDS is a furnished apartment with a maintenance crew for the appliances. Lambda is a hotel room: housekeeping handles almost everything, and you just keep track of your own belongings and who has your key.
questions.technical: EC2 (infrastructure): the customer manages the guest OS and patches, installed software, firewall settings via security groups, data encryption, and IAM. RDS (managed): AWS handles OS and database engine patching, backups infrastructure, and Multi-AZ failover mechanics; the customer manages database users, network access, encryption settings, parameter choices, and data. Lambda (serverless): AWS manages servers, OS, runtime patching, and scaling; the customer owns function code, dependencies, the execution role's permissions, environment secrets, and data. In all cases the customer owns data and access.

probes.q: What stays with the customer in every model?
probes.a: Their data, who can access it through IAM, and how it is classified and encrypted.

probes.q: Why can managed services improve security?
probes.a: AWS takes over patching and hardening, which removes common customer mistakes like unpatched servers.

questions.trap: Thinking serverless means no security responsibility. Overly broad IAM roles and vulnerable dependencies in function code are still yours.

domains.name: Hardware
domains.summary: What is physically inside the machines (processors, memory, storage, accelerators) and how AWS virtualizes them, so an SA can match a customer's workload to the right instance and explain why.

cheatsheet.def: A core is an independent processing unit; a hardware thread lets one core juggle two instruction streams by sharing its parts.
cheatsheet.probe: On x86 EC2 a vCPU is usually one hardware thread; on Graviton a vCPU is a full core.

cheatsheet.def: Small fast memory on the chip: L1 and L2 per core, L3 shared, each level bigger and slower.
cheatsheet.probe: Code that reads memory in order (good locality) stays in cache and runs far faster.

cheatsheet.def: About 1 ns for L1, about 100 ns for RAM, tens of microseconds for SSD, milliseconds for HDD and long network trips.
cheatsheet.probe: Each step down is roughly 10x to 1000x slower, which is why caching matters.

cheatsheet.def: A CPU has a few powerful cores for varied logic; a GPU has thousands of simple cores doing the same math in parallel.
cheatsheet.probe: Neural networks are mostly matrix multiplication, which is exactly what GPUs parallelize.

cheatsheet.def: AWS-designed AI chips: Inferentia for running models (inference), Trainium for training them, both programmed through the AWS Neuron SDK.
cheatsheet.probe: The pitch is lower cost per inference or per training run than comparable GPU instances.

cheatsheet.def: AWS-designed Arm-based processors for EC2, aimed at better price performance and lower energy use than comparable x86.
cheatsheet.probe: Software must run on arm64: interpreted languages usually just work, native binaries and images need arm64 builds.

cheatsheet.def: HDD spins a platter and moves a head; SSD uses flash with no moving parts; NVMe is a fast interface that connects SSDs over PCIe.
cheatsheet.probe: NVMe's many deep queues are why it beats older SATA SSDs on parallel I/O.

cheatsheet.def: IOPS counts read or write operations per second; throughput is data volume per second. Throughput is about IOPS times I/O size.
cheatsheet.probe: Databases with small random I/O need IOPS; log processing and big scans need throughput.

cheatsheet.def: 0 stripes for speed with no protection, 1 mirrors, 5 stripes with parity and survives one disk loss, 10 mirrors then stripes.
cheatsheet.probe: RAID 0 doubles the chance of losing everything; RAID 10 is the usual choice for fast, safe databases.

cheatsheet.term: VM vs container vs bare metal
cheatsheet.def: A VM runs its own OS on a hypervisor; a container shares the host kernel; bare metal has no virtualization layer.
cheatsheet.probe: Containers start in seconds and pack densely, but the isolation boundary is weaker than a VM's.

cheatsheet.def: The platform under modern EC2: Nitro Cards for networking, storage, and management, the Nitro Security Chip, and a minimal Nitro Hypervisor.
cheatsheet.probe: Offloading to dedicated hardware gives near bare-metal performance and keeps operators out of customer instances.

questions.q: What are CPU cores, threads, and clock speed, and which matters most?
questions.plain: Think of a kitchen. Each core is a chef. Clock speed is how fast each chef chops. Threads are like a chef keeping two dishes going at once, stirring one while the other simmers. More chefs help when you have many orders; a faster chef helps when one big dish has to be done step by step.
questions.technical: A core is an independent execution unit with its own pipeline and registers. Simultaneous multithreading (Intel calls it Hyper-Threading) exposes two hardware threads per core that share the core's execution units, filling idle slots when one thread stalls on memory; it typically adds a modest gain, not 2x. Clock speed (GHz) is cycles per second, but real speed is cycles times instructions per cycle, so a newer chip at a lower clock can be faster. Which matters depends on the workload: parallel servers and batch jobs scale with cores, single-threaded or latency-sensitive code with per-core speed. On EC2, a vCPU on most x86 instances is one hardware thread; on Graviton it is a full physical core.

probes.q: Why can't you just add cores to make any program faster?
probes.a: Only the parallel part speeds up. Serial steps and coordination limit the gain, which is Amdahl's law.

probes.q: Why did clock speeds stop climbing?
probes.a: Power and heat. Chips got more cores and smarter design instead of much higher GHz.

probes.q: When would you disable SMT?
probes.a: For some licensing, latency-critical, or high-security workloads; EC2 lets you set threads per core at launch.

questions.aws: EC2 sizes are described in vCPUs, and the CPU options setting lets you change active cores and threads per core.
questions.trap: Treating vCPU counts as equal across instance families. An x86 vCPU is usually half a core; a Graviton vCPU is a whole core.

questions.q: What is CPU cache, and why do L1, L2, and L3 exist?
questions.plain: Cache is the chef's countertop. The fridge (main memory) holds everything, but walking to it is slow. So the chef keeps the ingredients in use right on the counter (L1), a few more on a nearby shelf (L2), and a shared pantry for the whole kitchen (L3). The closer the shelf, the smaller it is and the faster to grab from.
questions.technical: Main memory takes on the order of 100 ns, hundreds of CPU cycles, so CPUs keep recently used data in small, fast SRAM caches on the chip. L1 is per core, tens of KB, split into instruction and data caches, about 1 ns. L2 is per core, hundreds of KB to a few MB, a few ns. L3 is shared across cores, tens of MB, around 10 to 20 ns. Data moves in cache lines, typically 64 bytes. Caches work because of locality: programs reuse recent data (temporal) and touch neighboring addresses (spatial). Code that walks arrays in order is fast; code that chases pointers randomly misses cache and waits on memory.

probes.q: What is a cache miss?
probes.a: The data is not in that level, so the CPU looks in the next, slower level and may stall.

probes.q: Why are arrays often faster than linked lists?
probes.a: Array elements sit next to each other, so one cache line brings several; list nodes are scattered.

probes.q: Why not make L1 huge?
probes.a: Bigger caches are slower to search and cost chip area and power; the layers balance speed and size.

questions.trap: Thinking more RAM fixes a CPU-bound program. If the hot data does not fit in cache, the fix is better locality or a CPU with more cache, not more RAM.

questions.q: Walk me through the memory hierarchy and rough latency numbers. Why should an architect care?
questions.plain: Imagine reading from L1 cache takes one second. Then reading from RAM takes about a minute and a half. Reading from an SSD takes about a day. Reading from a spinning hard drive takes about four months. A round trip across an ocean takes years. That is why architects keep hot data as close to the processor as possible.
questions.technical: Approximate orders of magnitude: registers under 1 ns; L1 about 1 ns; L2 a few ns; L3 about 10 to 20 ns; DRAM about 100 ns; NVMe SSD random read tens of microseconds to about 100; HDD seek about 5 to 10 ms; a round trip inside a data center around half a millisecond; across a continent or ocean, roughly 50 to 150 ms. Each tier is about 10x to 1000x slower and larger than the one above. Architecture follows directly: put an in-memory cache in front of a disk-backed database, keep compute next to its data, batch network calls, and serve users from a nearby Region or edge. The exact numbers vary by hardware; the ratios are what matter.

probes.q: Why put Redis in front of a database?
probes.a: Memory reads take nanoseconds to microseconds; a disk-backed query with network and parsing can take milliseconds.

probes.q: Why does chatty cross-Region traffic hurt?
probes.a: Each call pays tens to hundreds of milliseconds of round trip, and many sequential calls add up.

probes.q: Is network slower than SSD?
probes.a: A fast in-datacenter network round trip can be comparable to an SSD read; cross-Region is far slower.

questions.aws: This is why Amazon ElastiCache sits in front of Amazon RDS, why instance store NVMe is used for scratch data, and why customers deploy in the Region nearest their users.
questions.trap: Quoting exact numbers as facts. Give orders of magnitude and say they vary by hardware; interviewers care about the ratios.

questions.q: What is the difference between RAM and storage?
questions.plain: RAM is your desk: fast to work on, but it is cleared every night when the power goes off. Storage is your filing cabinet: slower to open, but everything is still there tomorrow. A bigger desk lets you work on more at once; a bigger cabinet lets you keep more.
questions.technical: RAM (DRAM) is volatile working memory: byte-addressable, about 100 ns access, and lost on power off. The CPU reads and writes it directly. Storage (SSD, HDD, network block or object storage) is persistent but much slower, with microsecond to millisecond access, and is read in blocks through the operating system. Programs load data from storage into RAM to work on it. When RAM runs out, the OS swaps pages to disk and performance collapses, or processes are killed for running out of memory. Sizing rule: RAM for the working set you touch often, storage for everything you must keep.

probes.q: What happens when a server runs out of RAM?
probes.a: It swaps to disk and slows sharply, or the out-of-memory killer ends processes.

probes.q: When do you pick a memory-optimized instance?
probes.a: In-memory databases, caches, and big analytics jobs where the working set must fit in RAM.

probes.q: Is EBS RAM or storage?
probes.a: Storage: network-attached block volumes that persist independently of the instance.

questions.aws: EC2 memory-optimized families (the R and X families) suit in-memory workloads; EBS and instance store provide block storage.
questions.trap: Saying 'my computer has 1 TB of memory' when it means storage. Keep the two words distinct in front of a customer.

questions.q: Compare HDD, SSD, and NVMe.
questions.plain: An HDD is a record player: a needle has to physically move to the right spot, so jumping around is slow, but it is cheap and holds a lot. An SSD is a wall of mailboxes: any box opens instantly. NVMe is the same mailboxes with many more clerks working at once, so lots of requests get served in parallel.
questions.technical: HDDs store data on spinning magnetic platters; each random read waits for the head to seek and the platter to rotate, milliseconds, so they do only a few hundred random IOPS but handle large sequential reads well and are cheapest per GB. SSDs use NAND flash with no moving parts, giving microsecond access and far higher random IOPS. Older SSDs used the SATA interface, built for disks, with a single command queue. NVMe is a protocol for flash over PCIe with up to 64K queues, each up to 64K commands deep, which cuts latency and unlocks parallel I/O. Choose HDD for cheap cold or sequential data, SSD or NVMe for databases and anything latency-sensitive.

probes.q: When is HDD still the right choice?
probes.a: Large, sequential, rarely read data such as logs, backups, and big data scans, where cost per GB matters more than random access.

probes.q: Do SSDs wear out?
probes.a: Flash cells tolerate a limited number of writes; drives spread writes evenly and keep spare capacity to manage it.

probes.q: Is NVMe a type of disk?
probes.a: It is an interface and protocol; the media underneath is flash.

questions.aws: EBS offers SSD types (gp3, io2) and HDD types (st1, sc1); on Nitro instances EBS volumes and instance store both appear to the OS as NVMe devices.
questions.trap: Calling NVMe a different storage medium from SSD. NVMe is the fast interface; the storage is still flash.

questions.q: What is the difference between IOPS and throughput, and how do you size storage for a workload?
questions.plain: IOPS is how many separate trips a delivery van makes per hour. Throughput is how many boxes arrive per hour in total. A pizza shop needs many quick trips (IOPS). A furniture store needs a big truck carrying a lot at once (throughput). You pick the vehicle for the job.
questions.technical: IOPS is input/output operations per second. Throughput is bytes per second. They are linked: throughput is roughly IOPS times I/O size, so 1,000 IOPS of 16 KiB is about 16 MiB/s, while 1,000 IOPS of 1 MiB is about 1 GiB/s. Latency, time per operation, is the third dimension. Transactional databases do small random reads and writes, so they need high IOPS and low latency. Analytics, streaming, and log processing do large sequential I/O, so they need throughput. Size by measuring the existing system's read and write IOPS, I/O size, throughput, and queue depth at peak, then add headroom. The instance itself also has an EBS bandwidth limit that can cap you before the volume does.

probes.q: The volume has IOPS to spare but the app is still slow. What else limits it?
probes.a: The instance's EBS bandwidth limit, queue depth, or the app doing I/O serially.

probes.q: Why does gp3 suit most workloads?
probes.a: You set IOPS and throughput separately from size, so you do not overbuy capacity just to get performance.

probes.q: When pick io2 Block Express?
probes.a: Critical databases that need sustained high IOPS, consistent sub-millisecond latency, and higher durability.

questions.aws: EBS gp3 is general purpose SSD with independently provisioned IOPS and throughput; io2 Block Express is provisioned IOPS SSD with 99.999% durability; st1 and sc1 are throughput and cold HDD.
questions.trap: Sizing only by capacity in GB. A big cheap volume can still be too slow; size by IOPS, throughput, and latency.

questions.q: Explain RAID 0, 1, 5, and 10.
questions.plain: RAID is how you combine several disks. RAID 0 splits a book across two shelves so two people can fetch pages at once, but lose one shelf and the book is ruined. RAID 1 keeps two full copies. RAID 5 splits the book across three or more shelves plus a clever checksum that can rebuild any one lost shelf. RAID 10 does copies and splitting together: fast and safe, but you pay for double the shelves.
questions.technical: RAID 0 stripes data across disks: capacity and throughput add up, but there is no redundancy, and losing any disk loses the array. RAID 1 mirrors: survives one disk loss per mirror, reads can be faster, and you get half the raw capacity. RAID 5 stripes with distributed parity, needs at least three disks, survives one failure, and has good capacity efficiency, but every write also updates parity (a write penalty), and rebuilds of large disks are slow and risky. RAID 10 stripes across mirrored pairs, needs at least four disks, offers strong performance and survives a disk loss per pair, at 50% capacity. RAID is not a backup: it does not protect against deletion or corruption.

probes.q: Is RAID a backup?
probes.a: No. Deleting a file or ransomware hits every disk at once. You still need snapshots or backups.

probes.q: Why would anyone use RAID 0 on AWS?
probes.a: To combine several EBS volumes or instance store disks for more performance than one volume gives, when the data is already protected elsewhere.

probes.q: Why not RAID 5 on EBS?
probes.a: AWS advises against RAID 5 and 6 on EBS because parity writes consume volume IOPS; EBS is already replicated within its Availability Zone.

questions.aws: EBS volumes are replicated inside their Availability Zone, so customers rarely build RAID for durability; they use snapshots for backup and RAID 0 only for performance.
questions.trap: Calling RAID 0 'redundant'. The R in RAID stands for redundant, but level 0 has none.

questions.q: What is the difference between a GPU and a CPU, and why do GPUs suit AI?
questions.plain: A CPU is a few brilliant professors who can solve any kind of problem one at a time. A GPU is a stadium of thousands of students who can each do simple arithmetic. If the job is grading a million identical math sheets, the stadium wins easily. Training and running AI models is mostly that kind of job: the same multiplication done billions of times.
questions.technical: CPUs have a small number of complex cores with deep caches, branch prediction, and out-of-order execution, built for low-latency, varied, branchy code. GPUs have thousands of simpler cores that run the same instruction across many data elements at once, plus very high memory bandwidth (GDDR or HBM). Neural networks are dominated by matrix multiplications and element-wise math that split into independent pieces, so they map well onto GPUs; modern GPUs add tensor cores specialized for low-precision matrix math. Programming is through CUDA and libraries such as cuDNN, which PyTorch uses under the hood. CPUs still run the data loading, orchestration, and many small or classical ML models.

probes.q: When is a CPU fine for ML?
probes.a: Small models, classical ML like XGBoost, low-volume inference, or when GPU cost is not justified.

probes.q: What limits GPU performance besides core count?
probes.a: Memory capacity and bandwidth, and keeping the GPU fed with data.

probes.q: Why use lower precision like FP16 or INT8?
probes.a: Smaller numbers mean less memory, more values moved per second, and faster tensor core math, often with little accuracy loss.

questions.aws: EC2 accelerated computing families include P (NVIDIA GPUs for training and heavy inference), G (graphics and inference GPUs), Inf (Inferentia), and Trn (Trainium).
questions.trap: Saying GPUs are just 'faster CPUs'. Each GPU core is slower and simpler; the advantage is massive parallelism and memory bandwidth.

questions.q: A customer wants to serve an open LLM on a single GPU. What hardware constraints do you think about first?
questions.plain: The model has to fit in the GPU's own memory, like furniture fitting through a door. A model's size is roughly the number of settings it has times how precisely each one is stored. Storing each setting with less precision, called quantization, is like vacuum-packing the furniture: it fits through smaller doors and moves faster, as long as you check it still works when unpacked.
questions.technical: First, GPU memory: weights take parameters times bytes per parameter, so a 3B model is about 6 GB at FP16 (2 bytes), about 3 GB at INT8, and about 1.5 GB at INT4, plus the KV cache, which grows with context length and concurrent requests, plus runtime overhead. Second, memory bandwidth: generating each token reads the weights, so decode speed is often bandwidth-bound, and smaller weights mean more tokens per second. Third, quantization quality: measure accuracy on a benchmark or the customer's own evaluation set, because INT4 schemes like NF4 often hold up well but not always. Fourth, the kernel path: some quantization formats lack fast kernels on a given GPU and run slower than expected. Then size batch and context to the leftover memory.

probes.q: Why can lower precision be slower?
probes.a: If the GPU or library lacks optimized kernels for that format, it spends time converting values back, which can erase the memory gain.

probes.q: What is the KV cache?
probes.a: Stored attention keys and values for tokens already processed, so the model does not recompute them; it grows with context length and batch size.

probes.q: When do you stop optimizing and use a managed service?
probes.a: When the customer does not need to own the model weights or infrastructure; Amazon Bedrock serves models without managing GPUs.

questions.aws: Options range from EC2 G and P instances or Inferentia-based Inf2 for self-hosting, to Amazon SageMaker AI endpoints, to fully managed models on Amazon Bedrock.
questions.resume: In my ModelScope project, I benchmarked Llama-3.2-3B and Gemma-2-2B across 8 quantization configs (FP16, INT8, INT4, NF4) on a T4 GPU. INT4 came in at 2299 MB, 62% below FP16, at 13.7 tokens per second, with MMLU within a point of baseline. INT8 was strictly dominated: 53% more memory and 2.1x lower throughput.
questions.trap: Assuming fewer bits is always faster. INT8 can be slower than INT4 or even FP16 if the GPU path for it is poorly optimized; always measure.

questions.q: What are AWS Inferentia and AWS Trainium, and when would you suggest them over GPUs?
questions.plain: A GPU is a general-purpose power tool. Inferentia and Trainium are tools AWS built for one job each: Inferentia for running finished AI models cheaply at scale, Trainium for teaching new models. A specialized tool can be cheaper for that job, as long as your materials fit it.
questions.technical: Both are AWS-designed machine learning chips. Inferentia powers Inf1 and Inf2 instances for inference; AWS positions Inferentia2 for large language and diffusion models with distributed inference across chips. Trainium powers Trn instances for training deep learning and generative AI models. Both are programmed through the AWS Neuron SDK, which integrates with PyTorch and other frameworks, so most model code is reused, but models must be compiled for Neuron and not every custom operator is supported. Suggest them when a customer runs a steady, large workload on a supported model architecture and cost per inference or per training run is the main concern. Stay on NVIDIA GPUs when the stack depends on CUDA-specific libraries or custom kernels.

probes.q: What is the main adoption hurdle?
probes.a: Porting: compiling with Neuron and validating operator support and accuracy, versus CUDA's mature ecosystem.

probes.q: How would you de-risk it for a customer?
probes.a: Run a proof of concept on their actual model, compare cost per 1,000 inferences and latency against a GPU baseline, then decide.

probes.q: Can customers use these without managing instances?
probes.a: Yes, through Amazon SageMaker AI, which supports Inf and Trn instance types.

questions.aws: Inf1 and Inf2 use Inferentia, Trn instances use Trainium, and the Neuron SDK is the common toolchain.
questions.trap: Mixing them up. Inferentia is for inference, Trainium is for training; the names give it away.

questions.q: What is the difference between x86 and Arm, and when should a customer move to AWS Graviton?
questions.plain: x86 and Arm are two different languages that processors speak. Most office PCs and older servers speak x86; phones speak Arm because it sips power. Graviton is AWS's own Arm chip for servers. If your software can be translated to Arm, you often get the same work done for less money and less electricity.
questions.technical: x86 (Intel, AMD) and Arm are different instruction set architectures, so compiled binaries for one do not run on the other. Arm designs have historically focused on power efficiency. AWS Graviton is a family of AWS-designed Arm-based processors for EC2; AWS states Graviton instances cost up to 20% less than comparable x86 instances and use up to 60% less energy for the same performance. Migration effort depends on the stack: Python, Java, Node.js, and Go code usually runs with little or no change, while native libraries, agents, and container images must have arm64 builds. Good path: build multi-architecture container images, test a slice of traffic, compare cost and latency, then move. Managed services like Amazon RDS and AWS Lambda offer Graviton options with no code work.

probes.q: What usually blocks a Graviton move?
probes.a: A closed-source binary or agent with no arm64 build, or performance-sensitive code tuned for x86 instructions.

probes.q: How do you spot Graviton instance types?
probes.a: A 'g' after the generation number, like m7g or c7g.

probes.q: How do containers handle both architectures?
probes.a: Multi-arch images: one tag points at an amd64 and an arm64 build, and each host pulls the right one.

questions.aws: Graviton is available for EC2 and managed options including Amazon RDS, Amazon ElastiCache, AWS Lambda, and AWS Fargate.
questions.trap: Promising every app gets cheaper on Graviton with zero work. It is a strong default, but test the workload and check native dependencies first.

questions.q: What is virtualization, and what does a hypervisor do?
questions.plain: Virtualization is turning one big house into several apartments. Each tenant thinks they have their own home, with their own front door and kitchen, but they share the same building. The hypervisor is the building manager who divides the space, keeps tenants from walking into each other's apartments, and hands out the utilities.
questions.technical: Virtualization lets one physical server run many isolated virtual machines, each with its own operating system. The hypervisor sits between the hardware and the VMs: it partitions CPU and memory, presents virtual devices (disk, network), schedules VMs onto cores, and enforces isolation. Type 1 (bare-metal) hypervisors run directly on hardware, used in data centers, such as VMware ESXi, Xen, KVM, and the Nitro Hypervisor. Type 2 (hosted) hypervisors run on top of a desktop OS, such as VirtualBox. Modern CPUs include virtualization extensions so the hypervisor can run guests close to native speed. This is what makes cloud computing economical: higher utilization and fast provisioning.

probes.q: What is a noisy neighbor?
probes.a: Another VM on the same host consuming shared resources and slowing yours; good hypervisors and hardware offload limit it.

probes.q: Type 1 vs type 2?
probes.a: Type 1 runs on the bare hardware; type 2 runs as an app on a normal operating system.

probes.q: Why does virtualization save money?
probes.a: Physical servers are often lightly used; packing several workloads on one raises utilization.

questions.aws: Every EC2 instance, except bare metal types, is a VM managed by a hypervisor; on current instances that is the Nitro Hypervisor.
questions.trap: Saying VMs share an operating system. Each VM has its own kernel; it is containers that share the host kernel.

questions.q: Compare virtual machines, containers, and bare metal. When would you use each?
questions.plain: Bare metal is owning a whole house. A virtual machine is an apartment with its own walls, plumbing, and front door. A container is a room in a shared apartment: it has its own lock, but everyone shares the same kitchen and pipes. Rooms are cheap and quick to set up; apartments are more private; the house gives you total control.
questions.technical: Bare metal runs the OS directly on hardware: full performance and access to hardware features, but slower to provision and less flexible. A VM runs a full guest OS on a hypervisor: strong isolation through a separate kernel, minutes to boot, more overhead. A container packages an app and its dependencies and shares the host kernel, isolated by Linux namespaces and cgroups: starts in seconds, packs densely, and gives consistent builds from laptop to production, but its isolation boundary is weaker because a kernel flaw affects every container on the host. Typical choices: containers for microservices and CI/CD; VMs for legacy or full-OS needs and stronger isolation; bare metal for licensing tied to physical cores, special hardware access, or running your own hypervisor.

probes.q: How do AWS Lambda and AWS Fargate get VM-level isolation with container speed?
probes.a: They run workloads in Firecracker microVMs, lightweight VMs that boot very fast.

probes.q: Are containers less secure?
probes.a: The isolation boundary is weaker than a VM's, so multi-tenant platforms put containers inside VMs.

probes.q: Why would a customer want EC2 bare metal?
probes.a: Software licensed per physical core, workloads that need direct hardware features, or running their own hypervisor.

questions.aws: EC2 offers VMs and .metal bare metal instances; Amazon ECS and Amazon EKS run containers on EC2 or on Fargate without managing servers.
questions.resume: At Oracle, I containerized NSX services on OCI with Docker and Kubernetes and autoscaled on custom Prometheus metrics instead of CPU alone, which held p99 SLOs at 2x peak load through release surges.
questions.trap: Saying containers are lightweight VMs. Containers share the host kernel; VMs each run their own.

questions.q: What is the AWS Nitro System, and why does it matter to customers?
questions.plain: In a normal server, the main processor spends part of its time doing chores like handling the network and the disks. Nitro moves those chores onto separate dedicated cards, like giving the chef a full kitchen staff so the chef only cooks. The customer gets nearly all of the processor, and a separate security chip and a very small manager program keep everything locked down.
questions.technical: Nitro is the platform under all modern EC2 instances. It has three primary parts. Nitro Cards are dedicated hardware with their own processors and ASICs, independent of the main board; they run the control interfaces EC2 uses to manage instances and provide all I/O: software-defined VPC networking, EBS, and instance storage, exposed to the guest as devices like NVMe and the Elastic Network Adapter. The Nitro Security Chip lets the Nitro Controller hold the main CPUs in reset until firmware is verified, and mediates firmware updates. The Nitro Hypervisor is deliberately minimal: it partitions CPU and memory and assigns devices, and little else. Benefits: near bare-metal performance, bare metal instances, faster new instance types, and a design where there is no operator access to customer instances.

probes.q: How does Nitro help security conversations with regulated customers?
probes.a: AWS documents that the system has no mechanism for operators to log in to Nitro hosts or access customer memory, which customers can review in the Nitro security whitepaper.

probes.q: What are Nitro Enclaves?
probes.a: Isolated environments carved from an instance's CPU and memory, with no persistent storage or external networking, for processing highly sensitive data.

probes.q: Why did Nitro make bare metal instances possible?
probes.a: Networking, storage, and management live on the Nitro Cards, so EC2 can still manage the server even without a hypervisor on it.

questions.aws: EBS volumes appearing as NVMe, enhanced networking through ENA, .metal instances, and Nitro Enclaves all come from the Nitro System.
questions.trap: Describing Nitro as just a new hypervisor. The hypervisor is the smallest part; the dedicated Nitro Cards and Security Chip are what change performance and security.

questions.q: A customer's ML training job is slow even on an expensive GPU instance. How do you find the bottleneck?
questions.plain: An expensive oven is useless if the prep cook cannot hand it trays fast enough. My first question is 'is the oven actually busy?'. If the GPU sits idle half the time, the problem is upstream: reading data, preparing it, or moving it. You fix the slowest step in the line, not the fastest.
questions.technical: Start by measuring GPU utilization and memory with nvidia-smi or CloudWatch agent GPU metrics. Low utilization with spiky patterns means the GPU is starved. Then profile one training step (PyTorch Profiler) to split time between data loading, host-to-device copies, compute, and synchronization. Common fixes: more DataLoader workers and pinned memory, prefetching, vectorized batch preparation instead of Python loops, faster storage or caching the dataset locally, mixed precision to raise compute throughput, and larger batches if memory allows. If utilization is high and it is still slow, the job is genuinely compute-bound: consider a bigger GPU, more GPUs with distributed training, or Trainium for cost. Check CPU too, since data preprocessing often runs there.

probes.q: GPU utilization is 30%. What is your first guess?
probes.a: The input pipeline: data loading or preprocessing on the CPU cannot keep up.

probes.q: How does storage affect training speed?
probes.a: Reading many small files from slow or remote storage stalls the loader; caching locally or using a high-throughput file system like Amazon FSx for Lustre helps.

probes.q: What does mixed precision buy you?
probes.a: Faster math on tensor cores and lower memory use, usually with no meaningful accuracy loss when done with loss scaling.

questions.aws: Amazon SageMaker AI training jobs expose GPU and CPU utilization in CloudWatch, and SageMaker Profiler helps spot data loader and kernel bottlenecks.
questions.resume: In USC Sports Analytics volunteer research, I cut DQN training time from 52 to 31 minutes, about 40%, by vectorizing replay-buffer sampling and removing a data-loader stall.
questions.trap: Buying a bigger GPU first. If the GPU is idle waiting for data, a bigger one just idles more expensively.

questions.q: How do you help a customer choose the right EC2 instance for a workload?
questions.plain: Choosing an instance is like choosing a vehicle. A delivery van, a race car, a moving truck, and a tow truck are all vehicles, but each is built for a job. I first ask what the workload carries: lots of thinking (CPU), lots of remembering (memory), lots of reading and writing (storage), or lots of math in parallel (GPU). Then I test on a couple of candidates rather than guessing.
questions.technical: Start from measurements of the current system: CPU, memory, disk IOPS and throughput, network, and whether it needs GPUs. Map to families: general purpose (M, T for burstable) for balanced apps; compute optimized (C) for CPU-heavy work like batch and encoding; memory optimized (R, X) for in-memory databases and caches; storage optimized (I, D) for local NVMe or high sequential throughput; accelerated (P, G, Inf, Trn) for ML and graphics. Then choose processor: Graviton (the g suffix) for price performance if the stack runs on arm64, Intel or AMD otherwise. Validate with a load test, right-size from real utilization, use Auto Scaling for variable demand, and pick purchase options: Savings Plans for steady use, Spot for fault-tolerant batch.

probes.q: What is a T instance and when is it a trap?
probes.a: A burstable instance that earns CPU credits while idle; it is a trap for steady high-CPU work, which drains credits and throttles or adds charges.

probes.q: What tool helps right-sizing?
probes.a: AWS Compute Optimizer recommends instance types from actual CloudWatch utilization.

probes.q: When is Spot appropriate?
probes.a: Stateless, fault-tolerant, or checkpointed work like batch jobs and some training runs, since AWS can reclaim Spot capacity with a two-minute notice.

questions.aws: Instance names encode the family, generation, processor, and size, for example m7g.large is general purpose, 7th generation, Graviton, large.
questions.trap: Lifting and shifting the on-premises server size. On-premises servers are often heavily over-provisioned; size from measured use and scale out instead.
